speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In too many cases, we actually know the victims.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We know their families and the pains they suffer.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We know too that this is a very difficult problem.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We want to take further action, but how?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: While the Bill is new, Members' concerns are not.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members of Parliament (MPs), including Mr Christopher de Souza, Mr Patrick Tay, and Minister of State Rahayu Mahzam, then a first-term MP, asked if victims would be given sufficient assistance when they approached the courts for help.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In 2021, deep in the trenches of COVID-19, my Ministry set up the Sunlight Alliance for Action.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It was a serious attempt to address online harms, especially those targeted at women and girls.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members like Senior Minister of State Sim Ann and Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim were actively involved.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Sunlight shone a spotlight on the prevalence of online harms and their severe impact on victims.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Arising from this effort, a new organisation, SG Her Empowerment (SHE) was born.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These include serious emotional, mental or physical consequences like depression or self-harm.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In 2022, Members debated the white paper on Singapore Women's Development.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Government made a clear commitment to tackle online harms.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Many victims are women and girls, but men and boys have also suffered in silence.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members may also access these materials through the SG Parl MP mobile app.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We can see that many victims add up to some very disturbing numbers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This included content supporting illegal activities, sexual content and violent content.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Many of these harms occur on platforms where people go for entertainment, such as Facebook, YouTube and Instagram.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In addition to POHA, the Government has made several moves to enhance online safety.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In 2022, we amended the Broadcasting Act to require social media services to disable access to egregious content, including content advocating suicide or self-harm.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In 2023, we introduced the Code of Practice for Online Safety.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Designated social media services were required to put in place systems and processes to enhance online safety, especially for children and youths.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These laws have helped in some measure to stem the tide of online harms.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, they were not a panacea, nor could they be.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The impact of technology evolves and is often understood only with time.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have therefore made it a point to review our laws regularly.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Most recently, in January 2024, Parliament debated a Motion on Building an Inclusive and Safe Digital Society.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Motion and other Parliamentary Questions filed by MPs have contributed many useful ideas.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They include calls by Mr Darryl David for victim-centric remediation; Ms Mariam Jaafar and Dr Wan Rizal for better platform accountability; Ms Tin Pei Ling, for more timely responses and respectful behaviours online; Ms Nadia Samdin, to lift the veil of online anonymity; Ms Hany Soh to address the use of deepfakes for extortion; Mr Yip Hon Weng, to firmly combat cyberbullying; and Mr Abdul Muhaimin, to deter hate speech.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They align closely with multiple studies conducted over the years by the Government, academics and non-government organisations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The first important finding is that victims often want quick takedowns of online harms.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Many valid reports are not even acted on.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The second important finding is that victims are daunted by the existing channels for seeking remedies and in particular, they find court processes complex and expensive.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The third important finding is that victims face difficulties seeking restitution.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is because they are often unable to confirm who was responsible for the harm.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They continue to be in fear and cannot find closure.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: OSRA aims to do this in three ways.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: First, OSRA will establish the Office of the Commissioner of Online Safety.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: An agency, the Online Safety Commission (OSC), will be set up to support the Office of the Commissioner.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: OSC will be empowered to issue directions to communicators of harmful content, administrators of groups or pages and platforms.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These directions require the recipients to act quickly on the harmful content.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: OSC will start by tackling online harms that are most prevalent and Singaporeans consider the most severe.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Minister of State Rahayu will elaborate on how OSC is intended to operate.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It provides a legal basis for the victim to take action.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Most importantly, it will allow victims to initiate legal proceedings against those responsible for causing or continuing the harm.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The proposed statutory torts will clarify the duties that users, administrators of groups and platforms owe to each other.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It will significantly reduce ambiguity about what online behaviours are considered harmful and unlawful.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Third, OSRA provides victims with the means to identify the person who caused the harm.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Not all victims want this, but for those who do, OSRA plugs a gap.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: While we have few counterparts to learn from, this does not deter us.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In setting up the OSC, we considered various models, such as mediation and dispute resolution.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Victims are at the very heart of the OSC's mission.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But the OSC's operational model and its oversight process are designed to be reasonable and fair to all.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is balanced against the need to act expeditiously and reduce the possibility of victim re-traumatisation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We also need to minimise long-drawn investigations and appeal cases.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In designing our set-up for the Office of the Commissioner of Online Safety, we drew lessons from Australia's eSafety Commissioner.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We learnt much from their generous sharing of experience to build a model that works for Singapore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, eSafety started small, focusing only on image-based child abuse material and cyberbullying of a child or young person under 18.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To put OSC on a firm footing, we will, similarly, also start off by tackling the most severe and prevalent harms.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Minister of State Rahayu will share more on the phased implementation approach.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: While we learnt important lessons from Australia's eSafety, I should point out, there are differences.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, the Commissioner of Online Safety in Singapore will be empowered to deal with a wider set of harms.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Commissioner can issue directions other than what is colloquially known as a "takedown".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For instance, it can issue a Right-of-Reply Direction that will allow the offending content to be seen alongside the victim's reply.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Commissioner can also seek the platform's cooperation to obtain identity information of perpetrators.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This victim-centric approach is the cornerstone of the OSC.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: After all, what Singaporeans have said they want most is a simple and effective way to protect themselves from online harms.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Importantly, it sends a signal that harms to victims inevitably become harms to society.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Our collective well-being is compromised when those who are harmed are denied restitution.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: With online harms becoming more prevalent, our barometer for acceptable online behaviour has been steadily eroded.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But just as we would not tolerate harmful behaviours in the physical world, we also cannot allow bad behaviours to become normalised online.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Through OSRA, we hope to avoid such an eventuality.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In its place, we want to lay the foundations for our citizens' online interactions by fostering trust in online spaces, Singaporeans can participate safely and confidently in our digital society.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We continue to welcome Members' views on how we can further improve online safety for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: (In Mandarin):   Harmful content online has seriously affected our online environment and goes against our social values.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When harmful content is encountered, the OSC can also issue directions requiring perpetrators or platforms to swiftly remove relevant content and stop its dissemination.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is precisely the outcome that most victims wish for.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Although perpetrators often hide their identities, we are discussing with various platforms how to ensure that perpetrators cannot hide forever.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Overall, the purpose of the Bill is not only to provide timely assistance to victims, but also to help them seek justice.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We also hope the Bill can serve as a deterrent, set new norms for online behaviour and create a safer, more positive online space. : Sir, our journey towards building a safer online world does not stop with OSRA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We are especially concerned about younger persons and plan to do more to ensure the usage of online services is age-appropriate.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We know anecdotally and from studies that youths can easily bypass age restrictions online.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They use false birthdays, spam email accounts or borrowed credentials for verification.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When one person figures out how to do so, they teach their friends, too.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Such behaviours can cause more youths to be exposed to inappropriate content or persons.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Hopefully, young users do not download age-inappropriate apps in the first place, but we know this is not enough.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This means extending age assurance requirements to social media services which attract many young users.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will explore better protections on other platforms, such as online games, where children and youths spend much of their time.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In addition, we will look beyond content to address unwanted interactions and excessive time spent on apps.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will review the additional measures needed to better protect younger users online.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As and when new technology arises, we will study them and update our safeguards, where required.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In the debate to follow, I suggest Members keep in mind three points.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: One, OSRA introduces many new features in our online safety ecosystem.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Nevertheless, there is much work ahead to ensure that these features can be effectively implemented.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Two, OSRA is designed to help victims in areas and ways that matter most to them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This was how we determined the types of harms, range of directions and thresholds of harms.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have also introduced safeguards to prevent overreach of the Commissioner and OSRA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Three, these considerations should, therefore, inform further proposals and suggestions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We should be careful not to distract the Commissioner and the OSC, or impose more conditions which will impede victims from getting timely, effective and accessible relief.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: With that, Mr Speaker, I look forward to the debate on this Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Part 1 consists of standard provisions, such as the purpose and interpretation sections.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Part 2 establishes the Office of the Commissioner of Online Safety, or the Commissioner.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Part 3 defines the categories of harm that will fall under the scope of the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Part 4 governs the statutory reporting mechanism; and Part 5, the types of directions that may be issued by the Commissioner.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Part 6 covers the investigative powers of the Commissioner.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Part 7 governs the oversight mechanisms that the Commissioner will be subject to.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Part 9 consists of provisions relating to service of documents and powers to make regulations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Parts 10 to 13 establish the statutory torts and the damages that may be sought under the torts, which Minister Edwin Tong will speak on later.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Part 14 deals with jurisdictional, procedural and miscellaneous matters, and Part 15 covers amendments made to other Acts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In my speech, I will be focusing on Parts 2 to 8 of the Bill, and will explain how the Bill will help to define what behaviours are unacceptable in the online world.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: These definitions were developed in consultation with the public, platforms and were guided by a Steering Committee.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Steering Committee was chaired by then-Minister for Law and Home Affairs, Mr K Shanmugam, and made up of Government agencies and experienced industry members.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Second, doxxing, which will cover the publication of a person's identity information that a reasonable person would conclude is likely to have been intended to cause harassment, alarm, distress and humiliation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Third, online stalking, which will be defined as engaging in a course of online conduct that involves online acts or omissions associated with stalking, and that a reasonable person would conclude is likely to cause harassment, alarm, distress or humiliation to the other person.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This is defined as the communication of online material that contains an intimate image or recording of a person, without their consent, that a reasonable person would conclude is likely to cause that person harassment, alarm, distress or humiliation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This includes images or recordings that may have been altered or generated by artificial intelligence (AI) or any other means.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: An offer to sell or distribute, and advertisements of an intimate image or recording, are also included.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Like intimate image abuse, this will include images or recordings that may have been altered or generated by AI or other means and will cover depictions of both physical and sexual child abuse.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: With the rapid development in AI technology and the advent of more powerful and easily accessible generative AI models, we have seen more deepfakes being used to cause harm to others.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This harm is defined as the communication of inauthentic material that a reasonable person would conclude is likely to cause harassment, alarm, distress or humiliation because it is false or misleading.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The material is regarded to be inauthentic where it is an image, video or soundbite that has been manipulated or generated through digital means to create a false or misleading depiction of the victim's words, actions or conduct, and is realistic enough such that a reasonable person would believe that the victim did say such words or engaged in such actions or conduct.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This category includes not only expressed depictions but also implied depictions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Seventh, online impersonation, which is defined as online activity where one person pretends to be another without their consent and would lead a reasonable person to believe that the activity is conducted by the second person.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: However, parody, satire or commentary which no reasonable person would believe is made by the victim, is not online impersonation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This category of harm will not be applicable to statements that tend to rally or call the public to undertake core political activities, such as calling for others to vote for a candidate in a Presidential or Parliamentary election.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The ninth category is the non-consensual disclosure of private information.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This harm is defined as the publication of any private information of a person without consent, and that a reasonable person would conclude was likely to cause that person harassment, alarm, distress or humiliation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The types of information that would be deemed as private would be context specific, and would depend on whether the information is already in the public domain.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Whether the individual is of the view that the information is sensitive may also be taken into account by the Commissioner.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Minister for Digital Development and Information will also be able to prescribe certain types of information as "private information".

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The 10th and 11th categories are the incitement of enmity and the incitement of violence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Enmity refers to feelings of enmity, hatred or hostility against any group.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Violence refers to unlawful force or unlawful violence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: These harms are what we term "group harms", as they aim to tackle harmful online content that is likely to harm groups in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: A group will be defined as a group of persons of any description and may include, for example, a group distinguished by race or religion.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Lastly, the 12th and 13th categories are the publication of false material and the publication of statements harmful to reputation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The former will cover statements about a person that are false and that a reasonable person would conclude are likely to cause harm.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The latter will cover statements that a reasonable person would conclude are likely to harm the reputation of the victim and likely to cause any other additional harm to the victim.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This is made possible because the online harm is identified through a single, discrete post, like the 13 categories of harms I described earlier.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In contrast, sexual grooming often occurs over the course of communication or exposure to various pieces of content, where each individual piece of content may not be harmful in and of itself.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Thirdly, OSRA is designed in way that relies on user reports.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Recourse can only be provided in cases where the victim recognises that they are victims.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Unfortunately, it is often the case that victims of sexual grooming or consumers of self-harm and/or suicide content, are not aware that they are victims.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: However, in such cases where these victims do come to the Commissioner for assistance, the Commissioner will work with the relevant agencies, including the Police, to provide the necessary assistance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Members might observe that not all of these 13 categories are new and some of them are already being addressed by existing law.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For example, online harassment is already being covered by POHA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Penal Code as well as the Criminal Law (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill, which was debated in Parliament earlier, both address intimate image abuse.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Such content might also be covered as egregious content under the Broadcasting Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The suggested additions to the categories of harm would also be covered by the Penal Code and the Broadcasting Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The group harms have also already been addressed by the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act and the Maintenance of Racial Harmony Act, for groups distinguished by religion or race.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The common law action of defamation, as supplemented by the Defamation Act, provides individuals with an avenue of recourse for defamatory statements or statements which harm a person's reputation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Some laws address harms that affect the public interest, such as the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act, the Maintenance of Racial Harmony Act and the Broadcasting Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Others provide individual remedies through legal action in Courts, such as POHA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The same SHE report also found that most respondents preferred the swift and permanent removal of content over taking legal action.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We acknowledge that the Internet evolves rapidly and the online harms ecosystem may change drastically over short periods, with new harms emerging or with bad actors finding new ways to cause harm.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Thus, OSRA has been designed in a way to allow us to adapt to changes in the online harms ecosystem.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Minister for Digital Development and Information will be able to prescribe additional types of online harms.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This power will be vital in ensuring that we address emerging harms as soon as possible.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We will ensure that this power is used judiciously and for harms that are particularly egregious to individuals, to prevent the unchecked expansion of the scope of OSRA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Part 2 of the Bill establishes the Office of the Commissioner of Online Safety.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It will be responsible for administering the statutory reporting mechanism to provide timely relief for victims of online harms.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Commissioner of Online Safety will be appointed by the Minister for Digital Development and Information and will be supported by Deputy Commissioners and Assistant Commissioners.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: While the Minister may provide broad guidance to the Commissioner, the Commissioner will be the final decision-maker for all cases.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We will also establish a new agency, called the OSC, that will support the Office of the Commissioner for Online Safety.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The OSC will be administratively supported by the IMDA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We have also considered the importance of transparency.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Members may also access these materials through the MP@SGPARL mobile app.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Members may refer to Handout 2 for an overview of the user journey with the OSC.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: First, prior to submitting a report to the OSC, victims will, generally, be required to report the online harm to the platforms.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: While we are setting up the OSC to provide timely relief to victims of specified online harms, platforms remain the first port of call.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Platforms must continue to play an active role and take responsibility for the safety of their users online.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This step will also not be required for doxxing.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Victims of these harms can submit a report directly to the OSC.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Our view has always been that platforms should take responsibility for keeping their users safe online.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This is evident from the approach we have taken under the Broadcasting Act.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For example, under the Code of Practice for Online Safety – Social Media Services, designated social media services (DSMSs) with significant reach or impact in Singapore are already required to submit annual reports to be published on IMDA's website.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: These reports contain information on the DSMSs' measures to combat harmful and inappropriate content, and metrics, such as the number of reports received from users, as well as the response times to act on these reports.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We intend for this to cover foreigners who are residing in Singapore for the long-term at the onset.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Where victims are under the age of 18, the parent or guardian of the victim may also submit a report on their behalf.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For example, earlier in November 2024, we saw deepfake nude photos of students at the Singapore Sports School being created and circulated by the student-athletes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In such a case, both the student victims and the parents of the victims depicted in the deepfakes would be able to submit a report to the OSC.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We have also considered situations where a victim strongly prefers that the report be filed for them.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In such situations, victims will be able to authorise other persons to file reports on their behalf.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For example, a hospital, if authorised, may file a report on behalf of a healthcare worker who is a victim of a specified online harm.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In the spirit of the reporting mechanism, OSC will only assess reports submitted.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: OSC will not actively monitor and identify cases of online harms.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Reports will be submitted through the OSC's website, which will be designed with the user in mind.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We are consulting other agencies and third-party organisations, such as SHE, in designing the website and the reporting form, to take into account user-centric language.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Accounting for victims' needs early is important, as survivors of online harms may, sometimes, avoid seeking external support to avoid re-traumatisation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The OSC's website will also provide victims and other persons with access to resources on online harms and advice on how to keep themselves safe online.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This will include, for example, information on the different types of online harms and what to do when you have experienced them.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The OSC is also exploring partnerships with third-party organisations which victims may be referred to for support, such as counselling services or further resources.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The details of this are still being worked out and we will provide more details in due course.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Each report will be assessed on its own merits and the OSC will be able to act on the face of the report submitted.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This is to ensure that the OSC can move fast to address the online harm.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Where necessary, such as where the information provided in the report is unclear, the Commissioner will be empowered, under Part 6, to conduct investigations, to better identify the relevant facts of each case.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The OSC will also develop internal practices and ensure that case officers are trained to handle each case sensitively.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The Commissioner will be empowered to issue directions to stop online harms from continuing to occur or to prevent further online harms from affecting the victim where there is reason to suspect that the online harm was conducted in respect of the victim or the victim group, as the case may be.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The threshold for the issuance of directions is modelled after the threshold set for the Police to take protective action in the Criminal Procedure Code and the Online Criminal Harms Act (OCHA).

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We will be putting in place oversight mechanisms to ensure that OSC directions are only issued where appropriate.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I will speak more on the oversight mechanism later.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The OSC may issue directions to three different parties: the communicator of the online harm, the administrator of a group or location where the online harm occurred, and the platform on which the online harm occurred.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Broadly, communicators and administrators may be issued directions that require them to remove specified material or disable a specified location, to restrain them from posting certain types of content or carrying out certain types of conduct or to require them to put up a victim's reply.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Administrators may also be issued other directions, such as directions that require them to put up a label to warn visitors that the online location has been subject to previous OSC directions or to restrict access by a Singapore account to the online location managed by them.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Platforms may be issued directions that require them to prevent end-users in Singapore from accessing specified content or online locations, to restrict interactions between an account and end-users in Singapore, to ban a Singapore account or to post a victim’s reply on its service.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As I mentioned earlier, two of the categories of harm – publication of false material and publication of statements harmful to reputation – differ slightly in terms of remedies that victims may receive.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Generally, victims of these harms will only be able to seek a Right-of-Reply Direction to allow them to have their side of the story heard.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We will be introducing new types of directions requiring recipients to act on content that can be distinguished by unique identifiers, such as usernames, keywords or hashtags.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The OSC may also issue what we consider as Enhanced Directions to certain prescribed online services.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: These Enhanced Directions impose additional requirements on the prescribed online service and may require the recipient to act on identical online harmful material, to take further steps to prevent online harm from occurring in the future or to reduce engagement of its users with a class of material.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Members may refer to Handout 3 for the full list of directions that the OSC may issue, and Handout 4 for illustrations of online harmful activity and possible OSC directions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In deciding whether to issue a direction and the type of direction to be issued for a case, the OSC may consider a basket of factors, including: the degree of the harm caused or likely to be caused; the number of persons harmed or likely to be harmed; the manner and circumstances in which the online harmful activity occurred; whether the conduct of the online harmful activity was reasonable, such as when a comment or post would be considered to be a "fair comment"; the likelihood of further online harmful activity being conducted; and whether the direction would be contrary to any public interest.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: These factors provide the OSC with much needed flexibility, to ensure that appropriate action is taken in every case.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The OSC will also publish guidelines detailing the factors that the OSC will consider in its decision-making process.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Such guidelines will also include illustrative examples of when the OSC will or will not act.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In cases where the OSC is made aware of non-compliance with its directions, the OSC may take further escalatory actions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: These actions include the issuance of orders following non-compliance, such as: access blocking orders, which may be issued to providers of Internet access services, to disable Singapore end-users' access to an online location; or app removal orders, which may be issued to providers of app distribution services, to remove the specified app from the Singapore app stores.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As these orders may affect all users in Singapore since they will no longer be able to access the apps or websites, they may only be used after careful consideration.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Part 8 of the Bill provides for offences and enforcement.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The directions and orders issued by the OSC are legally binding, and non-compliance with these directions and orders will be a criminal offence.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Where there has been non-compliance, the Commissioner will be empowered to conduct further investigations, such as requesting information or documents from individuals.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: These are the same Part 6 investigative powers that the Commissioner may exercise when assessing reports in the first instance.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In developing the penalties under the OSRA Bill, we have referenced other existing legislation, such as the Broadcasting Act, OCHA and the Penal Code.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The provision of false information to the Commissioner or the OSC will also be an offence.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Individuals found guilty of this offence will be subject to a fine of up to $20,000, or imprisonment for a period not exceeding 12 months, or both.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Entities will be subject to a fine of up to $50,000.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In some cases, it may be more appropriate to focus on rehabilitating the perpetrator rather than prosecuting them for non-compliance with an OSC direction.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: To that end, the Commissioner may put in place an online harms remedial initiative.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This initiative could include the completion of volunteer programmes by the perpetrator, which may be taken into account when considering prosecution for non-compliance with the OSC’s directions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As I mentioned earlier, we will be putting in place oversight mechanisms, which will be governed by Part 7 of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: These mechanisms ensure that the OSC will be able to move quickly and with confidence on the face of the information it has received.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Eligible persons may first apply to the Commissioner to reconsider the OSC’s decision.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For the reconsideration process, the OSC will re-assess the relevant case afresh, and may also take into account any new information that may be presented by the relevant parties after the initial assessment was conducted.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Applicants will be able to submit such new information to the OSC.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: When a decision has been made, the OSC will inform the applicant and other affected parties of their reconsidered decision.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The OSC may affirm, revoke, vary or substitute any earlier decision, direction or order issued.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Where the victim, recipient or prescribed person is dissatisfied with the OSC’s reconsidered decision, they may submit an application to the appeal panel to appeal against the OSC’s reconsidered decision.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Similar to the reconsideration process, the appeal panel will be able to affirm, revoke, vary or substitute decisions of the OSC in relation to the issuance or non-issuance of a direction.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The appeal panel will also be able to hear appeals on the issuance of an order following non-compliance.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Each individual will be given one chance to have their case heard by the independent appeal panel.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Should the individual continue to be dissatisfied with the outcome of the appeal, they may seek judicial review.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The establishment of a new office and the statutory reporting mechanism is a monumental task, one that will require close collaboration across Government.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We have to do the OSC right, so that we can do right by the victims.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This is why we will be implementing the reporting mechanism in phases.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The rest of the harms will follow progressively.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: These five harms are prioritised for a reason.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: They represent the most prevalent and serious harms faced by Singapore users online.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: These are also the online harms that Singaporeans are the most concerned about.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For example, The Institute of Policy Studies’ 2025 Online Safety Study showed that targeted harassment was seen by Singaporeans as “highly harmful”.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Members may refer to Handouts 1 and 5, for a broader overview of recent survey results and studies relating to online harms.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This will allow us to better manage the OSC's caseload and to properly develop the necessary guidelines, frameworks and capabilities to ensure that the OSC's decisions are consistent and appropriate in all cases.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Over the years, we have taken steps to educate and better empower our citizens to act against online dangers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For example, in 2021, we established the Sunlight Alliance for Action (AfA) to tackle online harms.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In the span of one year, AfA organised campaigns to raise public awareness about online harms and their impact.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: These campaigns also equipped youths to provide better support to their peers who were affected by online harms.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As co-chair of this AfA, I was informed by our partners about the experiences that many victims went through.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This is what drives me, to this day, to build a safer digital space.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The Sunlight AfA also inspired many of its members to continue their noble efforts to help victims.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: One example is the establishment of SHECARES@SCWO, a collaboration between SHE and the Singapore Council of Women's Organisations (SCWO).

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It is Singapore's first one-stop support centre for victims of online harms.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Efforts to enhance online safety require the involvement of every level of society, and the Government is ready to step forward to strengthen these efforts.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: With the establishment of the OSC, we will be able to provide timely follow-up actions for victims, help stop harms as quickly as possible and build a more robust support ecosystem for victims. : Mr Speaker, the OSRA and the OSC are just the one of the many steps that we are taking to enhance online safety.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I am heartened to note that online safety is a matter that both sides of this House are passionate about and I invite all Members of this House and the public to continue our conversations on how we can better enhance online safety.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The victims of online harms are not just statistics.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They may be our children, classmates, colleagues or neighbours.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Their confidence, studies and indeed their livelihoods can be shaken and seriously affected.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For one Primary 4 student, cyber-bullying reared its ugly head when she started using Instagram.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: She based her self-esteem on how many "likes" and "followers" she had.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: She would ask her friends to "like" her photos or "follow" her account to appear popular, and if a photo did not receive over 100 "likes", she would delete it.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: She was on medical leave from school for most of the year.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But what is worse is that it is not an isolated case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Online harms affect not only individuals and their families, but also the confidence and the trust of our society as a whole.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As a result, victims exit from public life or they choose to stay offline.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And proper discourse in the community becomes weaker.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If this continues, we will have a divided society, and a weakening of our social fabric and collective trust.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: About 98% of Singaporeans feel safe walking out alone, even at night.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In the offline world, we are mindful of how we behave towards one another.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We know not to threaten, harass or insult other people.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And in our everyday interactions, there are social norms that we know to abide by.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In public spaces, schools and also in work spaces.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Such norms allow us to function and thrive as a society.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But when it comes to the online world, these norms are not quite observed in the same way.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The sense of safety we have offline does not translate into the online space.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And in the course of our study, three issues stood out: first, fragmented standards and weak accountability in the online harms regulation space; second, economic incentives that unfortunately reward sensational content; and third, online anonymity that emboldens misbehaviour.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These three issues have very much shaped the thinking behind the construct and the framework of this current Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Thus far, the development of the rules and norms of the Internet has been largely left to the tech companies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Left on their own, different platforms will apply different rules, largely shaped by their own interests.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And in the absence of any common set of enforceable norms, it is not easy to expect or enforce accountability.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Instead, these differing standards will continue to exist and operate in a manner which allows wrongdoers to exploit the gaps.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This lack of accountability is exacerbated by the structural features of the Internet.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There is a misalignment between tech companies' profit motive and the need and desire to enhance online safety.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At the Online Harms Symposium co-organised by the Ministry of Law (MinLaw) and the Singapore Management University (SMU) Yong Pung How School of Law in 2023, former Facebook employee turned whistle-blower, Ms Frances Haugen spoke about how tech companies do have solutions to address online harms, but implementing them will eat into their profits and hurt their bottom line.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Social media platforms profit from the amplification of sensational and inflammatory content.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Viral, harmful content draws engagement, higher engagements draw eyeballs so their removal will impact revenue.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have some basis to believe that online safety considerations might well yield to profit generation, if left unregulated.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Today, tech companies have community standards which ostensibly address online harms.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Members can see some examples of these standards which are set out in Handout 7.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, most platforms do not necessarily adhere to their own community standards.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And this, we believe, is far from ideal, as victims are reliant on platforms to stop online harms.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At present, there is no framework which can give redress to victims for harms that happen at the speed and the extent to which they happen online.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: While victims may try and seek relief in court, there is a limit to how fast court proceedings can be and may also be costly.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And we all know that in these types of cases, speed of redress is crucial.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And most victims of such harms do not want to have to seek relief in Court, through the Court process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is also clear that online users behave on the Internet differently from the offline world.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Perpetrators are emboldened to act with impunity especially when they can remain anonymous.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, they experience what we call the "Online Disinhibition Effect", a term coined by Prof John Suler.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Prof Suler explains that anonymous Internet users separate their online persona from their in-person identity and they do not feel responsible for their behaviour online.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, there is little that victims can do to hold anonymous users accountable, simply because they remain anonymous and perpetrators know that they are unlikely to get caught and do not fear consequences.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To address these issues, the Government has taken proactive steps.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Minister Josephine Teo outlined the reforms that protect users.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Minister of State Rahayu explained how the new OSC will provide timely relief to stop harm.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Victims might require additional recourse, for example, compensation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And to do that, they will also need to know who lies behind that anonymous social media handle.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Bill therefore seeks to introduce a framework to close those gaps.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It will introduce clear statutory duties for online actors, defining what responsible conduct and therefore, what the standard of duty that is expected of them, ought to be.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It provides civil remedies for breaches of those duties, giving victims the right to seek justice in Court and it creates an additional avenue of relief, complementing the quick administrative recourse that can be obtained through the OSC, so that victims can choose the path that best suits their needs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: During the Online Harms Symposium that I referred to a short while ago, Ms Haugen likened Internet and social media regulation to the evolution of road safety, something that happened several decades ago.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In the 1960s, US car manufacturers vigorously resisted safety reforms.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But informed legislators persisted with greater regulation, coupled with a push, a very determined push from concerned citizens as well as investors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Through legislative changes, safety was made a core design principle in the manufacturing of cars.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And it has been estimated that between 1960 and 2012, over 600,000 lives were saved in the United States (US) as a result of this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In a similar way, not exactly the same, but in a similar way, we hope that this Bill will make online safety a design principle of the online space upfront, and not just an afterthought.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At the outset, our focus and intent is to empower victims.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is a very victim-centric approach and today you look at the example of one victim who tries to speak to the platforms, you heard the statistics that Minister Josephine Teo cited earlier, it is very difficult, and they are pretty much powerless today.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At the Government level, we have the Broadcasting Act, we have the Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Act (POFMA), we have OCHA that empower the Government to act in a variety of ways.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: OSRA provisions will empower private persons to obtain relief, and Members might, therefore, be aware that clause 4 makes it clear that a public agency cannot commence a claim under the Statutory Torts Framework.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I will now explain the types of online harms covered by the statutory torts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This framework will cover the same categories of harms that the OSC will act on, the same categories that Minister of State Rahayu took you through earlier, with some exceptions and refinements for coherence.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Harassment, doxxing and stalking will continue to be dealt with under POHA for communicators, but the new statutory duties for these harms will extend to administrators and platforms under this Bill, since POHA does not cover them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The online harms omitted from the statutory torts, mainly, false material, statements harmful to reputation and non-consensual disclosure of private information – are already well-covered under the existing legal framework, laws on defamation as well as on privacy and confidentiality.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This alignment ensures coherence in our legislation – no overlapping and no double remedy.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In this Bill, the statutory torts will also not cover Incitement of Enmity.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We think it is unwise to encourage such matters – which can be potentially explosive, emotive and divisive – to be dealt with litigiously, in a courtroom and so it will be dealt with by the OSC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The statutory torts will be implemented in phases, as you heard Minister of State Rahayu sketch out the OSC’s implementation of harms framework earlier in coordination with the OSC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, Sir, the Bill assigns clear duties to the key actors in the online ecosystem, and they are the communicators, the administrators and the platforms.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Clauses 90 and 91 impose two duties on administrators.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This duty covers administrators that are complicit in the online harms, and Members might be aware of the infamous chatgroup "SG Nasi Lemak" previously.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This will cover the administrators of such a chatgroup.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, when notified of harm, they must act reasonably – more specifically, they must take reasonable care to assess if there is harm and if so, to take reasonable steps to address it.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I want to make clear to Members that the duty to take "reasonable steps" does not require the platform to do constant surveillance and monitoring.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Their liability arises only when an actor fails to act reasonably after receiving proper notice.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They are not liable if, through no fault of their own, they did not receive the notice sent by the victim.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In assessing reasonableness, the Court will consider the circumstances of the case, including the seriousness as well as the persistence of the harm.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But if the same account repeatedly causes harm in the same way, simply taking down each time the post is put up may no longer suffice.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In such cases, taking stronger action, such as suspending or disabling the offending account, may be the reasonable steps required under clauses 91 and 94 and that is what I meant when I said you assess the entire factual matrix and situation holistically.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: What is “reasonable” will therefore depend on the facts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Courts can take into account factors such as the nature of the conduct; the context in which it occurred; and the effect and impact on the victim.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, putting up a post or creating a website to whistle-blow on serious misconduct may well be "reasonable" if done for a legitimate purpose and in a proportionate manner, even if it might cause harassment, or might be considered as online instigation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There are also safeguards to address concerns that administrators and platforms may be inundated with frivolous notices or notices with insufficient information.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Bill provides that the particulars, which an online harm notice must contain are to be prescribed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We set it out clearly in a prescribed form so that the categories of information is known upfront and this ensures that only genuine, properly documented cases trigger the duty to act, and the administrators and platforms have enough information to take "reasonable steps".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ultimately, it is the Court that will look at the facts of each case, weigh the totality of the evidence and decide whether a claim is made out and if so, what remedy should follow and against which party.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These are all fact-sensitive judgments that reflect the diverse realities of online interaction.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Bill therefore avoids the use of fixed or rigid formulas, to allow the Court to develop the law incrementally, while at the same time, keeping the focus squarely on online safety and responsibility.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Bill recognises that platforms and administrators need not proactively scan for all harms.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They only have to act responsibly once notified.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Take together, these duties encourage vigilance without imposing impossible burdens.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They reflect a simple idea embodied in many legal principles, which is, if you control the space, then you must play your part in keeping it safe.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If a victim successfully establishes a claim, the victim must have access to effective and fair remedies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The intent is to ensure that victims are properly compensated and that wrongdoers are not allowed to benefit from their behaviour.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For some harms, therefore, the victim's earning capacity or livelihood may be affected and they should be compensated for loss of future earnings or loss of earning capacity, as the case may be or as may be appropriate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In other cases, such as where intimate images have been put online and for sale and perpetrators profit from this harm, then, in those cases, an account of profits may be ordered so that the wrongdoer does not get to retain the benefits of the harm caused.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The regulations in this Bill reduce victims' uncertainty as to what remedies they are entitled to.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But ultimately, it is for the Court to decide on the appropriate orders, based on the facts of each case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We think that enhanced damages should apply to those who are the root cause of the harm, such as recalcitrant communicators or administrators who create harmful websites or chatgroups.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This framework is intended to incentivise and drive reasonable compliance and, in some cases, as quickly as possible.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And the enhanced damages framework also compensates victims for any additional harm resulting from failure to comply.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And we hope to drive overall a strong enough messaging with a deterrent impact on the actors in the online space.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Therefore, enhanced damages may be awarded to compensate the victim for additional harm caused by the refusal to stop the online harm, penalise the communicator or the administrator for bad conduct, and the Court will consider the overall justice of the situation, when assessing whether to impose enhanced damages.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These injunctions operate independently of any direction from the OSC, giving victims complementary routes to relief.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The OSC seeks to act quickly and takes public interest into account in making its decisions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Court decides any claim for statutory tort relief based on the applicable legal principles and a framework for remedies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Taken together, Sir, we believe that we have fashioned a suite of remedies that strike the right balance: accountability for wrongdoers; fair recourse for victims; and flexibility for the courts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The statutory torts are designed to change and strengthen norms – to make self-responsibility a default in our online spaces.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I come back to the time when the first motor-safety laws were introduced in the 1960s.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There was an American publication, Automotive News, which lamented the passing of these laws with the headline, and I quote: "Tough safety law strips auto industry of freedom".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There was fear; there was resistance in the industry.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But with the passage of time, history has proved those laws right.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They made cars safer, saved countless lives, changed attitudes and mindset, and re-shaped how the industry designed every vehicle thereafter.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We hope that this Bill, with a clear framework, can also have the effect of setting the right tone for online behaviour, shape mindset and attitudes, of both users as well as service providers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They define what is acceptable and what is not.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They will guide conduct not only through monetary damages, but through shared expectations made explicit.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Overall, our intention is that as our online norms mature, we will rely less and less on reports and lawsuits, because, like road safety, the law will have done what it set out to do, not just punish harm, but nurture the habits that prevent harm in the first place.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: From time to time, anonymity can serve a good purpose – it allows users to speak freely, sometimes, obtain assistance and, on occasions, allows marginalised groups to speak up.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But at the same time, it must not shield wrongdoing.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And unfortunately, many online users abuse the power and privacy which online anonymity affords them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I had earlier covered how online anonymity is a driver of online harms and leads to the Online Disinhibition Effect.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Anonymity also exacerbates the impact of harm on victims.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, victims may become more distrustful of those around them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They wonder who it is posting on their social media sites.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They do not know if the perpetrator is, indeed, someone they might know.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, victims will not be able to obtain legal recourse from perpetrators.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: By definition, they cannot commence legal proceedings, or enforce Court judgments, against an unknown person.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There are existing mechanisms currently available in Court, such as pre-action discovery and non-party discovery.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: All of these are mechanisms which can be used to obtain information about the identity of wrongdoers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To start with, clause 49 empowers the OSC to obtain information and documents for the discharge of its functions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This includes identity information of an end-user which is in the possession of platforms.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is akin to how law enforcement agencies are empowered to obtain such information for investigative purposes, akin but not similar.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This can take the form of the user's name or perhaps, verified phone numbers or credit card information, which can then be used to make further inquiries with telcos or banks.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This obligation to collect information is carefully scoped to target those users who are suspected of carrying out online harms.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is following close consultations that we had with industry partners who expressed difficulty with a general obligation upfront for platforms to collect information of all their Singapore users.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At the initial stage, disclosure will be limited to the purpose of enabling victims to bring their claim.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We intend to eventually extend this for other purposes as well, such as allowing victims to safeguard themselves from the perpetrator, and to take proactive future measures.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The measures are aimed squarely at those who hide behind anonymity to cause online harm.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They are not meant to affect ordinary users who act responsibly.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In fact, for the vast majority and for most users, nothing will change.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Most platforms today already require some form of verified contact or payment information at the point of registration.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Additionally, when the OSC discloses a perpetrator's identity to a victim, there will be safeguards to ensure that the information is protected and not misused.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Any breach of those conditions will be a criminal offence.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, the misuse of the information may itself attract legal consequences.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, if the victim were to use the information obtained from the OSC to dox the perpetrator, that could, itself, be an offence under POHA or under an online harm under this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They balance and they protect both the victim's right to know as well as the perpetrator's right against misuse.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And the provisions have been drafted with that goal in mind.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Minister Josephine Teo spoke about how the OSC will be empowered to issue directions quickly to address harmful content, and Minister of State Rahayu explained the appeal mechanisms available.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Her amendments speak to the removal of finality of an Appeal Committee's decision, and second, to add a right to appeal to the General Division of the High Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, we felt that we could not support them in this Bill and let me explain why.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These mechanisms will make the process slower, with less finality to the proceedings.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It will make it more complex and ultimately, less accessible for victims.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Allowing repeated appeals would prolong litigation and each new appeal means fresh rounds of arguments, delay and also uncertainty in dealing with harmful content, as well as renewed anxiety for those already hurt, who quite likely will have to remain engaged throughout the appeal process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We expect that there will be likely higher case volume in OSRA cases, which also adds to the administrative load of the OSC.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If a case goes on appeal to the High Court, lawyers will probably be instructed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In such an instance, will there be equality in how this might play out?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: One can imagine – most platforms are very well resourced, and likewise, a number of administrators and content creators too.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: What happens when an individual victim might need to seek redress against one of these giants, with deep pockets, in Court and with lawyers?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: With the additional prospect of having to bear substantial costs in the litigation if one does not succeed?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Overall, we fear that this will dissuade victims from coming forward.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And over time, this will render the framework toothless, not because of the provisions, but because individual victims will find it more difficult to seek redress and might shy away.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This will make the framework less inclusive, and we hope not to see that.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In contrast, we believe that the current framework already strikes the right balance.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The OSC's process is deliberately designed to be straightforward, fast and simple and focused on stopping harm quickly and hopefully, not spending time arguing about it.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We think that Ms He's proposed amendments, though well-intentioned, would probably make that journey harder and not easier.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It protects victims, sets fair expectations for online actors and strengthens trust and accountability in our digital commons.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If we proceed steadily and work together – Government, industry and users – I believe we can keep our online spaces open, but also safe; vibrant, but also responsible.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And as technology evolves, new harms will emerge.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We must be bold and innovative to stay ahead but also compassionate in how we protect those who are most vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This Bill gives victims a clear and practical framework to seek relief when harm occurs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It also sends a clear, unambiguous signal – that everyone who shapes our digital spaces in Singapore must act responsibly.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Through OSC, the Statutory Torts Framework as well as the End-User Identification provisions, we are building a coherent system of protection and accountability.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Each prong complements the other: the OSC is a safety net, providing rapid relief to victims of online harms; the Statutory Torts Framework provides private remedies, and it also is the standard-setter, encouraging all actors to play their part; and the End-User Identification measures ensure that no one can cause harm from behind a mask.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We started looking at developing this Bill as far back as 2021, even as the amendments to the Broadcasting Act and OCHA were being worked on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We spent close to five years carefully examining the issues.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We conducted numerous surveys and studies into the issue of online harms in Singapore, the findings of which have been presented to this House earlier.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We also partnered with the SMU Yong Pung How School of Law to organise the Online Harms Symposium, where distinguished speakers and panellists, including experts on online safety from around the world, shared their insight on key issues and solutions for online harms.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In addition to the Public Consultation exercise, we also met and consulted extensively with over 100 different stakeholders over the years.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This includes local and foreign experts, foreign regulators, victims of online harms, social service agencies, lawyers and the Judiciary, the Ministry of Education (MOE) and other educational institutions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We recognise that the impact of online harms may be felt and experienced differently across different communities.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have heard from various segments of society, including the youths, disability and the community groups.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We discovered, through these extensive engagements, a shared belief that the online world should reflect the same values of respect, decency and fairness that we all know and often assume, and which guide us in the offline space.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Around the world, societies are grappling with similar challenges – in Europe, the United Kingdom (UK), Australia and the US.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We are moving in step with these global efforts, but shaping our own path, our own course, contextualised and nuanced to what Singapore needs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Public education must teach users to protect themselves, and every user must take ownership of their safety and behaviour online.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But if we can do this together – build sound laws, responsible platforms and a thoughtful public – we will strengthen not only our digital safety, but over time, our social fabric.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And in time, our online norms will not erode, but endure – grounded in respect, anchored in responsibility and guided by the same values that make Singapore strong.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In particular, let me acknowledge two members from the private sector: Ms Stefanie Yuen Thio, joint managing partner of TSMP Law Corporation, member of the Sunlight Alliance for Action and founder and chairperson of SHE; as well as Assoc Prof Eugene Tan from SMU.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Every story helps us to shape the contours of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We thank them for their suggestions over the years.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have members from SHE and SHECARES@SCWO – Natalie, Hemavalli, Lorraine, Saira and Si Han – who together with their teams, served as vital pillars of support for those experiencing online harms today.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We also have representatives from YouthTechSG – Ben, Zoe, Beatrice and Kok Thong – who, together with many others, shared the perspectives of young Singaporeans with us.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We are deeply grateful for their partnership and commitment to making our digital spaces safer for all and we record our thanks and gratitude for the time that they have taken and the experiences that they have so generously shared.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: With powerful AI, harm scales fast and it is not rare.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In particular, as many of our Ministers and political officeholders have mentioned, for our youth, online and offline are one continuous reality.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: So, harm in one space, whether it is deepfakes, doxxing, non-consensual intimate content, bleeds into the other.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
