text: Mental health declines, some turn to self-harm, drop out of school or lose jobs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Embarrassments follow, harassment piles on and cancel culture amplifies the pain.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Sometimes a mental prison is worse than a physical one and we cannot keep telling victims to wait another three more months for relief.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: That is why, for years, I have consistently called for legislation to curb this danger.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In the 2022 Penal Code debate, I urged for laws to prevent cancel culture from taking root.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In the 2018 debate on online falsehoods, I argued that democracies depend on facts, transparency and truth in public discourse, and warned that social media algorithms turn some of the most sensational content viral and some of these contents are false and harmful.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It closes the gap and strengthens trust – the foundation of a "we first" society.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It protects people, it does not police speech.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Expression is not a licence to harass, and freedom comes with responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: At the same time, I have a number of clarifying questions to the Ministers for this landmark Bill.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: One, implication of the amendments added on top of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Also, the amendments called for a process to appeal to the General Division of the High Courts.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And the amendments call for the inclusion of serious harms like abetment or encouragement of suicide and sexual grooming into this Bill.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But I believe these are already addressed in criminal law, including the Penal Code, sections 306 and 376E; and the Vulnerable Adults Act 2018.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: To me, these amendments seem to be a substantive change to the due process proposed by this Bill, with implications to the victims – more legal cost, delayed justice.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: As such, I would like to ask the Ministers to inform us of the implications of these additional amendments put before Parliament votes.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: My second point is that, no wrong doors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We already have laws on harmful online content – POHA, Broadcasting Act, POFMA, the Foreign Interference (Countermeasures) Act and OCHA.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: If someone is harmed online, how do they figure out which law to use?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Will OSRA overlap with these or fit in with them?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Do victims have to report to several agencies or will the agencies coordinate?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And if OSC and the Courts disagree about whether online harm has happened, what happens then?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Who has the final say and how is the conflict resolved?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: How will OSC work with community groups and appropriate services to support victims, especially youth, of online harms?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Can we consider offering psychological support along legal relief?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And how will OSC make sure that the staff are properly trained so that they can help without causing further harm?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Four, Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) and disclosures.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Platforms must also, at the same time, meet data protection duties.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Will regulations clarify how Disclosure Directions interact with PDPA obligations, including purpose limitation and legal‑obligation exceptions?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And will good‑faith compliance with valid directions be recognised so platforms can act quickly without fear of breaching confidentiality?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: How will OSC enforce its directions outside Singapore and will claims under the statutory torts actually help in such cases?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The Bill lets OSC tell platforms to collect certain user information, but a person can ignore the request, ditch old accounts and open new ones.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In such cases, how will the Bill still get the perpetrator's user information?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: My final point, six, preventing abuse and protecting identities.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: What guardrails will prevent the statutory torts being weaponised for "lawfare", by that I mean frivolous claims or claims without merits to harass or pressurise respondents?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: As the Bill empowers OSC to identify users and disclose that information to purported victims, what safeguards are there to prevent misuse of that disclosed data for reverse doxxing?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In closing, Speaker, Sir, this Bill makes our online space safer, especially for our youths.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It strengthens trust, delivers speed as part of justice and holds platforms and perpetrators to account.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: With these clarifications, I support this landmark Bill.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: From cyberbullying, rise in hate speech, to AI generated content, online exploitation, misinformation and gender-based violence, we are having to deal with a wide variety of harms which have the added threat of going viral.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Singapore has a virtually 100% Internet connectivity rate and consequently, everyone is at risk from online harms.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Research in Singapore appears to bear out this fear.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The same survey also reported that two in five victims reported experiencing at least one form of severe adverse impacts, including suicide ideation and physical and mental health issues.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To further add to this, a World Economic Forum article published at the start of this year noted that there is a broader trend where online platforms move away from centralised content moderations and instead, rely more on user contributions to address potentially misleading or harmful content.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This has led to various groups being concerned that this shift would worsen the situation for vulnerable groups and create a less safe digital environment.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As I mentioned during the Committee of Supply for the Ministry of Home Affairs, in my cut on safe AI this year, women and children are two groups that have been found to bear disproportionately the harms associated with such online activities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: With the subject garnering greater concern in recent years, the Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Bill is now before us.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Workers' Party (WP) agrees that tough measures are required to tackle these harms to allow victims to seek better redress and healing, and to ensure that platforms act responsibly.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Whatever the online harms, be they categorised by content, contact, conduct or contract, or by types of harm, such as aggressive sexual or extremist values, the thing that unifies them is that their effect on victims or witnesses are cross cutting.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: All these harms have effects which are threats to physical or mental health, threats to privacy in the forms of violations or further promote inequalities or discrimination.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, our position is that the Bill before us leaves certain areas of concern unaddressed.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is, thus, in the spirit of strengthening our online protection regime to better protect victims of such harms that we propose these three main areas of amendment.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: First, the Bill leaves out certain harms which result in severe impact on victims.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Second, we have concerns about the legal procedures enabling the Commissioner to be the final arbiter and that certain clauses of what constitutes an online harm need further refinement.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Third, that there should be reporting requirements from the Commission, which will enhance public understanding and education about the harms, our protection regime and ultimately, build confidence in what we are doing to tackle it.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I will focus my speech on the first set of amendments and how we can better ensure that our tackling of online harms puts victims and vulnerable persons front and centre of our efforts.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: My other WP colleagues will also cover the other sets of amendments.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In our amendments, we proposed a statutory addition of two sets of activities and a definition of online harm activities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: First, sexual exploitation of children or vulnerable adults, otherwise, known as sexual grooming, with wording proposed in a new subsection O to the definition of online harmful activities contained in clause 3 and expanded definitions of what this comprises in the new clause A.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Second, publication of online material, encouraging or promoting suicide or self-harm, with our proposed insertion of new subsection O to clause 3's definition of online harmful activities and expansions on this in the new clause B.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In a study published by the Institute of Policy Studies in October 2025, child sexual exploitation and promotion of dangerous behaviours were identified as top harms and perceived as online harms of greater security.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is concerning, as in September 2025, it was reported that teenagers on Instagram were still able to access content relating to suicide and self-harm, and that its teen account's function did not appear to be stopping sexual content being uploaded by children.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Instagram is not the only platform noted for the risks associated with the promotion of self-harm and suicide.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In Singapore, SHE's survey ranked sexual harassment as the top online harms encountered by survivors and witnesses, with female youths aged between 15 and 34, more concerned about sexual-based harms.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Even though the OCHA covers certain sexual offences and various Codes of Practice have been introduced over the years, these harms do not appear to benefit from the full suite of mechanisms in this Bill, which I believe are more responsive and effective in tackling online safety issues that are highly context dependent and time sensitive.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In particular, I refer to the Bill's ability to request to restrain or stop the communication of a class of material by an administrator or communicator.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Furthermore, perpetrators seeking to groom minors or vulnerable adults may share online content that encourages, promotes or provides instructions of sexual communication or sexual activity to minors or vulnerable adults.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As the European Union (EU) has pointed out, the risk is that when a child is exposed to or engages with inappropriate sexual content, they risk ending up at greater risk of related content, be it in the form of becoming targets of or perpetrators of sexual grooming of minors, because it has become normalised or desensitised for them.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These children may also then become targets for sexual exploitation or streaming of child sexual abuse material.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Thus, the harm posed by content posted to glorify suicide or self-harm and sexual grooming of minors and vulnerable adults is substantial.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Thus, we hope that Singapore takes a strong stance against such online content by accepting our proposed amendments and including them under the scope of this Bill to provide more tools to tackle these types of online harm.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is complex, as harassment, humiliation and abuse of victims comes in various shapes and forms.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Harassment, as we all know, is not limited to just physical stalking, sending thousands of text messages or making dodgy phone calls.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For example, our Family Courts are now also enroute to recognising that it is not just physical abuse that causes real and sometimes lifelong and life-threatening harms to victims.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Increasingly, they know that other forms of abuse can be just as harmful and online media can be one means through which they are propagated.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We already have laws on the books regarding self-harm, sexualised grooming of minors and protecting vulnerable adults.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But they do not explicitly extend to online behaviour.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our amendments seek to harmonise the laws and extend protections given emergent risks in the online space.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, we have to understand that the harm experienced by victims does not end after a report or complaint is filed.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It could also extend beyond when the perpetrator has been sentenced, long after the justice system has taken its course.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Many withdrew from social media entirely, as documented in one of the case studies from the Institute of Policy Studies survey.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A handful of respondents even contemplated harming themselves physically or attempted suicide.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Even more crucially, for each person who steps forward, how many decide against pursuing matters through the justice system because it is daunting, because they are fearful of it or decide they did not want to re-traumatise themselves by recounting and reliving what has happened to them many times as they go through the systems to seek redress.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Thus, we also have concerns about the access to justice for victims who are contemplating pursuing justice under the statutory tort provisions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Many would be young people, students, workers who already feel powerless.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For them, the idea of commencing a lawsuit is unimaginable.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: So, how do we tackle concerns that a fragmented system of relief may emerge that those who are resourced can fight and those without must simply tolerate and try to move on?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Will the legal processes be simplified for victims to obtain remedies that they deserve?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Directions or orders issued by the Commissioner should also be granted swiftly.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And since under the Bill, the Commissioner is to use quasi-judicial powers who will sit in judgment, and handling reports and complaints filed by victims or agencies, the Commission must be staffed and resourced like a quasi-judicial body, not a customer service centre.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Decisions to be made by the Commissioner are not mechanical run-of-the-mill decisions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: They require legal, psychological, societal and cultural sensitivity.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This means that our processes to address online harms and provide redress and justice for victims must incorporate a victim-centric and trauma-informed approach.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Staff from frontliners receiving reports from victims, to decision makers within the agency should be supported by professionals who understand how best to continue to support and protect victims.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Trying to take a stand against harassment, humiliation and abuse requires much from victims.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It will run contrary to the intent of this Bill if victims instead find themselves with no support or even met with disbelief when seeking justice.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The principle behind tackling these harms would be to ensure that there is restorative justice, especially for non-criminal harms, which we, as a society, have decided do not warrant criminalisation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As for perpetrators, we too should try to get to the bottom of their motivations and what causes such behaviour.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As the Association of Women for Action and Research (AWARE) has recommended, would counselling orders for perpetrators be one of the tools that could be given to the perpetrators so that, where appropriate, they will receive appropriate treatment to stop them from re-offending after their sentence has been meted out?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In this vein, I believe that, aside from providing psychological support for victims, the Commission should prioritise education as an inoculator against these harms.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For OSC officers, this should mean ensuring evidence-based, up-to-date victim-centric education and training for those handling reports or complaints to continually incorporate latest victim-centric approaches to provide victims the support they need.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Ground-up knowledge sharing is also important, given that so much of online behaviour is driven by social media culture that is global, fast changing and trend-driven.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must continue and step up cross agency and sectorial education efforts for both children and adults to increase awareness of online harms and the help available to them.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These efforts have to continue to be informed by updated research on the evolving nature of the harms, how they are propagated and take on board the latest online trends, which often move rapidly.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Apart from targeting the broad public who may be or were exposed to harmful online content, they should also be proactive in nature and target perpetrators or those at risk of offending.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Educational efforts should also be sensitive to and address research findings that those exposed to online harmful content seem to display a higher probability of becoming offenders themselves and then be designed to target those who may be causing both criminal and non-criminal harms.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Now, I will turn to the other categories of amendments.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While we take a strong stance against online harm, we must balance it against the risk that overreach will strip away the normalcy of our online usage.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Commissioner can still issue directions or orders when it has reasonable grounds to believe that online harmful activity was conducted.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This will allow both online entities and individual users transparency.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: My colleague, Non-Constituency Member of Parliament (NCMP), Mr Andre Low, will elaborate more on these points.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These include the number of reports received by the Commissioner, the categories of these reports, the number of directions and orders issued by the Commission, the categories of persons or entities who have been issued with a direction or order, and findings by the Commissioner on the risk assessment and trends of online harm.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These proposed amendments are driven by the need to ensure that our laws are better understood and remain ahead of the rapidly evolving landscape of online harms.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: They also provide that groups disproportionately affected by online harms – women, children and vulnerable adults – would also have their interests represented.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: NCMP Eileen Chong will speak more on these amendments.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: With this Bill, we believe that there is an opportunity to act more effectively against material on suicide, self-injury and sexual grooming of minors and vulnerable adults.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We have the chance to legislate more clearly to ensure that victims can efficiently, effectively and safely get recourse for online harms.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We should also work to make online harms less likely to happen in the first place through education, research and by ensuring platforms are aware of their role in facing up to this challenge, all the while ensuring the justice system works effectively and as intended.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I believe that all of us in this House, as Parliamentarians, as Singaporeans and as human beings, wish online harms were less common and less hurtful than they are.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: That said, we cannot uninvent the Internet and we are at a point in time where the digital world has made it so easy for people to harm each another without having to directly experience the hurt they have caused others.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Some may recall an even earlier time, where snail mail is just known as mail.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But for today's generation, our children, students and younger workers, they have grown up knowing only a world that is integrated with online.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: For most of us, the digital space has become inseparable from daily life.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It is where we learn, we create networks, we work, and forms part of our identity.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: While the digital realm has brought immense good in connecting us, empowering creativity and expanding opportunity, it has also become a space where real harm can occur.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Over the years, we have seen painful examples right here in Singapore that remind us that what happens online can wound deeply offline.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In one tragic case, a teenage student took her own life after enduring prolonged cyberbullying from classmates on social media.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Hurtful messages and ridicule in the digital space compounded the pressures she faced in the real world.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: There was also the incident of a National Serviceman sentenced to jail after uploading his ex-girlfriend's private images onto a website, tagging her name and social media handle.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The images spread within hours and, despite takedown efforts, the victim continued to face humiliation long after.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: There are many more examples of online harms and these are not isolated incidents.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: They show that online harms are not just virtual.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: They are real, they are lasting and they are deeply personal.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: From the early days of Singapore's digital journey, we have always been mindful of the risks that come with greater connectivity and many have played their part in building a safer online space.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: At the ground level, numerous organisations have been promoting digital well-being and online safety education and many of my fellow People's Action Party (PAP) MPs have also done so in their constituencies.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In Pasir Ris East, we began our Digital Well-being and Safety lessons in 2020 and later expanded them through the M³ Goes Digital programme to reach more members of the minority community.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: A safe and responsible digital environment has long been a key advocacy point among PAP MPs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Globally, jurisdictions such as the UK’s Online Safety Act, the EU’s Digital Services Act, Australia’s Online Safety Act, Canada’s proposed Online Harms Act and New Zealand’s Harmful Digital Communications Act are grappling with the same question: how to protect users while preserving legitimate expression?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: To remain effective, our laws must first and foremost protect victims, provide quick and accessible recourse, for in the digital age, harm spreads faster than healing; and ensure that justice is fair, balanced and proportionate, shaping a safer and more respectable online space for all.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I therefore stand in support of this Bill, which takes a pragmatic and, as both Minister Teo and Minister Tong described as a "victim-centric approach," something which I agree.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It focuses on timely relief, clear accountability and shared responsibility across all stakeholders in the digital ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: That said, I would like to raise three areas for clarification: firstly, the definition and application of OSRA; secondly, how we can provide better support for victims of online harm; and thirdly, the possible unintended effects of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Minister Teo shared that the remaining eight will be followed progressively.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: While this provides a sound foundation, I seek clarification on how the threshold will be determined for online harassment?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Will it depend on the number of incidents, the severity of content, or the type of platform involved, something to which Minister of State Rahayu alluded to.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: How will the OSC determine what breached the online harassment threshold and how will we compare one versus the other?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I would also like to seek clarification about the timeline and criteria for introducing the remaining categories.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Also, if a victim experiences a form of harm covered only in a later phase, will the OSC have discretion to act on the case?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: For the law to be effective, the OSC's investigations and directives must be swift and timely.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Hence, may I ask, what is the expected case load under the first five categories?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: How do we ensure that this proactive reporting is not abused?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: How will OSC case workers assess the incidents?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Will they be doing it manually and how do we scale it up quickly?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The key point I am trying to make is, how do we adequately resource the OSC with the expertise, the manpower and the technology required to ensure that victims can get effective and timely relief?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We need to set the OSC up for success.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Lastly, the Bill empowers the OSC to issue directions to the communicator, administrator, or online service provider involved.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Can the Government clarify what qualifies as an "online service provider"?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Many Singaporeans are administrators of private chatgroups among friends, colleagues, classmates or even strangers such as in Build-To-Order chatgroups.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Some of the most hurtful cyberbullying can occur within such closed platforms.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: How will the Bill handle cases arising from private or semi-private groups, where the boundary between personal and public communication is slightly blurred?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Victims may take civil action through a statutory tort and claim enhanced damages in serious or malicious cases, a clear message that accountability applies equally online.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: However, the Bill does not address psychological and social support, especially for victims of cyberbullying, doxxing, or image-based abuse.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The emotional scars often outlast the digital content itself.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The OSC can also play a broader and more supportive role in caring for victims of online harm, acting as a one-stop point of contact that connects them to counselling services, community partners and social agencies that can provide the help they need.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In Handout 2, it is also noted that counselling support today is self-initiated by victims at the point when the harm is experienced.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But we know that, for many, this is often the most difficult time to reach out, when the victims may feel alone, frightened, or unsure of what to do next.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Can I suggest for the system to be a bit more proactive?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: So, when a victim files a report with the OSC, could there be an automatic prompt or offer for counselling support, so that help is not just available but actively extended?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This small change could make a big difference, ensuring that victims receive structured, compassionate and timely support at the moment they need it most.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The law must deliver justice but beyond that, it is must also help victims rebuild confidence and trust in our digital space.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: With such a framework, the OSC can be not just a regulator but a guardian of digital well-being for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Clearer legal rights may lead to more frequent or premature litigation, as victims, intermediaries, or even platforms resort to the courts as a first response rather than a last.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We must guard against creating a more litigious society, where disputes are too readily taken to court.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This would only make it harder for victims, many who are already distressed, who may hesitate to come forward because of the financial, emotional and psychological toll of litigation, and the pain of having to relive their trauma.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Some may also fear losing a civil case and being burdened with legal costs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This concern is even more acute when victims face large, well-resourced companies or global platforms.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Such entities could exploit the prohibitive cost of legal action to deter victims from pursuing justice.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: If every dispute were taken into lengthy court processes, many victims would refrain from seeking help altogether, something which Minister Tong has shared earlier too.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Justice must never depend on one’s capacity to afford it.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: That said, I urge the Government and the OSC to monitor the use of statutory torts closely, ensuring that they empower victims rather than intimidate them; promoting fairness, accountability and confidence in our online safety framework.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Mediation and conciliation should be encouraged as first-line remedies, and the OSC could monitor the civil actions to ensure the law remains fair and accessible to all.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Ultimately, this Bill must empower victims, not overwhelm them, making justice attainable, not intimidating; strengthening accountability without fostering a culture of fear or excessive litigation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Online spaces bring about many benefits for learning, working and networking, but it also comes with harms such as cyberbullying, sharing of private images without consent and doxxing, which can cause profound emotional impact.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: All this while, the Government and our people have worked to protect online users.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We already have POHA, OHCA and IMDA guidelines to ensure digital platforms behave more responsibly.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Many PAP MPs have also conducted programmes such as Digital Well-being and Safety, and at M3 Pasir Ris, we organised M3 Goes Digital to educate citizens about cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This new Bill complements those efforts and provides greater protection to victims.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: With that, I would like to seek three clarifications.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Our goal will be to build a safe and responsible digital space for all Singaporeans. : Mr Speaker, Singapore's online space must be a place of opportunity, not harm.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Bill represents another important step in our collective effort to make our Internet a safer and more trusted place for all.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This Bill builds on more than a decade of sustained progress and advocacy from the ground-up initiatives by community partners, PAP MPs who have championed digital well-being and online safety, to key legislative milestones, such as POHA and OCHA, and many others.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Together, these efforts reflect our continued commitment to protect Singaporeans from online harm while promoting a culture of digital responsibility.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The Bill before us today is not a standalone measure, but part of a long-term journey; one that combines education, legislation and compassion to safeguard every user, especially the most vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This, Mr Speaker, is the spirit of our digital future – a connected society that is also a caring one where freedom of expression is matched by responsibility and where justice online is real and reachable as justice offline.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I stand in support of this Bill and the shared goal it represents: to build a safe, responsible and inclusive digital Singapore for all.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Ms He Ting Ru has addressed the first question the Bill raises which is would it adequately protect the most vulnerable victims.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: She has outlined how we can strengthen that protection – I support these amendments.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I address the second question: will this Bill be fair, accountable and properly calibrated in its exercise of its powers?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Bill grants the Commissioner significant authority to issue directions, compel removal of content, impose obligations on service providers to reduce engagement with material without the creator's knowledge.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are necessary powers to address real harms, but there are also powers that should be carefully designed for their intended purpose and appropriately constrained by institutional checks and balances.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I will address three amendments that address our concerns about the Bill's architecture and six areas requiring Ministerial clarification.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First is raising the threshold for state action.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is the same standard used in comparable legislation overseas, including the UK's Online Safety Act and Canada's proposed Bill C63, or their Online Harms Act.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This requires evidence that would satisfy a reasonable person, not merely a suspicion.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the UK Act, they explicitly distinguish between "reasonable grounds to suspect" in order to begin an investigation as opposed to "reasonable grounds to believe" to take enforcement action.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We believe that this is the right approach.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The former permits inquiry, the latter permits coercion.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we are serious about protecting victims, we must be equally serious about ensuring the Commissioner's enforcement powers rest on evidence, not suspicion.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second set of amendments I will be addressing concern legitimate discourse.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Clauses 9, 11 and 19 define three online harms: online harassment, non-consensual disclosure of private information and instigation of disproportionate harm.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These definitions are necessary, but we think they are incomplete.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, a citizen posts fair criticism of a public official's conduct.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If a reasonable person were to conclude that that criticism is, "abusive or insulting", and it is likely to cause the official distress, under clause 9, this could be harassment.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the third scenario, a journalist publishes leaked documents exposing corruption in a government-linked entity, but under clause 11 this could also fall under the definition of non-consensual disclosure.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are no obvious exclusions for public interest and they do not go far enough in recognising that not all disclosures of private information are harmful and not all uncomfortable speech is harassment.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is drawn from the established common law defence to the tort of defamation.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For clause 11, we add that disclosure does not fall within the definition of if the public interest in disclosure outweighs the public interest in privacy.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We list seven examples – including exposing wrongdoing, informing the public on matters of significant concern and protecting public health and safety.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This amendment is modelled on a well-established balancing test in comparable common law jurisdictions, including the UK.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As drafted, it is also very similar to the test as codified in the Australian Privacy Act.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For clause 19, we add communication does not constitute instigation if it relates to a matter of public interest.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They ensure that the Commissioner's powers are used to protect victims, but not to chill legitimate speech.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They prevent this Bill from inadvertently silencing criticism, investigative journalism or public interest disclosures.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The third set of amendments that I will be addressing establishes independent oversight.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Clause 60 creates an appeal panel whose members are appointed by the Minister.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Clause 63 provides the right to appeal Commissioner decisions to an Appeal Committee drawn from this panel.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Crucially, clauses 63(5) and (6) state that no further appeals will be permitted beyond this Appeal Committee.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This makes a Ministerially-appointed committee the final arbiter.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is confined to three grounds, a point of law; secondly, that the harmful activity did not occur; and thirdly, that compliance is not technically feasible.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is similar to the appeal mechanism in POFMA.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This ensures that the Courts do not become a general review body for every single Commissioner's decision but remain available as an independent check on questions of legality, fact and feasibility.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When the state exercises coercive powers, especially a power that could affect livelihoods, reputations and businesses, there must be a route to independent judicial appeal of cases.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, some may say that our proposed amendments may introduce additional burdens on the Courts.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I also appreciate Minister of State Rahayu and Minister Tong's earlier clarifications as to the policy considerations at play here.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Minister of State Rahayu referred to the inherent right of judicial review, which is still available as there is no ouster clause within the Bill.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We appreciate that judicial review is always available, but the scope is generally limited, in this case, it will be generally limited to the process of the Commissioner making their decisions and not about the merits of the case itself.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The proposed amendment we have tabled is very limited in scope.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It proposes expanding this right of appeal to the Courts to three limited grounds.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We understand that a balance needs to be struck and we are striving to achieve that.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With reference to Minister Tong's suggestions that that there may be a David and Goliath situation if we avail of appeals to the Courts.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We believe that the existing provisions within the Bill, as drafted, notably section 63(4) which provides that there is no automatic stay on directions, even when an appeal process is proceeding, helps to ameliorate that concern.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There will be no continuing harm to victims as the appeals process is proceeding.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Furthermore, when we avail of the Courts, there are mechanisms that can address some of these concerns as well, such as in-camera private proceedings as well as gag orders to protect the identities of victims.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, I would like to address the scope of doxxing.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If a victim identifies their hitherto anonymous harasser online to warn others in the community, could a reasonable person conclude that this was intended to cause the harasser distress or alarm?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Bill does not answer this; so, I ask the Minister, will victims who expose their harassers in this manner be caught by clause 10?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If not, what safeguards exist in the Bill's design to prevent this?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Second, I would like to seek clarifications on standing to appeal where directions are given to platforms.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Clause 28 sets out who receives Part 5 directions.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When a direction is not issued to the communicator directly, can they still appeal?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The subsequent subsection says that they may appeal only if they fall within a description, the Minister may prescribe under clause 82.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, I ask the Minister, will the regulations be made to ensure that communicators have standing to appeal directions that restrict their content, even if those directions were not issued directly to them or will this remain subject to Ministerial discretion?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Third, the meaning of prescribed connection to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I understand Minister of State Rahayu has addressed this example.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: She has given the example of long-term residents in Singapore who will fall under the ambit of this provision.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, it is clear that Citizens, Permanent Residents (PRs) and long-term residents are eligible to make a report.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We would like to understand what else the ambit of prescribed connection in Singapore could mean.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does it cover a foreign spouse on a long-term visit pass harassed by someone in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Subsequently, does it also cover a former Singaporean resident who has now moved overseas, who is still being targeted by the Singapore-based individual?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, I ask the Minister who is protected by this Bill, who is excluded and whether the prescribed connection will be made clearer?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This means that if harmful content originates from, is hosted by or is facilitated by a public agency, the Commissioner cannot compel the agency to act.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Public agencies cannot be sued under the civil proceedings – provisions in Parts 10, 11 and 12.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, Mr Speaker, online harm is online harm, regardless of its source.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A citizen harassed through content on a Government platform or by a Government account experiences the same distress as one harassed on a private platform or by a private account.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, I ask the Minister, why are public agencies exempt from the Commissioner's enforcement powers and from civil liability?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What is the policy rationale for the asymmetry and what recourse does an individual have if they experience harassment, perhaps, from a rogue public employee using an official account?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Fifth, Engagement Reduction Directions and Class of Material Directions.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Clause 40 grants the Commissioner power to issue engagement Reduction Directions.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This allows the Commissioner to require a service provider to reduce the engagement of end users with a Class of Material Direction without removing it.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Clause 41(3) explicitly states that it is not necessary to give any person who may be subject to a Part 5 direction, an opportunity to be heard before the direction is given.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This means content posters are not necessarily informed, the content stays online.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It remains visible to the poster; it also remains visible to the victim.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: None will be aware that the contents' reach has been throttled.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The victim will continue to see the harm, wondering if the report achieved anything at all.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, my question to the Minister is simple: what is the envisaged use of this particular direction?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Surely, in cases of legitimate serious harms, one of the other more forceful directions is the better solution for victims, and if this is meant as a less forceful direction, why does the Commissioner see the need to intervene at all?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is a high risk that this will function as a digital dragnet that may capture legitimate content alongside harmful material.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Sixth, and finally, I address consistency in decision making.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Parts 10 to 12 of this Bill establish statutory torts that will be adjudicated by the Courts.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These will generate judicial precedence and publish decisions.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And secondly, will the Commissioner be bound by clarifications given today, in this House?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the Minister states that, for example, Clause 10's doxxing definition does not capture victims exposing their harassers, can future Commissioners be held to this clarification?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our amendments ensure that the powers are exercised on evidence with safeguards for legitimate speech and with independent judicial oversight, but oversight is meaningless if those affected cannot assess it.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, the Bill's ambiguities on doxxing, on standing to appeal, on coverage, on public agency exemptions, on shadow bans, on consistency in decision making, these are not minor.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They go to the heart of who is protected, who is excluded and whether the regime operates fairly.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope that in the course of this debate, that we can get clarity and comfort on these questions.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, I urge the Minister to accept our amendments.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the Minister declines, I ask for clear answers to the questions I have raised.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think Singaporeans deserve a regime that protects victims and respects fairness in equal measure.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: This is not just a Bill about digital platforms or statutory duties.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: It is about people, especially our young, our parents and those whose lives have been shaken by what is said or spread online.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: A harmful post, an exposed address, a doctored photo – once uploaded, it spreads in seconds.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: That is why the speed of takedown must match the speed of harm.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: In an earlier debate, I shared the story of a young lady, Ms K, living in Punggol who was doxxed by her best friend's ex.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: He had created an account, just for doxxing and had put up one post with her face, name, place of work and where she used to study.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: When she came looking to me for help, the post had been up for two weeks.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: But even with the help of her loved ones, friends and, indeed, the extended Punggol family reporting the doxxing, the post was still not taken down even after a month had passed.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: I reported this as well, but was told, two weeks after I reported, that the platform is experiencing high volumes of reports and that I should report on the post, and not the account.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: It finally took several interventions by Government agencies and a certain trusted reporter/flagger NGOs to get the post taken down.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: By then, the post was already seen by a few hundred people, Ms K was aghast, but relieved and thankful.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: That is, until a few weeks later, she contacted me again, to tell me that her friend's ex, had doxxed her again, this time on the same account and on another platform.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: If this House feels weary just hearing about this, imagine how defeated she felt.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Victims should not have to file multiple reports to multiple agencies.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: This should not be measured not in days, but in hours.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Online harm does not wait and neither should help.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Because someone under siege, an hour can feel like forever.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: In extreme cases, how do we guard against misuse of the system, and prevent it from becoming weaponised against the very same people it had set out to protect; (b) given that platforms themselves face high reporting volumes, how will OSC manage a potentially large caseload without compromising response speed; and (c) finally, while the first schedule covers harassment and doxxing, other categories, such as online impersonation and deepfake abuse, will only be implemented later.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Could the Minister share the timelines and what recourse victims have, if their harm type is not yet covered or even identified?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: They are amplifiers of information, of emotion and, sometimes, of harm.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: When harm is done through them, they must be part of the solution, not silent observers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: I hope that with this Bill, delays in response will no longer be acceptable.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Platforms must design systems that detect and throttle the spread of harmful content; provide real-time cooperation channels within OSC; and be transparent about how quickly and how often they act on Takedown Directions.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Families should not have to fight for accountability post by post.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Responsibility must also rest with those who profit from the platforms that host them.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Real safety depends not just on legislation, but on the strength of our community: one that notices, listens and steps forward when someone is in distress.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: In Punggol Shore, we started a community initiative several years ago – the Punggol Positivity Pizza Movement.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: It began with our youth leaders and families who wanted to create a visible, warm symbol of encouragement for our young residents.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: If you're going through a hard time, please reach out, because your community loves you." Through the Positivity Pizza movement, volunteers from every corner of Punggol Shore – seniors, youths, women's groups, sports teams and religious organisations – have come together to crochet pizza plushie keychains, with a heartfelt goal: to make 20,000 pizzas, one for every young person living in Punggol Shore.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Each slice carries a message of solidarity, "It's not okay to be not okay, reach out and your community has your back." The inspiration for this movement came from a young resident, C, whom I met at a local mall.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: I had known her since her primary school days and when I asked how she was coping with secondary school, she confided that she was struggling with online bullying and thoughts of self-harm.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: As we spoke, she noticed a small keychain plushie on my bag and she said softly and shyly to me, "Ms Yeo, that is very cute.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Know that you have started a movement that has touched thousands of lives.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Our Punggol Shore handcrafted pizza slices have become small but mighty ambassadors of empathy – connecting neighbours, bridging generations and providing that kindness, even if it is handmade and in real life, can still go viral.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: If cruelty can spread fast, then kindness must spread faster.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: When we see a friend being bullied or humiliated online, do not scroll past.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: When we teach our children to stay safe online, let us also teach them to be kind online.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: So that our parents, our seniors and our young persons alike, can learn not only to protect themselves, but also how to support one another.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Because real safety, Mr Speaker, does not come just from stronger laws.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: It must also come from stronger community bonds.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: (In Mandarin):   In the online world, a harmful post or a malicious photo can spread across the entire island within minutes.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: We must also care for and protect one another.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: At the same time, I want to call upon all major online platforms to work together with us.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Let us join hands to create a safe, caring and responsible online environment.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Our online world must reflect the same values that we keep our physical neighbourhoods safe and that is, respect, responsibility and care.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, I support the objectives of Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Bill.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This can provide more timely channels for victims of online harm to seek help, improve online safety, deter and prevent online harmful behaviour and promote rational and responsible online conduct.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can and should, ensure that victims receive more timely and comprehensive relief.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the same time, the WP believes this Bill can be further optimised and therefore proposes several amendments to the Bill.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We suggest expanding the definition of "harmful online content".

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This would enhance the scope of the Bill's jurisdiction.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Furthermore, we can also strengthen the fair and just implementation of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Bill will establish the OSC to assist victims of online harm through unified regulatory and appeals mechanisms.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The report content should include the number and types of reports received, processing times, the content of orders and directions issued, online harm risk assessments and trend analyses and personal privacy protection measures taken.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Publishing annual reports can make the mechanism more transparent and provide public reassurance that this Bill is effective. : Mr Speaker, I want to begin by expressing my support for the intent of the Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Bill to provide victims of timely means of redress, promote and improve online safety, deter and prevent online harmful activity, and promote accountability as well as responsible and reasonable conduct online.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MDDI's Perceptions of Digitalisation survey found that 84% of Singapore residents encountered harmful content last year.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The SHE report also shows that female youths were twice as likely to experience sexual harassment online.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They can be severe, life-altering threats to safety and peace of mind.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Because online harms can be constant, invasive and hard to escape, they can be as harmful, if not more harmful than physical harm.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We know that the current system is inadequate.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Victims of online harmful activities face challenges reporting such behaviours to online service providers.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They report the content; they wait hours, usually days.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Still, most platforms acted appropriately on only half of the harmful content reported.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For harms that are, by nature, constant, invasive and hard to escape, five days feel like forever.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This Bill offers victims more tools, ways to get harmful content taken down faster, and to hold perpetrators accountable.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the same time, a good idea still needs good implementation.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Given how this Bill grants significant powers to a new agency, the OSC, that will safeguard our rights in this fast-evolving space, I believe it warrants further examination of the Bill with care and rigour.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It will receive and triage reports, investigate whether thresholds of harms are met, issue directions and orders, monitor their compliance and handle appeals.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a lot of responsibility and it is crucial to get three things right: capacity, independence and transparency.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, will the Commission have what it takes to do the job?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It will be on the frontlines dealing with cases that will require an exacting mix of legal expertise, technical knowledge and sound judgment under pressure, all set amidst the fast-moving digital landscape.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Given these responsibilities, I second my colleague He Ting Ru's point that the Commission should be staffed and resourced like a quasi-judicial body, not a customer service centre.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I look forward to the Minister's clarification of what is the anticipated resourcing for the Commission in terms of manpower and budget.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will it include lawyers and technologists who can keep up with the fast-evolving digital landscape, mental health professionals who understand trauma, and people with lived experience of online harms?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Additionally, Minister Teo also rightly pointed out that victims are at the heart of the Commission, and she also importantly flagged the need to minimise the traumatisation of victims.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How will the Ministry ensure that there are trauma-informed care and processes for both the victims who engage with the Commission and Commission staff who will have extensive interactions with these victims?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Second, will the Commission remain independent when it matters the most?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Commissioner is appointed by a Minister and is subjected to Ministerial Direction.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Commissioner will make important assessments on the factual veracity and reputational harm of statements, a profoundly difficult and at times, contentious exercise.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Unlike public agencies, political officeholders themselves can make reports to the Commission.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This means that the Commissioner may find herself having to make judgments about factual accuracy and reputational harm, judgments that could, in some cases, involve content critical of political officeholders, possibly including the very Minister who appointed her.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To be clear, this is not a question about the integrity of any future Commissioner or Minister.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is about how good governance is not solely built on trust in individuals but also on systems that work, and which remain independent and accountable.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For the Commission to become a trusted institution that endures, we need to ensure that it is structurally resilient against potential conflict of interest and/or abuse.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I welcome the Minister to clarify what mechanisms there are to ensure the Commission and Commissioners will remain operationally independent, particularly when handling content that is politically sensitive.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Third, how will Singaporeans know that the Commission is working as intended?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What kinds of harms are the most common and are we adapting to emerging threats?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I invite the Minister to clarify how the Commission’s effectiveness will be measured and to whom it will be held accountable.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We believe that the Commission can and should do better to counteract the opacity of online service providers in regulating online harms.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is the standard practice of the Commission’s foreign counterparts with similar mandates – the Australian eSafety Commission, the UK’s OFCOM and the EU’s Digital Services Coordinators.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Australia and the EU even go a step further to enshrine mandatory review of the legislation after a fixed period to ensure that they remain relevant.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I was heartened to hear Minister of State Rahayu Mahzam state that the Commission will consider publishing regular reports for public awareness.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Public reports by the Commission will help build public confidence in its work.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They will also help researchers, civil society groups and even Government agencies better understand what is happening online so we can respond more effectively.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And related to transparency is the question of consistency.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Beyond aggregate reporting in the form of annual reports, there is also the question of how the Commissioner makes individual decisions for each case and whether they create precedent.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As the Bill does not require for decisions made by the Commissioner to be published, my colleague, Andre Low, has sought clarification on whether the Commissioner will be bound by prior decisions or if each case will be decided with fresh discretion.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This matters because consistency in decision making is fundamental to fairness.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Published decisions, even in anonymous or partially redacted form, provides predictability and prevents arbitrary outcomes.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would also like to thank the Minister for his clarification that the framework on end-user identity disclosure is developed through close consultation with industry partners, and I appreciate the graduated approach.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One defining feature of the Bill is the powers that it grants the Commissioner to unmask anonymous users.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When perpetrators know they can be identified and held accountable, some might think twice before posting that intimate image, sending a threatening message or coordinating a harassment campaign.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They deserve the option to pursue justice beyond content removal.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They will have the option to pursue civil remedies under the new statutory torts.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They can seek damages for the harm they have suffered.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But none of that is possible if they do not know who they are taking to Court.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, while I support this power in principle, the bigger question is how it can be implemented responsibly.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Because, Mr Speaker, identity disclosure is a one-way door.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have seen the bad that can happen when someone’s identity is exposed.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They include some of the very harms this Bill targets, like doxxing, and in extreme cases, even extend to actual physical harms.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I welcome the Minister’s assurance that these measures are not meant to affect ordinary users who act responsibly.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Bill allows identity information disclosure for a prescribed purpose based on “reasonable suspicion” of harmful activity, short of a formal determination.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This means that someone could be unmasked based on an allegation that may not ultimately be proven.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They do not prevent someone from using identity information for vigilantism or sharing it with others in the window before enforcement.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Academic literature on online safety recognises the dual nature of online anonymity.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It can enable authentic expression while also necessitating education to promote constructive dialogue.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It enables marginalised voices to speak up, facilitates frank discussion of sensitive topics and protects some from discrimination or violence.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And this is why we are not arguing against end-user identity information disclosure.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are urging that we get the balance right so it works as intended.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Deter perpetrators while empowering victims, yet also carefully calibrated to prevent misuse and protect legitimate anonymity.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The threshold should be clear enough for consistent application, yet flexible enough to account for context and severity.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this regard, I would still appreciate the Minister’s clarifications on the following.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Minister had earlier mentioned that it would enable victims to bring their case and eventually consider extending it to other purposes.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Could the Minister clarify how broad this scope could be?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I was heartened to hear Minister mention about limiting its use for legal remedies.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will there be consequences if they subsequently chose not to pursue the prescribed purpose?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And finally, Mr Speaker, no enforcement mechanism, however well-designed, can eliminate online harms.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our goal should not be to create a system where Singaporeans constantly defer to regulatory power.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We must continue to empower Singaporeans young and old to navigate the online world safely, think critically about what they encounter and act responsibly.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While it is important that victims have practical solutions to seek timely recourse, it is equally important to prevent that harm in the first place.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How do we build a generation of digitally literate, resilient Singaporeans who can recognise risks, respond appropriately and support others?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should actively work to normalise the reporting of harmful content, promote positive online behaviour and challenge the bystander effect.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Research consistently shows that bystanders often fail to intervene or report, not from apathy, but from uncertainty about whether intervention is appropriate or how to do it effectively.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is also the potential for the Commission to be a resource that helps all Singaporeans navigate digital spaces more safely and constructively.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Enforcement is but one pillar of work for the Commission’s global counterparts.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Australia’s eSafety Commission and the UK’s OFCOM also invest in supporting, conducting and evaluating research on online safety.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Conducting demographic-specific research can help us form a better, more up-to-date understanding of the changing nature of online risks both in terms of content and medium and help inform policy-making.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
