text: It also feeds into the development of accessible, regularly updated resources to increase confidence, skills and online safety of citizens.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Victims of online harmful activity need and deserve better recourse than what is available today, and the establishment of the Commission is a necessary step towards that.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the near term, with the establishment of the Commission, we may see more reported instances of online harm, not because more harm is committed, but because fewer people will suffer in silence.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will be a positive development as it means that people trust the system enough to use it.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the long term, online harms will evolve as quickly as technology itself, because they are driven by perverse incentives, financial profit, manipulation or malice.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is why getting the Commission's design right matters.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It needs to be capable, independent and transparent enough to adapt to whatever comes next.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Instead, it will be in something harder to measure, but more important, do Singaporeans feel better equipped to identify and respond to online risks?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Do we feel supported and empowered to seek help?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are we more likely to intervene and report harmful content?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is our online discourse becoming more constructive and less toxic?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If more Singaporeans can answer yes to most or all of the above questions, then we know we have made good progress in building not just a safer digital space, but a healthier digital society.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The Internet has transformed how we live, work and connect, driving innovation, enabling ideas and creating digital marketplaces where transactions occur at unprecedented speed.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Yet, as with every invention, it has also created new opportunities for harm, for deception, harassment and abuse.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This Bill is therefore both necessary and timely.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The first, empowering victims through civil remedies; the second, introducing a new thought of online impersonation; the third and last, addressing inauthentic and manipulated media.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Together, these measures strengthen accountability, protect dignity and promote responsibility in our digital spaces.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This allows victims to seek redress directly without depending solely on state prosecution.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: As the online sphere becomes central to daily life, individuals should have both the agency and responsibility to safeguard themselves – contributing to a safer shared online environment.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: They no longer need to wait for perpetrators to be unmasked or for criminal proof beyond reasonable doubt.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Victims can act to restore their good name, remove false content and prevent further misuse of their identity.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This reform affirms that digital identity is personal identity – restoring dignity and control to victims and signalling that accountability does not end at the keyboard.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: With the rise of generative AI, manipulated images and fabricated videos are increasingly used to mislead the public, exploit reputations and erode trust.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: As technology blurs the line between truth and fabrication, our laws must evolve.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Timely action against false and deceptive imagery will help preserve the integrity of public discourse and protect individuals from reputational harm.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: First, on the Right-of-Reply User Directions under clause 34.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Can a victim pursue both concurrently, or only if the Commissioner declines to issue a direction?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Clarifying this interplay will help lawyers and users understand how best to obtain swift redress.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Second, on directions and orders under clause 26.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: While immediate intervention is sometimes essential, will the Commissioner conduct a preliminary screening before issuing directions?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This ensures that powers are exercised not only quickly but proportionately.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Relatedly, would the Ministry consider issuing guidelines to clarify which harms will be prioritised for urgent attention?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This would also help manage public expectations, streamline workflows within the OSC and enhance confidence in its impartiality.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Such a measure could serve as a more proactive alternative as compared to retrospective proposals like an annual report, which for example calls for the publication of annual reports and risk assessments for the preceding financial year.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Given its wide-ranging powers over privacy, speech and accountability, public confidence in its competence and neutrality is essential.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Mr Edwin Tong acknowledges that public education is essential, but I would also like to clarify if OSC is taking this educational role, promoting public awareness of online safety, informing users of their rights and responsibilities, and guiding victims to seek help because an informed public is our very first line of defence.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It represents a comprehensive and forward-looking framework to make our digital space safer and more accountable.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Globally, we see similar efforts: from the UK’s Online Safety Act 2023, Germany’s Network Enforcement Act and the EU’s Digital Services Act.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Yet Singapore’s approach goes further by recognising new civil wrongs such as online impersonation and inauthentic material abuse, empowering victims beyond mere takedown or criminal models.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: At the same time, I think we can also learn from others: proactive risk mitigation in the UK, systemic harm prevention in the EU, and clear removal timelines from Germany.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: These remind us that while the digital frontier is global, regulation can reflect and must reflect our local context.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I commend MDDI, MinLaw, the Attorney-General’s Chambers and all involved agencies for developing this landmark legislation.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This Bill continues Singapore’s proactive response to online harms, giving victims real avenues for redress and ensuring that our digital space remains one of safety, trust and accountability.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I have some queries that cover about 10 clauses in the Bill as tabled by the Government for Second Reading.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Explanatory Statement does not shed light on what the ambit or scope of these two types of directions are.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What general or special character directions does this clause envisage, which are not already fully captured or foreshadowed by the Bill?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister clarify what are some of the directions that the Minister envisages to give under this clause, or is this clause to be understood as a general one that confers broad and inchoate powers to the Minister?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Clause 8 empowers the Commissioner to issue advisory guidelines.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As much as public attention on this Bill has focused on online harmful activities and the statutory torts that arise from them, I believe one important barometer for the success of the Bill will lie in its capacity for preventive education.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Australian government's eSafety Online Commissioner's website is a useful guide to take note of as a one stop site to assist victims navigate the difficult terrain of online harms and educate young and old Singaporeans about the impact of their words and actions online, with a view to establish acceptable norms of online behaviour.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, can the Minister share the scope and outreach plans the Government has under this clause to address online harms, with particular focus on juveniles and young adults?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Does it intend to copy the Australian approach with adjustments for the local context, or does it, for example, intend to work closely with the Ministry of Education to consider novel approaches?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Are there specific autochthonous approaches on preventive education that pertain to online conduct and behaviours the Ministry plans on introducing suited for local circumstances?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Clause 11 on the non-consensual disclosure of private information is not clear as to what private information entails.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While the clause leaves open clarity for future regulations, as drafted it reads too widely to be of practical application, and is thus unsatisfactory.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On a plain reading, it begs more questions than it answers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The clause states that private information is information about a person that is not widely available to the public at large.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Explanatory Statement to the Bill does not aid at all to clarify the ambit or context of "not widely available", and what it means.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I hope the Minister can shed light on this clause and briefly outline how regulations will address the ambit of private information in this clause.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If the private information is, for example, found behind a paywall of an exclusive and expensive online publication with limited circulation, would that information be construed as not being widely available?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Clause 20 covers a specific online harm, namely incitement of the enmity, which means the communication of online material that a reasonable person would conclude incites, or is likely to incite feelings of enmity, hatred or hostility against any group in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, in finding the same, clause 20A of the Bill considers relevant factors, such as whether the material dehumanises any person or persons, or otherwise portrays them as less than human.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, in the event a foreign embassy puts up a post that tends to incite, would the Commissioner issue an order against the embassy, an online service provider, or Singaporeans who share the post, or all three?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Clause 22(1)C also includes an individual who has a prescribed connection to Singapore to make a report to the Commission.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The interpretation section of the Bill does not define this prescribed connection, unlike how it defines prescribed online service provider.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister clarify if the Bill can be expected to extend to all work pass holders in Singapore, including foreigners, or even diplomatic staff who make reports to the OSC seeking relief outside the excluded online harmful activities covering incitement of enmity and incitement of violence?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I move to Part 6 of the Bill covering information and end user identity matters.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Commissioner is empowered to require any person to provide in any form or manner any information or document, whether kept in Singapore or not.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This includes requiring the person to provide an explanation of the information or document, including providing access by way of username, password or any other authentication information.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Clause 49(4) states that the Commissioner is entitled without payment to keep any information or document.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister confirm, notwithstanding Minister's comments about the usual police procedures, if anything in this part of the Bill allows the Commissioner to, for example, seize or retain a mobile device or laptop on grounds of an investigation into an alleged online harm under this Bill?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While I accept the relevant law is different, it would be useful for the House to understand how our laws interface with how promptly and the extent to which social media platforms can comply with them, and if not, why not?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Part 7 of the Bill covers reconsiderations and appeals.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This clause does not require the Commissioner to provide reasons for his decision.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister share the rationale behind the treatment or the differentiated treatment, because from a layman's perspective, both are essentially appeals?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One approach to consider is for the Government or the Commissioner to provide reasons in both cases, or the Commission to provide reasons in both cases.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Doing so would be helpful in reducing the number of appeals if the Commissioner's decisions are clearly explained at the outset, subject to the usual privacy concerns.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister explain the approach taken in the Bill so as not to give the impression that the first appeal to the Commissioner to reconsider the decision is not perfunctory?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In this particular case, while it is foreseeable that the form of an online harm notice will be forthcoming, can the Minister shed light on what constitutes a reasonable response time from the online service provider?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The illustration to this clause makes reference to the word "promptly" when a social media service responds to an online harm notice.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This suggests that the interpretation of "reasonable" ought to be construed as "forthwith" or "almost at once".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Would this be a correct reading and expectation of how quickly an online service provider is expected to react?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 4.17 pm until 4.40 pm.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: First, I speak from a position of advocacy that began in 2021.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As a lawyer assisting victims of online harms on a pro bono basis, I have seen firsthand how online abuse can devastate victims, not only emotionally, but socially and professionally.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This Bill will be a powerful tool to help victims stop the immediate harm, obtain justice swiftly and crucially, avoid being re-traumatised by a long and painful process.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Second, this is a novel piece of legislation.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It places Singapore at the vanguard of legal innovation in the online safety space, with provisions not yet seen even in comparable jurisdictions such as Australia.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Third, drawing from my experience on the ground, I urge that we keep the victim's perspective front and centre by ensuring process and access to swift, affordable and final justice, without unnecessary delay or re-traumatisation.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In 2021, I founded Defence Guild SG, a ground-up network of pro bono lawyers who assist victims of online harms and sexual harassment.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This was started following the lewd online poll involving female religious teachers in our Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Together with fellow lawyers, we wanted to send a clear message that such acts have no place in our society and that victims deserve access to legal protection and recourse.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The initiative, supported by the Lawyers@M³ Network and the M³ movement, provides legal advice and assistance for survivors who may not qualify for legal aid.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But this is a small but important step to close the gap for those who fall between the cracks and those who cannot afford representation.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Yet, they are in need, desperate need of justice.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Through Defence Guild SG, I have seen how online harassment often extends beyond the screen as it affects confidence, careers and even the will to participate in the community.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many victims suffer in silence because justice feels distant, complex and often expensive.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In 2022, together with PAP MPs Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin and Ms Hany Soh and the PAP Women’s Wing, we developed an Online Harms Resource Toolkit to empower community activists, women and girls, with practical guidance on what to do and where to seek help.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This effort complements existing legislation by building bottom-up community awareness, not just laws on paper, but empowerment in practice.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In Parliament, I have also consistently raised questions on legal aid and tribunal access for online harm victims.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I spoke on the Online Safety Bill in 2022 and the Online Criminal Harms Bill in 2023, pressing for accountability of platforms, standardised reporting and swifter takedown processes.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: That is why I welcome this Bill because it directly strengthens the protection that many of us, on the ground, have been advocating for years.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My second point on the forward-looking and the novel features of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: First, it introduces new statutory torts for online harms.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This bridges the gap between the public regulation and private redress.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Unlike Australia's eSafety framework, which relies mainly on regulator-led penalties, our model empowers victims themselves to seek justice directly with enhanced damages or an account of profits where appropriate.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This development does more than create new rights.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: By codifying what responsible digital conduct looks like, the law educates all users that our online actions carry consequences and that respect, civility and accountability are non-negotiable.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is both technically astute and morally sound because this will address not only the symptom, but the system that can cause the perpetuation of online harms.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I urge caution in two areas: first, the over-extension of "fair comment" and "public interest" defences; and second, allowing extensive appellate processes that risk re-traumatising victims.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some may argue that comments made in the public interest should be exempt from liability.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But while fair comment is important, it must never be a carte blanche excuse for online abuse or harassment.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singapore’s jurisprudence has long recognised that freedom of expression comes with duties and limits; particularly when words cross into the realm of targeted harassment, doxxing or intimidation.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our current legal framework already strikes a careful balance by weighing public interest and fair comment alongside intent, tone, persistence and also impact.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This ensures that genuine whistleblowing or responsible criticism remains protected, while malicious campaigns disguised as "commentary" are not.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We must retain this proportional approach by allowing robust discourse, but drawing a clear line where speech becomes conduct that harms.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In online harm cases, Mr Deputy Speaker, speed is justice.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Victims are often individuals like students, parents, working adults who are facing powerful platforms or determined harassers.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A specialised tribunal system offers the right balance: quick, affordable, trauma-sensitive decisions, with limited appeal only on points of law.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If we open the door to full appeals, victims may find themselves trapped in lengthy and costly litigation.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Most of the time, it is the party with the deep pockets that can bear this war of attrition.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In any event, the recourse to judicial review is always there as another check and safeguard.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It ensures that executive and administrative decisions are made within the bounds of legality, fairness and rationality.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our courts have consistently held that judicial review is not an appeal on merits, but a safeguard against illegality, irrationality and procedural impropriety.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Within the context of this Bill, that principle remains fully preserved.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The decisions of the Commissioner and of any tribunal established under this Bill are not insulated from scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I believe that this is a balanced approach: it maintains judicial oversight to prevent abuse of power but avoids turning each case into protracted litigation.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In doing so, we uphold both the integrity of our legal system and the need for timely justice for victims of online harm.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Justice must not only be fair; it must also be fast and final for those in pain.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this regard, would the Minister agree that our current legislative framework already strikes a fair balance between safeguarding free expression and protecting individuals from harm?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And that, for the sake of victims of online harms, we must, we must avoid approaches that prolong their trauma, by allowing perpetrators, or well-resourced platforms or providers or any other party to hide behind technical defences, escalate legal costs and drag victims through a drawn-out process that ultimately denies them the swift justice and protection they deserve?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This came about after the incident involving a lewd online discussion that demeaned the female religious teachers and asatizah in our community.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Together with my fellow lawyers, we wanted to send a clear message: That such behaviour has no place in our society and our country.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: That no one can hide or conceal themselves online and do these things without facing any consequences.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the span of just a week, over 20 lawyers came forward to offer their pro bono services.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is a small but significant step because there are gaps in our legal system where people may have been left behind; who are unable to bear the cost of legal fees, but are too hurt to remain silent.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Through Defence Guild SG, I have seen that cyber harassment does not simply end at the screen.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It extends into real life; shaking self-confidence, destroying careers and crushing a person's spirit.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this fight of ours, we are upholding not just the law but also the values that we hold dear, that justice, compassion and wisdom must go hand in hand; both in the physical world and online. : Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, let me conclude by giving voice to some of the victims who have reached out to me and my colleagues.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One victim J shared that she had been "subjected to prolonged and persistent online harassment since 2014", but could not afford the cost and time for injunctive relief.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Another named Y, a Singaporean who was studying overseas said she remained "fearful of returning to Singapore" because the harassment had so deeply affected her sense of safety.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A third victim S, a single mother, suffered from severe depression and anxiety, described how her personal information was circulated in unsolicited emails to various parties.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Each and every one of them are desperate for help quickly and would have to turn to the system for protection.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Their stories remind us, all of us that behind every case, every case number, every matter is a human being: seeking peace, not revenge; dignity, not exposure; closure, not spectacle.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Let us make the online world safer, so that our generations to come may inherit not a space of fear, but one of respect and responsibility.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As I once pledged with my colleagues, my pro bono lawyers at Defence Guild SG: let us stand together, against violence and harassment here and online so that the world we live in today will be a better one when we leave it for our children.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I have met with residents affected by online harms and Singaporeans have written to me asking for reforms.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: From how we stay in touch to how we work, shop, learn and govern, the Internet has evolved into more than just a means of communication – it has become a second life.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: And the divide between the online and offline worlds continues to blur as technology becomes increasingly interwoven into our daily lives.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Our laws need to keep pace with modern day advances and the threats of today.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The recent report by SHE, "404 Help Not Found: Lived Experiences of Online Harms Survivors" sheds light on the harsh realities that define today’s digital landscape.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: As a child, Zane experienced bullying in school.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: His peers took to online platforms weekly to spread negative remarks about him.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Later in life, during his polytechnic years, Zane experienced doxxing.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The perpetrator shared his name, school and course on Twitter and threatened Zane.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: These incidents had an impact on Zane in his growing years.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: He kept his pain to himself, fearing retaliation and judgement.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The emotional toll eventually caught up with him.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: During his National Service days, Zane experienced panic attacks and had to seek professional help.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Zane's journey reflects how cumulative online harms can leave deep psychological scars; ones that linger long after the screen goes dark.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: And what happened to Zane is not rare.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It is a glimpse into a culture where online harm has become casual, even accepted.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Where cruelty hides behind screens, and victims often suffer in silence – many times too afraid, too tired and too ashamed to seek help.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It is important for us to be deliberate in shaping the tone of our online world for our children, our friends and our neighbours.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Because the wounds may be invisible, but they are real – and they last.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The Bill is a step in the right direction.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In the age of AI, where false and harmful content can spread faster and cut deeper, such protections have never been more important.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The youths in particular are particularly and especially vulnerable to online harms.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: To find out what the youths thought of the Bill, I spoke with YouthTech SG, formerly known as Cyber Youth Singapore.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: YouthTech SG is a youth-led social movement and charity.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: One of their divisions is YouthTech Institute which focuses on helping young people navigate the risks and opportunities of technology, including online safety.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: They wrote to me and expressed their support for the Bill, describing it as a signal for Singaporeans to foster a more cohesive, civil and wholesome digital environment.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: They also welcomed the Bill’s introduction of new avenues for youths to seek help and relief when harmed online; options that previously did not exist.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: While the Bill makes important strides in fostering a responsible digital environment, the online culture is ultimately one which requires users to build and that endeavour goes beyond legislation.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Having reviewed the Bill, I find that the Bill is a meaningful step forward.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It is unlikely to be a quick or perfect fix given how common online harms are and how deep rooted they are in our daily lives, but it signals our shared commitment to build a kinder, safer Singapore – both offline and online.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I support this Bill and would like to share a few reflections and seek some clarifications.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: My first observation: the creation of the OSC and the scope of its enforcement powers is noteworthy.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: While victims often suffer immediate harm, current means of redress are reportedly slow and sometimes ineffective.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The unfortunate reality is that victims are often left to navigate complex and sometimes opaque complaint processes, and structural challenges may further hinder platform responsiveness.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The OSC plays a vital role in addressing these gaps.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Moreover, clause 26(1) provides that the Commissioner may issue a Part 5 direction if the OSC has reason to suspect that the online harmful activity was conducted.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This allows OSC the flexibility to swiftly take down online harmful activity.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I see that Australia had similar experiences from which we can draw some lessons.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The Australian eSafety Commissioner has the power to issue directives to address online harmful activities.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Speaking at a 2023 symposium organised by MinLaw and the SMU Yong Pung How School of Law, the eSafety Commissioner from Australia highlighted the value of a dedicated and independent safety regulator in addressing online harms.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In a Straits Times article, dated 26 September 2023, it was reported that she said: "Often when people come to us, they just want their images taken down, they don’t want to be tethered to their former partner through litigation, which, of course, can take a long time.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I don’t think we would have the same degree of success with the platforms, particularly where there are grey areas, if we didn’t have these (remedial) powers." To this extent, I note that there is a requirement for victims to first file a report to the online platform before approaching OSC.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: And therefore, the accessibility and ease of reporting on the platforms will be critical in ensuring access to justice for victims through OSC.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I seek clarifications on how the Ministries plan to work with the platforms to enable this.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Should the victim report all incidences he or she is aware of at the same time?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Or will we land in a situation where the victim is required to repeatedly go through the process of reporting to the platform and then to OSC for each piece of material?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Can a victim apply to OSC for the pre-emptive ban of similar materials resurfacing?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Member Zhulkarnain had mentioned the advantages that OSC offers in being a more responsive and less adversarial mechanism as compared to traditional litigation.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I will not repeat that, but I stand in support of his point.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Victims of online harm may be reluctant to seek redress due to fear of repercussions, whether from the perpetrator, societal stigma, workplace consequences, or familial pressures.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This hesitation is particularly pronounced in cases involving intimate image abuse, doxxing, or harassment, where the victim’s identity is often central to the harm itself.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I am heartened to see that the Ministry has been sensitive to this issue.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This would mirror existing protections under the Children and Young Persons Act, where proceedings involving minors are automatically anonymised, and the Women’s Charter, which provides automatic identity protection in the form of prohibition of publication or broadcast of information identifying victims or witnesses.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This is applied under the Women's Charter in cases involving sexual offences.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Extending automatic anonymity to victims of online harm, particularly those from vulnerable groups, would not only reduce procedural burden but also encourage victims to avail themselves to the options under this Bill.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Beyond the courtroom, I would be grateful for further clarity on how the Ministry intends to safeguard the confidentiality of victims during the reporting process.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Specifically, how will the Ministry ensure that victims’ personal information remains protected, while also upholding the rights of alleged perpetrators to be informed of the nature of the allegations made against them?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: My third observation relates to the new statutory tort of online instigation of disproportionate harm.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Civil action under this tort requires proof of actual or reasonably foreseeable loss or damage, while some heads of losses, such as financial losses, may be easier to prove, others, particularly psychological injury or emotional distress, have traditionally presented evidentiary challenges.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I would be grateful for the Minister's clarification on how the latter cases will be treated.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: My fourth observation is that the Bill seeks to address "inauthentic material abuse", which is any audio, visual or audiovisual material that has been digitally altered or generated that is false or misleading depiction of the victim’s words, actions or conduct, but is realistic enough that a reasonable person would believe that the material emanated from the victim.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In this regard, a depiction of the victim saying or engaging in anything includes a depiction of the victim’s likeness saying or engaging in that thing.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The Bill would benefit from clarity on how likeness is assessed in the context of AI-generated content.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Must there be an intent to impersonate or mislead?

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In my view, these clarifications are especially important since resemblance may be subtle, stylised, or partial.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In closing, Mr Deputy Speaker, I welcome this Bill.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It is a timely and necessary step towards preventing the propagation of online harmful activities.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This is especially important today, when many of us, including young and old, spend much of our time online.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The youths in particular are especially vulnerable to online harms, and I am heartened that this Bill provides additional avenues for their protection.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In particular, I am encouraged by the Ministries’ efforts to consult widely and engage with the youths while drafting this Bill.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The youths form a significant demographic that would be affected and protected by this Bill.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In their letter to me, YouthTech Institute shared with me that they participated in the public consultations and dialogues organised by the Government.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: They voiced their concerns and provided feedback on how the Bill can continue to stay true to its policy goals without chilling legitimate online participation by youths.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: They tell me that their feedback was seriously taken in and considered.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: The courts hear the evidence, the verdict is pronounced, sentence is spent.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Yet, far too often, the second sentence is delivered online by self-appointed vigilantes.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Almost immediately, commenters weave threads of public shaming: images, addresses, workplaces, friends – all exposed, shared, argued about.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: One legal practitioner recounted a man in his 30s with mild autism, whose personal traits, speech, appearance and insecurities were relentlessly attacked online in gaming communities.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Whether or not the original crime was serious, the secondary assault online multiplies harm and deepens exclusion.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: The person who already faces legal consequences now must contend with perpetual digital scrutiny, unable to move forward even after "paying their dues".

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: And sometimes, the person targeted online is not even guilty at all.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: In 2020, many will remember the case of the woman who refused to wear a mask at Shunfu Mart and claimed to be a "sovereign".

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: In the rush to identify her, online users wrongly accused another woman of being that person.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Within hours, her photographs, company details and even the names of her colleagues were posted across social media.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: She and her firm faced a barrage of racist and xenophobic abuse, even though she had absolutely nothing to do with the incident.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: The victim later described feeling bewildered and frightened, a bystander suddenly thrust into the centre of a public storm.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: It was a textbook case of doxxing and mistaken identity.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: And it showed how quickly online outrage can spill over into real harm, even for those completely uninvolved.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: If that is what can happen to an innocent person, imagine what happens to someone who has actually made a mistake, served their sentence and is trying to move on.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: We already have laws against doxxing in Singapore: amendments to the Protection from Harassment Act make it an offence to publish someone’s personal details with intent to cause harassment, alarm or distress.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: And yet, enforcement is limited: the Singapore Police Force investigated fewer than 10 cases of doxxing in the first four months of a recent year.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Because doxxing often lies in a grey area where exposure is legal, for example, a court report, but the layering of personal data and commentary turns exposure into attack.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: I return to the question: when someone serves their sentence, should society still punish them?

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Worse still, when harm hides under the guise of public interest or fair comment.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: If a so-called fair comment is sent repeatedly every day to a victim, their family, or their employer, it ceases to be comment.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: We must be clear about where legitimate expression ends and abuse begins and ensure that enforcement is consistent so victims do not hesitate to come forward for fear of uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: If we allow perpetual online shaming, we deny redemption.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Employers, neighbours, friends, all filtered by search results, by rumours, by what the digital crowd decided to publish.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: This Bill helps guard against that unending sentence.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: It lets the Courts and the Commissioner intervene.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: It says: the past does not have to be a life sentence in the digital realm.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Many victims of online harm may lack the legal literacy, confidence or financial means to approach the Commissioner or file for redress.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: The process should therefore be simple, affordable and trauma-informed with clear guidance and support for vulnerable groups such as youths, persons with disabilities and lower-income users.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: A centralised "one-stop" reporting channel that connects the Singapore Police Force, IMDA and the Commissioner's office could make seeking help far less intimidating.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Second, prevention must go hand in hand with enforcement.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: We cannot legislate empathy, but we can educate for empathy.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Public campaigns and digital citizenship programmes, especially in schools and workplaces, should teach not only what is illegal online, but what is unethical.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: It is as important to cultivate digital restraint as it is to punish digital harm.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Third, we should examine the appeals framework carefully.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: The Bill currently limits further appeals after an online safety Appeal Committee's decision.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: That finality provides efficiency but there is a risk that victims could still face drawn-out proceedings or repeated challenges from offenders exploiting procedural loopholes.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: We should ensure that the appeals process is fair but finite, one that safeguards due process while sparing victims prolonged distress.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Because our society should not allow people to be condemned twice: once by the Court, and again by the crowd.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: I ask that as we debate, we remember those caught in the crossfire of legal punishment and digital vengeance and build protections so that justice ends where it should.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: The burden of proof and the effort to seek redress often fall on those already traumatised.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Hence, whether at the individual or society level, we must have in place effective and firm mitigation across policy, enforcement, technology, education and civil society to tackle the ills of online harms.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: As mentioned, this House has debated these issues before.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: In January last year, I moved the Motion on Building an Inclusive and Safe Digital Society together with our then-Digital Development and Information GPC colleagues.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: During the Motion debate, we reaffirmed our commitment to adopt a whole-of-nation approach to sustain trust by building an inclusive and safe digital society.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Members who participated actively discussed, amongst other things, online harms.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: In all, the then-Digital Development and Information GPC members and PAP MPs who spoke set out a total of 13 Calls to Action, which included: Calling on Social Media Services to be accountable for the proliferation of harmful content and malicious ads on their platforms.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Calling for the Social Media Services (SMSs) and App Distribution Services (ADSs) to step up in measures to better protect young users from being exposed to age-inappropriate or harmful content.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Calling for these SMSs and ADSs to improve timeliness in responding to user reports on harmful content on their platforms.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Here, I must stress that the importance of timely interventions cannot be understated.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Thankfully, both sides of the House supported the Motion.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Therefore, I am glad that we are now taking a step further in building an inclusive and safe digital society through stronger legislation and measures against online harms.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: These measures address the problems victims often face – speed and uncertainty.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Allow me to share a story of my resident's fiancée back in 2014.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: My resident's fiancée's ex-boyfriend uploaded very compromising photos of her onto websites such as "Revenge Porn", which was outlawed by California but was still available online because the sites were hosted overseas.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: These photos were taken while they were still in the relationship and when there was still trust.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Following the uploads, there were many unsavoury comments by people she knew and did not know and after a while, even her friends started to notice it and asked her about it.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Imagine the shame, the embarrassment, the kind of distress that she had to endure.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Quoting my resident, he stated, "to complicate matters, the website is hosted in the US.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: The company is registered in Amsterdam and even the individual, who happens to my fiance's ex-boyfriend, who uploaded the photo is unable to remove them without the website host's approval who, ultimately, would only do so if the removal fee is paid.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Since then, my fiancée has lost sleep, could not eat or work in peace, especially not while witnessing the links to her compromising photos appear on search results while looking up her name." At that time, POHA was just introduced and yet to take effect.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: But the issue at hand was real and pressing.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I recall we had to approach various agencies to try to figure out how to stop it and protect the fiancée.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Eventually, we managed block access domestically to protect her.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: We have more legislation in place and stronger enforcement capabilities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: There is greater societal awareness and to be fair, the social media industry has also been more responsive than before.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: We may no longer find the "Revenge Porn" website now, but we can still remember the fairly recent "SG Nasi Lemak" Telegram chatgroup.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: The format and vectors have changed – from public websites to private chatgroups and dodgy apps.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: And so, our legislation and interventions must change too.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: So, I believe the clearer definitions in this round of amendments will accelerate investigation and enforcement.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: The longer harmful material remains public, the greater the lasting damage.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Yet, victims today still find the reporting process confusing and daunting.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Reporting to social media platforms often feels like a "lucky draw", you cannot be sure whether they will agree to remove the post or when they will do so, if they agree to do so.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: The ordinary users, that is, the "small fry", are often disadvantaged.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: It is not that there is no legal recourse at present.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: But when a victim is already stressed out by the fire burning online, how can she/he find the mental space to navigate the laws and take the right actions?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: As it is, the relevant statutes addressing harmful online content and conduct include a wide range – POHA, Broadcasting Act, POFMA, Foreign Interference (Countermeasures) Act and OCHA.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: How can a victim navigate these laws and will OSRA, which is the Bill that we are debating now, overlap with existing laws and frameworks?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Must the victim make reports to multiple agencies, or will agencies coordinate amongst themselves?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: In the 2014 case that I shared earlier, my resident and his fiancée felt lost, even I felt somewhat exhausted trying to help them navigate the various agencies.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: How will the new OSC help, or not help, to overcome this?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: That being the case, we must also guard against abuse of this new mechanism.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: What measures are in place to prevent OSC being made use of by devious characters to make vexatious reporting or be weaponised to fix another person due to private disputes?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Without timely finality, resourceful perpetrators can exploit appeals to delay takedowns, prolong exposure and continue with the abuse.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: All things equal, some considerations simply should take priority.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Hence here, protection against harm must be prioritised.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I refer to hon Member He Ting Ru's proposed amendment.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I had a little bit of concern that I wish to set out here.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I find the use of "fair comments" here somewhat fuzzy and highly subjective.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I do not think that these are helpful to victims of online harm.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Perhaps, the Ministers, in your responses, can comment and shed more light on the possible consequences of such amendments as proposed by the hon Member.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Ultimately, legislation and enforcement are necessary but not sufficient.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: In 2021, PAP's Women's Wing launched a campaign, #ActionForHer, to encourage Singaporeans to take action to support women.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: In 2022, the campaign focused on tackling online harms.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: There were pledges to action, and a toolkit on "Supporting Residents Facing Online Harms", just to name a few.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: And as part of the campaign, youth activists from my branch, MacPherson, decided to do more and organised the #ActionForHer Webinar Series to discuss topics pertinent to their peers and with a strong focus on protecting women in the virtual space.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I am sure there are many other examples of positive ground-up efforts by different volunteer groups and organisations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: We should certainly recognise and encourage such efforts, to encourage positive social behaviours and norms.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: (In Mandarin):   Online harm, whether it is harassment, non-consensual intimate images, deepfake scams or coordinated disinformation, damages mental and physical health, economic security, public discourse, safety and public trust in digital systems.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Online harm differs from physical and verbal harassment.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Online harm spreads rapidly, often exponentially and frequently beyond our immediate control.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Content published today can be copied, archived, indexed and repeatedly shared, leaving long-term, or even permanent, damage to victims' reputations and livelihoods.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Therefore, the Internet often favours perpetrators, while being unfair to victims.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Anyone can easily publish information, but victims, especially ordinary users, find it difficult to remove harmful content.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: The burden of proof and seeking redress often falls on those who are already traumatised.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Therefore, both at the individual and societal levels, we must establish effective and robust mitigation mechanisms in policy, law enforcement, technology, education and civil society to address the consequences of online harm.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I am therefore pleased that we will now combat online harm through stronger legislations and measures.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: As technology continues to develop, new methods of cyber threats and online harms will also emerge.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Therefore, legislation and intervention measures must also keep pace with the times.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: We may not be able to totally stem out such risks or threats at one go.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: We must continue to evolve our legislation and ensure there is teeth in the enforcement.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Meanwhile, it is not enough to just put in place such hard measures.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: If anyone is willing to take on a larger share of the responsibility, we can protect more people and reduce the harms or damage to individuals, so that ordinary citizens can be free to live full and meaningful lives.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: (In English): As technology continues to develop, new methods of cyber threats and online harms will also emerge.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: We may not be able to totally stamp out such risks or threats at one go, but we must continue to evolve our legislation and ensure there is teeth in our enforcement.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: That being said, it is also not enough to just put in place such "hard" measures.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: We need the whole-of-society to believe in upholding a safe online space as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: So, if we can do more, if everyone is willing to take on a larger share of the responsibility, we can protect more people and reduce the harms or damage to individuals, so that ordinary citizens can be free to live full and meaningful lives.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Before that, Ms He Ting Ru, do you have a clarification of a speech by a Member before you?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I have a clarification on Ms Tin's speech from earlier.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I think I heard Ms Tin said on my amendment to change the standard from "reason to suspect" to "reasonable grounds to believe", I believe the Member said that this might actually prolong the process and cause further harms to victims.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I just wanted to clarify how she thought that this would be the case.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Ms Tin, would you like to respond to the clarification?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: And this is what I meant by if we change from "reason to suspect" to "reason to believe", it may therefore extend that exposure to harm on the victim and therefore, cause more harm to the victim.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Ms He, do you have a clarification arising out of Ms Tin's response to you?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I just want to explain our thinking behind why we actually called for the amendment.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: However, when there is ambiguous harm that is worthy of further investigation, our thought process was that where this might not satisfy reasonable grounds to believe and therefore, we will actually use investigative powers, and for the Commissioner to satisfy himself that it is appropriate to take action.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: So, do you have a specific question for Ms Tin or not, Ms He?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Ms Tin, would you like to respond to any of that?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: I do have a question in response to that.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: I am not sure whether I am allowed to.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Perhaps, in the thought process that Ms He had articulated, could she share some examples of what such ambiguous situations may be so that I can have a better understanding of her thought process?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Ms He, would you like to respond to that?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: So, I think for something that is ambiguous, for example, what is considered harmful to a reputation, that would be something that sometimes, it could be a little bit ambiguous; and therefore, that is when, perhaps, there is a bit of a chance for the investigative powers to be used to investigate further.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Do either Ms Tin or Ms He like to say anything before we move on to Mr Alex Yeo who is the next speaker?

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: We operate every day in the digital world.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: It is part and parcel of our lives.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: While digital connectivity has brought undeniable benefits, a potent side effect has been the proliferation of online harms.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Online harms are all pervasive, have the capacity to go viral very quickly and often bring immeasurable harm to the victims.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Victims find it difficult and challenging to seek recourse or relief from the mental and emotional toil that online harms inflict on them.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: For many, there is an innate helplessness in not knowing how to make it stop; how to make it go away.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Ironically, even though it is the digital world, they have nowhere to run and nowhere to hide.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Many jurisdictions like us are also grappling with this phenomenon.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Australia, New Zealand, Germany, the UK, the EU, the US and India have enacted varied legislation to address this.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In Singapore, the introduction of this Bill is, therefore, a timely one.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: I appreciate the policy intent of this Bill and the actionable levers that it seeks to introduce to address online harms in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: I shall highlight three aspects that stand out for me.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: The Commissioner will take a holistic approach in considering each report to carry out his or her duties effectively and in good time.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Over time, it is hoped that this will promote accountable and responsible conduct that moves us towards a safer online environment in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: I just like to make two observations to the inclusion of fair comment as an exception in certain clauses.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Let us take clause 9 – online harassment – as an example.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: At the outset, I will say that I appreciate the good intent of the amendment.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: It is to carve out an exception of fair comment on a matter of public interest so that any such communication of online material will not constitute online harassment.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Mr Andre Low, for example, gave an illustration of a public official: a person who made or gave a purported fair comment to a public official that could be perceived as an online harassment.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: First, I note that the amendments do not propose a definition of what constitutes fair comment.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: As such, we have to look elsewhere for interpretation.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: One possible area is in existing defamation law where fair comment is a defence.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: But in simple terms, if the comment or opinion that a fair-minded or reasonable person could honestly made based on facts and importantly, it must be made without malice.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: With that in mind, let us look at what constitutes online harassment in clause 9 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: It is the communication of online material that a reasonable person would conclude is threatening, abusive, insulting, sexual or indecent, and likely to cause a victim harassment, alarm, distress or humiliation.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: If we are to compare both definitions of online harassment and fair comment side by side, could a fair comment reasonably constitute as online harassment?

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Even with the example provided by Mr Andre Low, based on the definitions, is it possible for fair comment to be threatening, abusive or insulting?

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: If the answer is no, then, the amendment, in my opinion, is unnecessary.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In fact, I am of the respectful view that a fair comment should be a comment or opinion conveyed in a respectful, civil and courteous manner.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: I am sure such a comment will not be captured under clause 9 as online harassment.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: This leads me then to my second observation.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: As I had shared earlier, my reading of the intent of the Bill is for the Commissioner to make an assessment that is first, victim-centric, how the online communication is received by the victim.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Second, focused not on its content, but rather on the nature and manner in which the online communication is conveyed.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: And third, provide victims with quick and effective relief.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: To necessitate the Commissioner to make further legal assessment on whether an online communication is fair comment, especially in light of my first observation will, in my opinion, distract from and potentially defeat the purpose of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Having said that, Mr Deputy Speaker, while I rise in support of this Bill, I would like to take this opportunity to seek some clarifications on how the Government intends to address online harms suffered by a particularly vulnerable class of victims, children or minors.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In my maiden speech, I spoke about the concerns surrounding our children and their exposure to the digital space.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Several Members of this House also raised similar concerns.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: I had shared that, as a father of two Gen Alpha children, one of whom will be a teenager soon, no matter how much we try to regulate their interactions with the digital world, my wife and I worry.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Where parents once told their children to beware of the strangers outside of the home, today, we must also guard against "strangers" and dangers lurking within, in the digital world.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Even the home is no longer a safe sanctuary for our children.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Digital connectivity has dramatically altered the experiences of the growing up years.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In the analogue world of the past, if you had an unpleasant experience at school or with your friends, you could go home, get "away" from the problem.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In fact, they become viral, multiplying and reinforcing the awfulness of the experience or encounter.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: It becomes the last thing you read or see before you sleep and the first thing you see or read when you wake.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: For a child or a youth, this incessant barrage could lead to unthinkable devastating consequences.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: We have all read of such cases happening all over the world.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: I do not need to raise them here.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: First, how will the proposed Office of the Commissioner of Online Safety distinguish online harms between adults, children or youths?

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Second, whether the proposed Office of the Commissioner for Online Safety will take a differentiated approach in the reporting regime and the provision of remedies and reliefs when the victim is a child or a youth.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: I will elaborate on each of the above in turn.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Under the Bill, most of the classes of online harms depend on the "reasonable person" test.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: This is the test that the Commissioner will apply to assess and conclude whether the reported online material fulfils the criteria of an online harm.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Currently, this is a single, uniform test to be applied to persons of all ages.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: I accept that the Commissioner is within his or her remit to apply a differentiated standard of the "reasonable person" depending on whether the alleged victim is an adult or a child.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: This, however, as we can all appreciate, could be an extremely delicate exercise.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: There is, at present, little guidance provided in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Other jurisdictions have drawn this distinction in their legislation.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In fact, it appears that the Australian eSafety Commissioner has set up different channels in dealing with a range of different persons: adults, educators, parents, young people, children, seniors and women.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: I believe that the perception of harm, such as what is threatening, abusive or insulting, between an adult and a child and even between minors of different ages is different.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: The type of online materials that may cause harassment, alarm, distress or humiliation to an adult as opposed to a child or youth, will also be different.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In fact, I thought Minister of State Rahayu had actually — when she shared Handout 4, if I can bring the House to Handout 4, paragraph 7 under (A) Online Harassment says this: "However, if the facts were different and B had disagreed with A, only by calling A's stance stupid and flawed, this is not necessarily online harassment.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Criticism, even if strongly worded, is not online harassment if it does not involve what a reasonable person would conclude is threatening, abusive, insulting, sexual or indecent language, which is likely to cause harassment, alarm, distress or humiliation".

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: It is my humble opinion, Mr Deputy Speaker, that when words such as stupid and flawed are addressed to a child or a minor, it is perceived very differently.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: And so, when we look at the reasonable person test, we must be mindful that it must be viewed in the context of age and maturity.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: My only wish is to make the point that there needs to be a distinguishment between how we view online harms between adults and children.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Studies have also shown that online harms impact children differently from adults.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: For example, online harms are likely to have a longer-lasting impact on children.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Cyberbullied children experience depression, anxiety, suicidal ideation and self-esteem deficits that persist into adulthood.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Reports and surveys suggest that in the cases of cyberbullying of children or minors, under-reporting is prevalent.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In February 2024, the then Ministry of Communications and Information released findings from their youth online gaming survey.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Only about 8% spoke to their parents about the experience.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Of the parents surveyed, one in four parents were not aware of who their child gamed with.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Studies elsewhere have also reflected the under-reporting phenomenon.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: The common reasons for this are the belief that they should "deal with it themselves", that is 50%; the fear of losing Internet access or face device restriction, or 31%.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In other surveys, embarrassment, shame, fear of judgement or reprisal are also reasons children or youths cite for not reporting cyberbullying.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Ensuring that the reporting mechanism is one that provides confidence to our minors and a safe space to share their experiences and fears without judgement, is vital and crucial.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: There are many reasons why a child or a youth may shy away from sharing cyberbullying incidents with parents or family.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: A compromising indecent image of themselves, for example.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Will there be a reporting mechanism that would allow children or minors to directly report cyberbullying, even in the absence of a parent or a trusted adult?

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: How will we reassure and encourage our children and youths that such a reporting mechanism is safe for their use?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Andre Low, do you have a clarification of a Member who gave a speech prior to you?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre
text: I have a clarification of Mr Alex Yeo.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre
text: Before I proceed with my substantive clarifications, I think I want to get a preliminary clarification from the Member.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre
text: Is the crux of his point on the fair comment issue that essentially he thinks the amendment we have proposed is extraneous because it is already covered by the definition of the harm?
