speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre
text: So, I think my response to that would be, I believe Mr Yeo was referring to the defence of fair comment, the defence, the tort of defamation.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre
text: I think it has been stated that the test for fair comment involves four elements, but none of that refers to malice.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre
text: So, as stated in the case of Review Publishing v.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre
text: Lee Hsien Loong, there are four elements to the test.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre
text: So, the element of malice actually comes later as a rebuttal to the usage of this defence.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: So, is that a clarification of your own volition, or are you seeking a response from Mr Alex Yeo?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre
text: Yes, I would like to seek a response from Mr Alex Yeo.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo
text: When I say that fair comment is unnecessary, I mean that there is no example in my mind, given the definition of fair comment.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo
text: And I agree with Mr Andre Low, I did not want to list out all four elements and then list out the rebuttal to the defence, and so on, because I did not want it to be too legalistic in my speech.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo
text: And if you look at what it is, as I said in my speech earlier, online harassment under clause 9 requires a communication of online material that is threatening, abusive, insulting, sexual or indecent, and causes a victim humiliation – and something else, I cannot remember, my notes are over there – but the point is that, suffice that the point to be made, Mr Deputy Speaker, is that a fair comment would not be caught under section 9, and therefore, it is unnecessary.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Andre Low, do you require a clarification arising out of that?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Yeo, do you have anything else to add?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This Bill matters – to every parent who has ever worried about what their children see online, to every small business owner targeted by scams or false associations and to every young person who has faced abuse, ridicule and humiliation online, sometimes spilling offline.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This Bill tells them something powerful: that the law sees their pain.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: That we are serious about safeguarding the dignity, privacy and well-being of every person online without stifling creativity, innovation, expression or enterprise.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is principled and practical – the product of years of careful consultation and iteration, including insights from last year’s Motion on Building a Safe and Inclusive Digital Safety in this House.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In that debate, I called for an inclusive and safe digital society even in the age of AI.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I said that platforms that profit from attention must also take responsibility for harm, including AI-generated content such as deepfakes.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Perpetrators and platforms can no longer hide behind the anonymity of code or contract or algorithm.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It holds intermediaries and platforms accountable when they fail to act reasonably upon notices.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We move beyond "blame the victim" or "blame the platform" to reasonable duties on everyone with power to prevent harm – users, group owners and administrators, and service providers and platforms, paired with liability for frivolous or abusive notices to prevent weaponisation.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: By defining administrators’ duties, we give WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord group owners clarity: act reasonably and promptly when put on notice and you will be fine.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Even though the first phase focused on five online harms, the planned inclusion of inauthentic material or deepfake abuse and online impersonation recognises how AI is changing the very texture of online truth.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I have to admit that preparing to debate this Bill was quite a challenge, given the number of consequential changes to related laws such as harassments protections, remedies for identical reports, recognition of humiliation as harm.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I commend the Ministry for the hard work aligning our justice system with the digital reality.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: First, for the new civil torts, what factors will courts consider?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: A short practice note would guide platforms, administrators and users, to act correctly and swiftly.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What are the expected service levels from report to direction and typical reconsideration timelines?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: A fast track for high-risk harms would be reassuring.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: When identity disclosure is required to pursue relief, what privacy safeguards and purpose restrictions will apply?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We should deter abuse while protecting victims’ and bystanders’ data.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I also have five suggestions where we might go further.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Today, duties are triggered after harm occurs, hence victim redress.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: A limited, risk-based set of anticipatory duties – not blanket surveillance but responsible design – would help to prevent harm.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Platforms should explain, in principle, how their systems amplify or reduce harmful content.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Much like how banks must disclose material risks, systemic accountability requires visibility.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Third, strengthen rehabilitation, digital literacy and AI awareness.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Sometimes it comes from ignorance, inexperience or immaturity.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Courts should have discretion to combine compensation with digital-literacy or restorative programmes, especially for younger offenders.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Long term safety is not just about punishment.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is about cultivating a culture of respect online.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Platforms could publish anonymised statistics: notices received, actions taken, average response times – so that the public can trust and policy-makers can measure progress.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Fifth, as technology evolves – so must the law.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Periodic reviews are essential to ensure the framework remains effective, especially for emerging technologies like generative AI and immersive platforms.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Gen AI tools like ChatGPT can create harmful content.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This could include, for example, documentation of model training or data governance, or disclosure of AI safety plans as has been passed in California.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Any adaption must also reflect the unique harm pathways, user prompts leading to AI outputs, in contrast to social medica and be risk-based to safeguard Singaporeans without stifling innovation.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But in times or rapid technological change, our task is not to fear the future.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Uncertainty should not make us pessimistic, it should make us better builders of systems that are inclusive, safe and resilient.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Our laws must remain principles-anchored, technology-neutral and future-ready.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I have also studied the amendments proposed by the hon Member Ms He Ting Ru and other Members from the WP with interest.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I appreciate the desire for safeguards against overreach, but as many have said today the law must put victims front and centre.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: A "fair comment" exception risks confusion and loopholes.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Harassment is clearly defined, "fair comment", as seen by the debate earlier, is vague and legally complex – and may give bad actors an easy excuse.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is delay, it is harm, it is injustice.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The hon Member Mr Andre Low has made some comparisons to other jurisdictions – UK and Canada.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We are not here to copy the UK and Canada.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But he also seems to believe the thresholds, the blanket threshold that applies for this instance to also to victim redress.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And I actually wonder if the Minister can clarify that.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In practice, Ofcom's own guidance shows it can and does act on complaints and indications of harm.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: When Ofcom or the platform can act to prevent further harm in the early-stage assessment phase, while evidence is still being gathered.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: That does not seem dissimilar to the balance that this Bill strikes.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The "reason to suspect" threshold ensures victims are seen and helped immediately, while safeguards prevent abuse of the system, including appeals for reconsideration.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This is practical, principled and humane lawmaking, putting people over procedure.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Bill already provides for a clear appeal architecture – reconsideration by the Commissioner, then an independent Online Safety Appeal Panel and Committee.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This ensures that powers are reviewable, not arbitrary.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Parents worried about cyberbullying, or professionals whose reputations are harmed online, do not care about legal theory.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They care about timely, practical action – recognition of their harm and real, enforceable recourse and real accountability.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And a system that prevents someone else from being hurt in the same way.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This Bill gives them justice that is felt, not just written on paper.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Our goal must be quick relief and effective, accountability, not endless second guessing and legalese.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And that is why I did not support these amendments.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is the woman who is a victim of doxxing; the honest small business owner whose reputation is destroyed overnight; the retiree who is targeted and manipulated online, losing his life savings; the woman whose private images become public forever; the young creator attacked for speaking up.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But is also every Singaporean who has ever hesitated before posting something kind, for fear that cruelty will follow.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This Bill protects all of them – and reminds us all of our responsibility.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Safety online cannot be legislated into existence; it must be built through culture, enforcement and example.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Some may ask: why does this matter so much for Singapore?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Because the Internet is where our children learn, our businesses grow and our communities gather.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: When people feel safe online, they feel they belong.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And when they feel they belong, they can speak, create and care for other another.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Our laws already protect people in physical spaces – at work, at school, in our homes better than most other places.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This Bill extends the same promise into our digital spaces.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: When I asked what she wanted most, she told me, "I just want to feel safe when I’m myself online." That, at its heart, is what this Bill is truly about.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This Bill does not just respond to online harm.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It rebuilds trust in the digital public space.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It tells society: "We can be both open and safe".

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, I urge all Members today: let us pass this Bill with a united voice and continue refining it, so Singapore remains not only the safest place to live, but the safest place to be yourself, online and offline.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is where we work, socialise, play, engage services, amongst many other things.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Unfortunately, "online" has also become "where" and "how" malicious actors inflict harm on others.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And the harm inflicted in the virtual world has far-reaching and deep implications in the physical world because they tend to permeate the very being of the individual victim and our communities, with potentially long-lasting damage.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A resident teenager came to my meet-the-people session recently.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: She shared with me the daily fear she lives under, being subjected to online harassment from a perpetrator based overseas, and who has been able to somehow gain access to her private online accounts to blackmail her and even threaten others, her friends in her social network.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is why I cannot agree with the amendments proposed by the WP to raise the threshold for the Commissioner of the OSC to give directions from "reason to suspect" to "reasonable grounds to believe".

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As Mr Andre Low says, "this is not mere semantics".

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The higher threshold proposed by the WP will mean that the Commissioner will need to take more time to put together the "reasonable grounds to believe" before giving directions, during which the victim continues to suffer in silence.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I agree with Mr Andre Low that we need institutional safeguards to ensure fairness for all parties, but I would argue these safeguards have already been provided for in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Clause 58 provides for the application for reconsideration of the Commissioner's decision.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Clause 63 provides for the appeal against the Commissioner's reconsidered decision by the appeals board.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And further, clause 69 makes the provision of false information an offence to be dealt with in the courts.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, what these institutional safeguards mean is that the Commissioner can act swiftly to protect the purported victims while also injecting urgency on the part of the accused to clarify, seek reconsideration, make an appeal if they feel that the order was not the right one or if it was made with incomplete facts but it gives them urgency to do so and gives the victim justice.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, given the rapid and exponential impact of online harms, this approach strikes the right balance.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, this Bill alone is not a silver bullet to the threat of online harms, nothing can be given the complexity of it and we will require the enforcement capabilities, as well as local and international partnerships to implement the Bill effectively.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, I hope you can allow me to raise a few points and clarifications for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Also, is the Minister able to provide any guidance on how the courts should calibrate the penalties to be meted out?

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Because as a general principle, Parliamentary intent is key in the application of the law, and we should, as far as possible, make it clear for the purposes of administration of justice.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Next, I touch on the extra-territorial aspect of the offences under consideration.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Operationally and practically speaking, will the OSC’s arm of the law be long enough to reach the wrongdoers who may be located overseas?

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Who will be our key regional and international partners?

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will the overseas Internet service providers and app distribution services comply with OSC’s order?

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Relatedly, does the Bill contemplate online harms perpetuated by foreign actors, perhaps as a means of foreign interference?

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Like the non-digital world, the Internet comprises dark and less overt corners as well.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, while the Bill provides a comprehensive framework to deal with offences committed through the mainstream channels, are there sufficient and effective safeguards and capabilities against circulation by dark social media, dark traffic or perhaps even the dark web?

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For the membership or following of certain obscure forums can far outnumber groups on more familiar platforms such as Instagram or TikTok.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The risk of involvement of organised or syndicated crime groups could further significantly enhance the scale of harm.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Identity protection tools such as the Virtual Privacy Network (VPN) will add a layer of complexity to detection and investigation, enforcement efforts.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To be clear, I am not proposing the policing of private conversations.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, we ought to do our best to eliminate or reduce the gaps where they are.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Has MDDI formulated a projection of OSC's workload?

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a to-be newly established agency, the OSC will have to deal with multiple issues on various fronts, besides the core work itself, including administrative matters, logistics, human resource and financing.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Before that, do you have a clarification, Ms Chong?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Of a speaker before you in this debate?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: I have a clarification for Mr Foo Cexiang.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: I would just like to seek a clarification regarding the Member's point on fair comment, and if the Member can elaborate on what he means.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: Because surely, a person cannot be guilty until proven innocent, because anyone can lodge a report to this Commission, and I would urge Mr Foo to refer to Part 4 of the draft Bill.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: And if the Commission has to assess and take action based on a single person's viewpoint, however valid as it may be, surely it should be based on reasonable grounds to believe that something has actually occurred, rather than just a reasonable suspicion?

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang
text: There is no judgment on whether somebody is guilty.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang
text: In fact, that is why it allows the reconsideration of the order and upon thereafter, an appeal as well.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang
text: As for the second clarification that the Member made was how would you come to the conclusion that there is something to suspect vis-a-vis reasonable grounds to believe.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang
text: And I think that is something that the Commissioner will need to take judgment of, based on the facts available to him or her.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang
text: Because for them to have reasonable grounds to suspect, and I do not want to prejudge what the Commissioner's decision will be, there must be information that is provided from the victim, admittedly, but it will also be based on actions that has been done by the perpetrator.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Ms Chong, would you like to raise any clarifications arising from Mr Foo's point?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: I think to Mr Foo's point about how the Commissioner's assessment will be based on the report that is filed as well as the actions taken by the perpetrator, would Mr Foo not agree that if it is based on a report filed by the victim, then it is alleged actions by a perpetrator, and the Commissioner or the Commission would then need to investigate to ensure that this action has indeed happened, and therefore warrants any directions or orders.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang
text: And for that, I refer to clause 69 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Andre Low, do you have a clarification for Mr Foo?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre
text: We have all seen scenarios where influencers have cat fights online.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre
text: We want to avoid a situation where the Bill is weaponised by one party against another and that is, why we have proposed that the threshold be set at a higher level.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Is that a clarification of your own volition, or are you seeking a clarification?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Is that a clarification of your own volition, or are you seeking a response from the hon Member Mr Foo?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre
text: Yes, I am seeking a response from the hon Member Mr Foo.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang
text: I think the hon Member brought up the issue or the case of two different groups of bickering online influencers.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang
text: And I would put it to the hon Member that, in such instances, where it is a bickering that is made out in the public, online world, the Commissioner and all the officers in the OSC will have access to this information, they will be able to come to their own judgment, whether or not there are reasonable grounds to suspect online harm.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Would either Mr Foo or Mr Low seek to raise any further clarifications before we move on with the debate to Mr David Hoe?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The Internet is central to how we learn, we work and we connect.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Yet the same space that empowers can also wound.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Online harassment, doxxing and impersonation cause not only reputational harm and damage but also emotional and psychological harm.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In my years with working with students, I have seen how online words or even emojis can weigh heavily on a young mind.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: What begins as a passing comment or post can linger for weeks.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It shapes how young people see themselves, how they trust others and how they engage in the world.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But we know that online harm affects beyond youths.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Behind every statistic is a person whose confidence, rest or peace of mind has been shaken.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When digital interaction becomes constant and instantaneous; the pursuit to respond, to perform and stay visible has grown.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: You can ask many of the MPs here.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For many, that brings new forms of stress and exposure, the kind that erodes stress and confidence quietly but deeply.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This Bill therefore is not merely about regulating conduct.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is about reinforcing dignity, trust and wellness and well-being in our digital lives.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It recognises that feeling safe online is part of feeling secure in daily life.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Each day that harmful content remains online, it deepens harm.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So, consider the Singapore Sports School deepfake case in 2024, where manipulated images of students were circulated.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Counsellors reported anxiety and social withdrawal among those who were affected.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: A faster redress system could have reduced that distress and restored a sense of safety to our youths.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This reflects a simple principle: we step in early, we support recovery and we prevent harm from deepening.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In the many community dialogues that I have held, parents often share that when their child is targeted online and they do not know where to run or turn to.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: To them, Police reports feel daunting, platform responses are slow, or may I say, very slow.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The OSC will fill that gap with a trusted, accessible pathway for relief.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The Bill introduces statutory torts for online harms, such as harassment, stalking, doxxing and impersonation.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It defines responsibilities for both perpetrators and for platforms.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When expectations are clear, behaviour improves without constant enforcement.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Ultimately, a safer online space grows from shared values from individuals, from families and institutions choosing responsibility over convenience.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I stressed, just as in my last Bill, platforms must do their part.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For too long, victims have waited days for responses while hurtful content spreads unchecked.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These platforms hold immense influence over public life, and with influence comes duty.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This Bill reminds them that their responsibility to people cannot end at their servers' edge.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This Bill changes that, for platforms will now have a duty of care, not merely a policy preference.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And when young people see that harmful actions carry consequences, lessons on digital citizenship gain meaning.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It teaches them that civility is not weakness, it is strength.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Authorised bodies, including trade unions and professional associations, can now represent victims.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This is significant because it extends workplace safety into the digital realm.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Unions, such as the Healthcare Services Employees Union (HSEU) and the Singapore Teachers' Union (STU) can now act when members face online harassment in the course of duty.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Over the years, we have seen so many examples and I am glad that this Bill comes in very timely.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As a labour MP, I have met educators, healthcare workers and young professionals who face online criticism that turned pretty personal.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They told me it is not just the comments, but the silence that followed, not knowing who to turn to and whether who would stand with them.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: That sense of isolation is something we must change.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And I am glad this Bill enables the unions and institutions to act swiftly because the ability that can make the difference between despair and recovery is now here.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When unions step in, they offer more than legal aid.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They offer reassurance, solidarity and care – support that protects both moral and mental well-being.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Those numbers remind us that online harm is not abstract.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It touches people who serve us daily with empathy and commitment.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In my community work, I have also heard from residents and parents who say they feel exposed online, sometimes hesitant to speak up for fear that comments or images may be twisted or misused.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And this Bill offers a safety net, from institutional support to clear remedies and assurance that no one has to face such harm alone.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Will the OSC set clear service benchmarks, for example, acknowledgement within hours and resolution within defined days, and include escalation lanes for frontline public officers and workers, such as healthcare workers or educators?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: A delayed response to these workers who serve us in the frontlines prolongs their distress and can affect their confidence in carrying out their duties.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For workers who engage publicly, like the teachers, nurses and the social workers, harmful posts can spread faster than formal action, and platforms must act quickly to protect those who serve the public.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: My third point is on protection of privacy when identity disclosure is ordered.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Confidentiality is not about data, it is about psychological safety.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Victims are more likely to seek help when they know their identity will be treated discreetly and with care.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: My fourth point is on sectoral readiness and guidance.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Such inter-agency readiness, even if outside of this Bill’s scope, will make the OSC's work more effective and ensure that victims receive consistent, trauma-informed support.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: My last point is on union and professional-body activation.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Unions are often the first line of support when workers face online abuse.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Clear guidelines and authorisations allow them to move quickly to offer legal protection, pastoral care and reassurance before harm escalates and I hope the Ministry can consider this.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It provides timely relief to victims of online harassment through the establishment of the OSC; it sets clear responsibilities for individuals and platforms so that all parties act more responsibly; and third, it allows unions like NTUC and professional associations to represent members who become victims so they do not stand alone when attacked in cyberspace.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Fundamentally, this Bill does not merely protect digital safety, it also safeguards our mental health and well-being, stability of the family and social cohesion.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We want a society that has the courage not just to speak up, but to do so in a civilised manner, one that is active online but also mindful of the impact of words and actions.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When citizens feel safe enough to interact politely and respectfully, both in cyberspace and the real world, we will strengthen trust, compassion and the sense of solidarity in our nation. : Mr Deputy Speaker, this Bill protects more than digital boundaries.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It complements our wider efforts in preventive health and mental well-being by reducing one of today’s quiet stressors: online hostility.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When a teacher, a nurse or parent knows that the law stands behind them; when a student or a young person feels that their dignity will be defended; when the union can stand with its members in solidarity and assurance, then trust grows.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But laws can make clear what we stand for: respect, responsibility and care.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This is how we build a digital society that strengthens, not fractures, our people.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Notwithstanding the clarifications I raised, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This Bill is close to my heart, because I have met Singaporeans who suffered from the harms described in Part 3 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For them, the humiliation and emotional distress that they have gone through are overwhelming.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This Bill, if implemented well, will go some way to deter perpetrators of online harms and give victims of online harms much clearer routes of recourse.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Against this backdrop of my support for this Bill, I would like to seek clarifications on how this Bill works in practice across five areas.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: My first clarification is about the operational tempo and service standards of the Commissioner’s office.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: On operational tempo, the Bill rightly allows victims to seek the Commissioner’s intervention without first going to court.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Beyond "being fast", we also need to communicate what is being done fast.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This means that efforts should be made to lay out the process as clearly as possible to the general public, so that the victim knows what actions will be taken and what to expect from the moment they decide to make a report.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: You see, it makes a difference by telling someone that within a certain number of hours, they will receive a response versus telling someone that over the next X number of hours, actions a, b and c will be taken and they will be updated at the end.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As part of implementation, the Commissioner should consider issuing advisory guidelines that set out triage principles, communication milestones, indicative response time across various categories of online harms by severity.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Hence, I wonder if the Commissioner’s office can consider setting and publicly communicating service standards or target response times for various categories of online harms by severity.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Saying this, I am cognisant that speed also requires resourcing.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The Commissioner’s office should be staffed and supported to act with urgency.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I would welcome the Ministry’s plan for resourcing so that operational targets are achievable rather than aspirational.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I also think that it is more appropriate to leave service expectations and operational key performance indicators (KPIs) as guidelines as compared to statute because hard timelines in primary legislation like this Bill may risk overwhelming staffing when spikes in online harm cases occur.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Hence, the guidelines can be updated swiftly and calibrated to capacity at the agency level, so that the bar can be set at achievable and meaningful levels.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: To strengthen this approach, the Commissioner should also consider having a standing advisory group of relevant practitioners such as technologists, clinicians, child-safety specialists and academics to refresh workflows, KPIs, and give guidance on online harms periodically.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: My second clarification involves accessibility and public readiness.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Clause 23 of Part 4 provides that victims can report online harms to the Commissioner, but it is also equally important that they know how to do it.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Online harm victims will also include those who are less technologically savvy.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It is hence vital that we ensure that the process of online harm reporting is kept simple, multilingual and accessible.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This could mean: (a) ensuring that the online and mobile service platforms use plain English, not technical jargon, and official languages to communicate to the public and guide victims of online harms through reporting; (b) proactively providing step-by-step guides via major online and mobile platforms, so that they know how to file an online harm notice; and (c) at the same time, setting up offline helplines and community touchpoints for those who are digitally less-confident users to keep them informed of the work of the Commissioner and the Office.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Clause 94 in Part 12 of the Bill also allows victims to send an online harm notice to an online service provider.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This is a positive step towards direct accountability.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But for this to be utilised effectively, online services must make sure that reporting is easy to find and use.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In this regard, would the Government, along with the Commissioner and the Office, study how major platforms will implement their online harm reporting in practice and consider whether they are accessible, especially to the vulnerable users.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For instance, sending an online harm notice within a mobile app or website should never require a user more than 20 minutes navigating multiple different landing pages and entering unnecessary inputs that the provider would already have gotten from the moment they had registered for an account.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: You see, these design features are not cosmetic, because they determine whether victims can exercise their rights effectively.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Thirdly, we should also consider the practical aspects of civil proceedings and cost of justice.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Hence, civil action involves practical hurdles, legal costs, disclosure processes and emotional strain.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The Commissioner and the Office should also consider communicating the availability of these resources from the onset, because at the end of the day, justice should never be determined by income.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This upfront assurance will reduce the barriers to entry to report and deter the actions of perpetrators.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: My fourth point of clarification is on issues related to damages, humiliation and redress.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This may go further in helping the victims to rebuild their lives.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Relatedly, public communications and victim-facing materials by the Commissioner and the Office should be trauma-informed and non-stigmatising.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They should state plainly that the responsibility lies with the perpetrator and not invite interpretations that the clothing, occupation, social activity has caused harm to be done unto them.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This is important because victim-blaming deters reporting and delays help-seeking, and compounds humiliation and distress.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Such upstream measures would ensure that our protections are not only reactive but proactive making the digital environment safer before harm occurs.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Hence, I hope that the Government will actively work with major online and mobile platforms on this.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But to make online safety real, we must pair law with speed, prevention, and accessibility.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This is how we build an online environment that is safe, fair and inclusive, while upholding responsible speech and due process.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Online harms, such as image abuse, circulation of obscene materials, including child abuse materials, AI-generated images, doxxing and so on.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Previously, Parliament had also passed other Acts, like OCHA, to deal with online scams, hate speech and so on.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: In other words, we have been keeping our criminal laws up to date and fit for purpose, and these updated laws provide our people the assurance of statutory retribution for online harms.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Operating alongside our criminal laws, OSRA, before us today, will provide statutory relief, including injunctive relief and statutory torts and civil remedies for online harms.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Taken together, this body of laws, while providing justice to our people experiencing online harms, can also help deter online harmful actors, thus further protecting our people in the online commons.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: I will say that on the whole, the Government has done a tremendous job architecting our laws to protect and secure the online commons for our people, in a very thoughtful, thorough, yet calibrated and pragmatic manner.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: This is an important thought, because after OSRA is passed today, if it is passed, the focus will increasingly turn towards the enforcement of these laws, the implementation of policy and the painstaking work of building up organisations, capabilities and practice to deliver on the intended legislative and policy outcomes.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Implementation is policy, and the focus will turn towards implementation.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Minister Josephine alluded to this in her speech as well.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And so, the point I wish to make is this: that in implementation, let us have trust that the Government will go about this implementation in the same thoughtful, thorough, yet calibrated and pragmatic way as it had architected our laws for the online commons.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Being a later speaker in this debate, I have had the privilege to hear many colleagues who spoke earlier.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Most called for sufficient resourcing of OSC to handle workload and do its job, and most also called for clear service levels – time taken between reporting and relief – to give Singaporeans certainty and assurance of the relief they can expect when they report to OSC.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Speed of relief is, indeed, so crucial for victims of online harm.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And this Bill, which provides for the establishment of a dedicated agency to deliver such relief to victims of online harm, could not have come soon enough.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And so our natural instincts will be to say, "Let us get the relief out to the victims who need it today, who needed it yesterday.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Let us get this relief out quickly." But the reality is that building up an organisation, building up capabilities, especially fast-cycle capabilities, takes time.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: We cannot rush the building of fast-cycle capabilities, paradoxically.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: So, I hope all of us, including and, perhaps, starting from this House, can give the Government the time and space needed to build up OSC properly, so that it can deliver the quick, effective, on-point relief that we, ultimately, are all seeking out for victims, present and future.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: On workload and resourcing of OSC, my thoughts are as follows.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: How might we be able to resource OSC to deal with a potential workload like this?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: I am going to posit that we may never be able to resource it enough, because, fundamentally, there will be, to a large degree, what we call supply-induced demand for the OSC's services.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Meaning, the more services the OSC supplies, the more demand it may actually induce and therefore, demand will likely keep running ahead of supply.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And so, beyond doing our level best to resource OSC to keep up with demand, the central task of implementation, in my mind, is to keep the gap between supply by OSC and demand for OSC tight.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: This means we must also find a way to manage demand, to manage expectations – manage our expectations – on OSC.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Rather, I say, let us give time and space for OSC to establish a baseline, to establish its rhythm and give time and space for supply and demand to find an equilibrium and most importantly, give time and space for all of us to go through the necessary discovery process on relief standards collectively – as a society.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And then, we can look to codify these service levels and standards at the right time.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, I rise in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: For the young, or whom we call the digital natives, the Internet is their classroom to the world, where they learn, play and form friendships.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Yet, this classroom has few teachers at the door.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: I have met parents who tell me their children can mute a chat or delete a post, but they cannot delete the hurt or the humiliation that came with it.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: I support this Bill because it recognises two simple truths: that people need protection and platforms need accountability.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: However, I would like to seek clarifications on the points below.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Both laws allow victims to take civil action, but if their boundaries are unclear, victims may end up filing under multiple laws – OSRA, POHA and common law, all at once.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: That could inflate time and cost, which runs counter to OSRA's intent for quick and affordable relief.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: I hope the Ministry can issue guidelines or practice directions to make these boundaries clear on when OSRA applies and when POHA remains the better channel.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Clarity will help claimants, lawyers and judges navigate cases efficiently, reducing unnecessary litigation.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Yet, the current text does not distinguish between victims who are minors and adults.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: I hope OSC will develop tiered response protocols that give priority to victims under-18, especially when harm is ongoing.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: If we can respond quickly to a child being targeted online, we can often prevent lasting damage.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Online safety should be seen as part of raising happy and healthy children, not separate from it.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Our online space must give children room to explore safely – to learn, play and make mistakes, without being preyed upon.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: I hope that OSC can also work closely with relevant Government agencies and non-governmental organisations to educate and empower victims to speak up.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: It is imperative that the protections and recourse available to victims, especially those from vulnerable groups, are easily understandable and accessible.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Doing so will help to encourage victims to seek help early and safely.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: I have received feedback expressing concerns that victims may run the risk of being exposed to further harm by seeking recourse under the proposed new legislation.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: To ensure that the new legislation achieves its intended purpose of protecting victims, adequate safeguards should be implemented, including to safeguard the victims' identities and to ensure that the process is fair.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: In this regard, I am heartened to see that the Bill contains certain safeguards, including clause 54, which imposes secrecy obligations on persons who may receive sensitive information in the course of carrying out their duties; and Part 7, which establishes mechanisms for reconsiderations and appeals.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: In addition, I have received feedback that seeks clarity on the types of information that would be considered "private information" for the purposes of clause 11 of the Bill, including sexual orientation, gender identity, sexual diseases or sex-related occupation status.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Although the definition of this phrase in the Bill is worded in wide terms and the illustration makes it clear that non-public information relating to medical conditions constitutes private information, it would, perhaps, provide clarity and assurance to potential victims if regulations, which are contemplated under clause 11(2) of the Bill, are swiftly introduced following the passage of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: I have also received feedback regarding the list of persons who are eligible to make a report to the Commissioner on behalf of a victim under clause 22(2)(a) of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: In particular, there are concerns that there may be victims, who are under the age of 18, who may either be estranged from their parents or guardians, or are fearful of informing them of the online harm that is occurring to them.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: For example, due to shame associated with the information that is being published about them online, a minor could be fearful of informing his or her parents.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Could the Minister clarify the recourse that the minor would have in such a scenario, please?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: This Bill builds on lessons from other countries.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: UK and Australia have implemented similar online safety laws, and it would be useful to understand whether their experiences led to fewer harms or faster response times.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: If certain measures have proven effective, we should localise and adapt them early.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Could the Minister clarify the principles that would give the Commissioner's imposition of deadlines for compliance with directions issued under our Act, and whether guidelines embodying such principles will be published, please?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Large platforms have legal teams, moderators and automated filters.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Smaller and community-based platforms, including start-ups and local networks, may not.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Otherwise, we risk a two-speed digital economy where global platforms comply easily while smaller innovators struggle to keep up.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Regulation should lift everyone, not leave the smaller players behind.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: It must, therefore, be adequately resourced, not only with technical and legal expertise, but with experienced officers who understand the social and emotional dimensions of online harm.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: However, this is different from an annual reporting, as service standards are listed out clearly and pre-emptively, rather than post-incident.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: This is akin to how teachers would set out clear rules in their classrooms prior to conflicts and bullying.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: The success of OSC should lie in whether parents, children and all users of our online space feel safe even before logging online.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: In time, I hope the Commission will also act as an educator and facilitator, promoting digital literacy and empathy across communities.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, OSRA is like a set of classroom rules in our digital school to ensure every Singaporean, especially our young, can learn, share and express themselves safely.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, I support the Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Bill.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: However, the Government should also pay attention to the following during implementation.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: First, clarify the distinction between this Bill and POHA.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Second, prioritise cases of online harm involving minors.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: But beyond regulation, it also reminds us of our shared duty to build a safe digital environment for our young.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   I support the Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Bill.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Victims of online harassment or malicious disclosure of their privacy will receive more timely and comprehensive protection and will be able to seek compensation.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Commission will be able to instruct distributors of harmful content, platform administrators and platform operators to remove harmful content, restrict perpetrator accounts or publish victim responses.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These measures will help curb many forms of online misconduct and are crucial for building a responsible and healthy online ecosystem.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The enactment of this Bill is a landmark achievement in shaping a civilised, responsible and trustworthy online environment.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I sincerely thank all relevant departments and the public for their efforts and contributions over the past five years.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am gratified and encouraged to see everyone working together to make the online environment safer and more civilised.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Internet's appeal lies in connecting people and ideas around the world, fostering understanding and solidarity.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, it has also been abused for disseminating pornography and violence, cyberbullying and inciting racial or religious conflict.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many of these misdeeds are carried out anonymously and this trend is escalating.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Currently, the avenues for help available to Internet victims are extremely limited.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Beyond the direct psychological and emotional harm, we are also seeing increasing indirect impacts.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many people are beginning to self-censor, even choosing to reduce their Internet use to protect themselves and their families.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If we do not address this issue promptly, this online environment will further deteriorate.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I welcome the establishment of the new OSC to enable victims to seek timely remedies.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I cheer the Government's decision to enhance information and identity disclosures.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Especially important is the introduction of statutory torts.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I support the Ministry's plan to progressively expand coverage.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At the same time, I would like to ask, when would the other online harms be progressively included?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They shared that their addresses, car numbers and details of when they are resting are being shared online, as are videos and photos showing their family members, neighbours and visitors.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If so, what actions will the OSC take?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition, the POHA provide protection from online harassment as well.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How can victims decide on when to seek help from OSC or POHA?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With this new legislative framework, new standards will be set for online behaviour and communication.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Over time, these guidelines will guide our Internet users.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I urge relevant departments to continue raising public awareness of this new framework and its corresponding penalties.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Internet abusers must understand that they can no longer easily hide behind seemingly anonymous avatars and commit offences, they would be punished if they do so.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the UK, the Online Safety Act can impose penalties of up to S$31 million.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This highlights a clear and urgent need to enhance current mechanisms for help seeking relief.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Bill is, therefore, a crucial and timely step to ensure that the safety and civility we value in the physical world, on our streets, extend to our digital lives.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: An anecdote that Minister Edwin Tong had alluded to as well.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For a victim whose intimate images have been non-consensually recorded and distributed publicly, five days can be catastrophic.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am, therefore, concerned about the need for timely relief and clarity of the administrative process for victims of online harm.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Bill rightly grants the Commissioner wide discretion to carry out its own investigation and empowers to issue legally enforceable directions to take down content and restrict accounts.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will the perpetrator being investigated be made aware of the investigation, and at what stage?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What information will be disclosed to the perpetrator about the complaint made against them?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I understand the Commissioner is already working with SHE in the design of this initiative, including referral to SHECARES@SCWO for counselling and pro bono legal advice.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will the Commissioner consider engaging other organisations who provide victim care and support, like AWARE's Sexual Assault Care Centre and Project X, to improve trauma-informed processes and joint case management and outreach to encourage more victims, especially those in minority communities, to be assured when seeking help.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For victims under immense stress, clarity on the steps involved for bringing a complaint and the expected time for resolution is vital.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With great power holds great responsibility, and the transparency of the process can help reassure and encourage help-seeking efforts.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A month-long public consultation on the proposed legislation, which received broad public support and directly informed the final Bill.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our citizens have asked for accountability and this Bill delivers.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It empowers the victim, yet holds the perpetrator accountable, and sets clear expectations for platforms.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is a necessary act of legislative fortitude to protect our citizens in an increasingly complex digital world.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: With the growing prevalence of cyberbullying and the rise of illegal black markets and harmful online chatrooms that benefit profit from disseminating obscene and dangerous materials, this Bill could not have come at a more timely moment.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: It is even more important that Singapore will be among the first countries to introduce comprehensive legislation on this issue, a significant milestone that did not happen overnight.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: It took years to get here; years of heart, hope and hard work by the many stakeholders and public officers.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: In supporting this Bill, I have four clarifications: two concerning the contents of the Bill and two concerning its enforcement.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Currently, many major social media platforms, such as Instagram and TikTok, have internal reporting mechanisms and community guidelines, which will need to be aligned with the new legislation.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Some of these platforms already provide warning labels for potentially distressing images, for example, content that may contain self-harm, violence or sensitive materials.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: However, I note that there may still be grey areas.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Certain artistic or educational materials, which are excluded from the definition of obscene materials under clause 9(2), may still be distressing for some users.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: In the UK, for example, their Online Safety framework has included protections for what is called "epileptic trolling", content that is designed to trigger seizures and other materials that may trigger individuals with mental health conditions.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: My second question concerns an issue close to the hearts of many Singaporeans, especially our senior youths and that is cyberbullying.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: This has become an issue of serious public concern in recent years and there is growing anxiety that our youths and senior youths' young children are being exposed to obscene and harassing behaviours online.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: A further concern relates to enforcement, especially in cases where harmful content is disseminated through transnational online platforms.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: A lot of these harmful materials are transnational in nature, or if not, the online platforms themselves that host these materials are transnational themselves.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Some global companies have proactively aligned their internal policies with global legislation on online harms, while others have not been as forthcoming.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: And if work has already started, what are the current stakeholder sentiments and negotiations done to ensure that such online platforms, in particular, adopts and abides by the Online Safety Bill?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Under the current framework, victims must first report harmful content to the relevant service provider and in more serious cases, escalate it to the newly established Online Harms Commission.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill also provides for victims to bring civil actions against offenders or platforms in cases of online harm.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: As the hon Member Mr David Hoe has also mentioned, many Singaporeans may lack the financial resources to pursue such claims.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The technology and social landscape will continue to evolve, and while this Bill marks an important step forward, the work should not stop here.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Ensuring a safe and trusted online space requires a holistic approach, one that looks beyond legislation to how we build a supportive and resilient ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: This includes strengthening community networks and drawing on the support of stakeholders, such as social and religious organisations, as well as deepening public education efforts.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Together, these efforts will foster a culture of responsibility, empathy and care in our digital spaces.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill represents a crucial step forward in safeguarding our digital spaces and ensuring that our laws keep pace with the realities of the online world.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: I hope this brings safer spaces online, with protection and recourse for all.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This legislation is a thoughtful and compassionate response to the growing challenge of online harms, such as cyberbullying, intimate image abuse, doxxing and online stalking.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These are not just breaches of privacy, but attacks on dignity and are harms that leave deep scars on victims, scars that are no less real for being inflicted through screens rather than in person.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When people experience online harm, every hour of delay multiplies their suffering.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That is why we need to act quickly.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our citizens deserve an agency that can act swiftly on their behalf, providing the support and relief they need during what can be a highly vulnerable moment.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am deeply grateful to the Minister and the entire Ministry team for their dedication in crafting this important piece of legislation and I hope to explore several queries where additional clarity and detail would help us achieve our common goal of protecting Singaporeans online.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, on extraterritorial enforcement and international cooperation for cross-border protection.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Bill wisely grants extraterritorial reach, recognising the global nature of online harm.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A perpetrator in another country can cause immense damage here.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I appreciate that the Bill includes important tools, such as access blocking in section 44 and app removal in section 45 and that it establishes calibrated penalties that reflect the seriousness of non-compliance.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These provisions show careful thought about practical enforcement.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Like Mr Foo Cexiang, I hope the Minister can share how the Government intends to enforce this law outside Singapore's territory other than access blocking and app removal orders.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I note that access blocking can be circumvented with technology like VPNs; apps can be accessed by means other than app stores, for example, through web versions.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What are the concrete steps for enforcement of directions and orders against overseas actors?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are there plans to expand the available slate of mechanisms and means of enforcement, or if there are any international cooperation protocols for extraterritorial enforcement?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Let us build international partnerships that match the borderless nature of the Internet with equally borderless protection for victims.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, many Members have already pointed out the need to adequately resource the Commission.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Commission's promise is clear – to offer swift relief for those facing online harm.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The victims who turn to the Commission will be in their most vulnerable state.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Let us make sure the system they encounter is not just efficient, but also humane, staffed by people who listen, understand and act with compassion.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Section 64 establishes an Appeal Committee to review the Commissioner's decisions.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Appeal Committee has been granted powers to affirm, revoke or vary decisions and directions, providing an important internal check on decision-making.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Given the significant powers being granted to the OSC, including directions carrying criminal consequences and orders with substantial penalties, I believe that clear accountability mechanisms will strengthen public trust and confidence in the system.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Judicial oversight by direct appeal would ensure accountability, fairness and transparency and thus strengthen the credibility of the OSC.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To address concerns of ensuring swift and low-cost resolution for the relevant parties, there can be prescribed short timelines, standard forms and low court fees.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This would be a similar approach to that under POFMA.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I appreciate that section 5(1)(e) requires the Commissioner to collaborate with IMDA and other public agencies, and section 24(4)(d) allows appropriate referrals.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This reflects understanding that protecting Singaporeans online requires coordinated effort across Government.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many situations, including doxxing with intent to harass, non-consensual sharing of intimate images and image-based child abuse, constitute both harm under this Bill and criminal offences requiring Police involvement.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will there be a framework to automatically refer certain types of online harm cases to the Police?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When agencies work seamlessly, victims would not need to repeat their trauma at multiple doors, ensuring that the system itself becomes a source of healing, not exhaustion.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Fifth, on potential over censoring by online service providers (OSPs) and administrators.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: OSPs and administrators may over censor content to avoid risks.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They may err on the side of caution and may remove content upon receiving any purported online harm notice that superficially appears to have some basis, unnecessarily silencing voices.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Unlike the Commissioner's decisions, which can be reconsidered or appealed against, their decisions are not statutorily subject to reconsideration or appeal.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While there is a statutory tort available to OSPs and administrators against people sending frivolous or false notices, people adversely impacted by their decisions have no statutory recourse.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In most cases, there will be an imbalance of power and resources such that those impacted will have little or no means to pursue recourse.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can we avail to people whose content have been removed by OSPs and administrators, statutory torts similar to sections 91 and 94 if OSPs and administrators fail to respond reasonably to online harm notices by unreasonably removing their content?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would the Ministry consider mechanisms for recourse, a form of appeal or review, to ensure that fairness applies not just to victims of online harm, but also to users who are wrongly penalised by overzealous moderation?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Building on this strong foundation, I hope we might explore opportunities to extend these protections even further.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our young people are creative and curious, exploring online spaces we might not immediately think of as social media.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Games like Roblox, Minecraft and Fortnite bring children together but include private messaging functionalities where risks can emerge.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Messaging platforms, like Discord, WhatsApp and Telegram enable connections but can also expose young users to unwanted contact and harmful content.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We should ensure these powerful tools are designed with their safety in mind.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Broadcasting Act amendments and Codes of Practice represent genuine progress.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope we can continue this important work, advancing "safety by design" principles across the entire digital ecosystem our children and young people inhabit.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This must be coupled with continued public education across all segments of our society, especially parents and young persons, on digital safety, so every child and young person can explore, learn, create and connect safely.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Online harm spreads in the same way a fire does: fast, invasive and devastating, and every second counts.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With this Bill, we are ensuring that when victims cry out, the system answers not with delay, but with decisive, immediate protection.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A law is only as strong as its capacity to be enforced.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We are all in agreement that victims should have access to swift and effective relief.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Statistics and stories tell us this is what victims primarily want.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We also all agree that the implementation of OSRA is key and that the OSC must always be fair and consistent in its decisions with accountability through due processes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There is consensus that platforms also need to do their part in creating safer online space for their users.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I am heartened that both sides of the House are aligned in wanting to do more to help victims of online harms.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Where we differ is in some of the details.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: What is important are the outcomes when the OSC commences operations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We all want the OSC to succeed, and in this vein, I ask Members to give OSC the time and space to stand up what we all agree are new and novel functions, so that it can progressively build its muscles to help victims.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I acknowledge that Members have questions about the statutory reporting mechanism and how the OSC will carry out its functions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Understandably so, given that this is a new agency that we are setting up, I will address Members' questions thematically.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: First, on the scope of the OSRA Bill and its interaction with other laws.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Members have noted that there are several statutes addressing harmful online content and conduct.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This includes removing the harm as soon as possible.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: With the OSRA Bill and the set-up of the OSC, we hope that victims will be granted more timely relief with a new channel for support.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Besides timely redress, the OSRA Bill also expands the scope of online harms covered in our current criminal and regulatory regime.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: With this, we hope to protect victims not just from existing but future harms.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Therefore, the OSRA Bill is complementary to the existing laws and frameworks.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Most importantly, it supports victims in ways they have asked for, putting a stop to the online harm as soon as possible.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
