text: Ms Tin Pei Ling, Mr Henry Kwek and Dr Choo Pei Ling have asked how victims can navigate the various laws, and whether they would need to make multiple reports when seeking help for online harms.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Gabriel Lam and Ms Elysa Chen raised the need for clear processes and guidance on how victims can approach the various agencies like the Police, IMDA and the OSC.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This means that regardless of which agency a victim first approaches, they will be guided on the appropriate help.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I also take Mr David Hoe’s point that the process of online harm reporting should be kept simple and accessible.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We will bear this in mind as we refine the OSC’s operational details.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Some Members have also asked about the scope of the harms covered by the OSRA Bill.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling raised the point that victim’s exposure to online harms may be prolonged if we are unclear about what constitutes online harms in the OSRA Bill.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: With the OSRA Bill, we sought to clearly capture the key characteristics of each harm.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: To aid public understanding, explanatory notes and illustrations are included, where appropriate.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I would also like to refer Members to Handout 4, which gives further illustrative examples.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: While we have given definitions for each of these harms in the OSRA Bill, the OSC will assess each case based on its unique context and facts.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I think Members would know that no two types of online harm will be the same.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Some flexibility must be accorded to the OSC to act according to the harm concerned.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Ms He Ting Ru suggested that we consider including sexual grooming and the publication of online material that encourages or promotes suicide or acts of self-injury as specified online harms that OSRA covers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We agree with the Member that these are egregious harms, and I have explained why these harms would be better addressed through other legislation in our online safety framework.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Such content includes child sexual exploitation material and content advocating or instructing on suicide or self-harm.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: If such online content is connected to the commission of criminal offences, action can be taken under the Penal Code or Online Criminal Harms Act.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: If sexual grooming is displayed through online harassment or stalking conduct, the victim will have recourse to seek directions from the OSC.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For the victim, who is under 18 years old, a parent or guardian can make a report on their behalf.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: On the suggestion to add "fair comment" exception to online harassment and public interest exception to the harms of non-consensual disclosure of private information and online instigation of disproportionate harm, I would like to highlight to Members that these factors will be taken into consideration as the Commissioner assesses each case.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: If we included the suggestions and make them exceptions to the online harms, communication that meets the "fair comment" or "public interest" criterion will automatically not be actionable by the OSC.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In comparison, the current formulation allows the OSC to consider a basket of factors when deciding whether to issue directions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This allows the OSC to weigh whether something counts as "fair comment" or "public interest", while also considering the features of the post, and not immediately say it cannot act.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, if a member of a public raises in good faith or exposes serious wrongdoing, this will be taken into account as part of OSC's case assessment.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We should not pre-emptively restrict the OSC from considering any one factor.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Leader of the Opposition, Mr Pritam Singh, and Mr Ng Shi Xuan sought clarity on what would be considered private information.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Ng has asked whether the harm of non-consensual disclosure of private information would cover information such as sexual orientation and gender identity.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As we implement this harm in future, the Minister may issue regulations to clarify the types of information that is or is not private information.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Ms Mariam Jaafar highlighted the need for the OSRA Bill to be technology-neutral and future-ready to deal with harms generated by algorithms and AI.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I wish to assure the Member that the 13 harms under the OSRA Bill are generally technology-neutral.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As shared in Handout 4, if person D uses an application to digitally alter an image of person C fully clothed into a nude image and posts it online without consent, that would be intimate image abuse.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We recognise that online harms are constantly evolving, and new harms may emerge over time, especially with the proliferation of new technologies.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The OSRA Bill allows the Minister to prescribe additional types of online activity that are likely to cause harm to persons in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We will continuously review the online landscape and expand the list of harms, if there is a need to, in future.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For the harm of “inauthentic material abuse”, Ms Cassandra Lee asked for clarity on how "likeness" would be assessed in the context of AI-generated content and whether there needs to be intent to mislead.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The OSC will assess based on objective standards whether the content is a false or misleading depiction of the victim’s words, actions or conduct; and if it is realistic enough such that a reasonable person would believe that the victim said such words or did such actions or conduct.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Such content may cross the thresholds of likely to cause the victim harassment, alarm, distress or humiliation, even if there was no intent to mislead.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Ms Elysa Chen asked about how the harm of "publication of statement harmful to reputation" interacts with defamation under common law.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This enables a victim to put out their reply or their side of the story quickly in order to protect their reputation, which matters especially in the online world where allegations spread with great speed and ease.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We see this as a complementary pathway for the victim, that may be an alternative to, or concurrent with, a defamation suit.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: A victim may find sufficient relief in a Right-of-Reply Direction, that they no longer need to resort to a defamation suit.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Or, they may still need or want to sue, for example to seek monetary damages.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In either case, putting their reply out helps to limit the damages suffered.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Ms Elysa Chen asked how the OSC would ascertain disproportionality in the case of "online instigation of disproportionate harm" (OIDH) and if there will be guidelines published for what constitutes disproportionate harm.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As illustrated in Handout 4, disproportionate harm can take on various forms, such as physical harm.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The Bill currently lists non-exhaustive factors that the OSC may consider when assessing the requirement of disproportionality, such as whether the act instigated is or is likely to constitute a criminal offence and the nature and severity of the harm mentioned.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The OIDH framework does not mean that members of public can no longer call out certain problematic behaviours, or express views on issues of public interest.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Even as we reject mob behaviour, we continue to uphold the principle that there must be space for online discussions, within the bounds of civility and respect.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Some Members, including Ms Valerie Lee and Ms Elysa Chen and Ms Eileen Chong, asked about the set-up and composition of the OSC.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The appointed Commissioner for Online Safety will be someone of suitable seniority and experience.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We will also ensure that the OSC is appropriately staffed with individuals that have the relevant experience and expertise, and have a good understanding of our society and online norms, so as to address reports as they come in.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Henry Kwek and Ms He Ting Ru asked about training for OSC officers and if the OSC will be working with community partners to support victims of online harms who need psychological and legal support.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: They will also refer victims requiring further support beyond the mitigation of an online harm to community partners.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr David Hoe suggested having a standing advisory group of relevant practitioners to provide guidance on online harms periodically.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Under the OSRA Bill, the Commissioner is empowered to consult with any person that the Commissioner thinks appropriate, for the purposes of performing the Commissioner's functions and duties.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This could include the relevant experts and practitioners in the field of online safety.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We also took into account Singaporeans' Internet-use practices, such as the time spent online.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Depending on the volume of the cases, we will calibrate and reallocate resources, as necessary, to resource and size OSC adequately.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Cai Yinzhou asked about the rules that will govern how the OSC carries out its investigations to determine further action.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Each case will be assessed based on the nature and severity of the harm, and investigations will be carried out fairly, working with the relevant agencies to determine the appropriate follow-up actions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The relevant parties will be notified at the appropriate junctures, as the OSRA Bill accords the OSC powers to require documents or information and to examine and secure attendance of persons for investigations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Overall, the focus will be to ensure that the victims are not denied timely relief, even as we accord due process to all involved.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Foo Cexiang also proposed expanding OSC's powers, such as by giving its officers powers under the Criminal Procedure Code.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The scope and nature of every law is different; hence the respective officers are accorded different powers to ensure they are fit-for-purpose.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In considering how OSC might conduct investigations in various scenarios, such as investigating reports to determine whether to issue a direction or offences under OSRA, we had accorded OSC the appropriate powers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: On the suggestion for the Commissioner to submit an annual report to Parliament, the OSC will consider publishing regular reports on its website for public awareness on online harms and the OSC's work.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The OSC will require time to assess what and how to put up information that would complement its processes, as it gradually stands up its operations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We are, therefore, taking a more adaptive approach towards the OSC's publication of reports, as opposed to legislating this as a requirement.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The regular reports may include information on aggregated caseloads and anonymised case information, insofar as these do not re-traumatise victims.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Members are also welcomed to file Parliamentary Questions to request such information, if it is not already published in the public domain.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: On the suggestion for the OSRA Bill to require platforms to publish annual reports on their measures to enable users to seek recourse from harm and response times, among others.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I would inform Members that under the Code of Practice for Online Safety – Social Media Services, designated social media services (DSMSs) with significant reach or impact in Singapore are already required to submit annual reports to be published on IMDA's website.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: These reports contain information on the DSMSs' measures to combat harmful and inappropriate content, and metrics, such as number of reports received from users, as well as the DSMSs' response time to act on these reports.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: IMDA also publishes an Online Safety Assessment Report.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We will continue to drive the point on platforms' accountability through the OSRA Bill.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: On the phased implementation of OSC's reporting mechanism, Mr Sharael Taha, Ms Yeo Wan Ling and Dr Choo Pei Ling asked about the timeline for introducing remaining categories of harm.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Sharael Taha and Ms Yeo Wan Ling also asked what happens when a victim experiences a form of harm covered only in a later phase.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: A phased implementation approach is necessary so that OSC builds its capabilities in a sustainable and scalable way, focusing the right level of attention to each case, to ensure a positive user journey.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It will also manage the OSC's caseload, allow officers to properly develop the necessary guidelines and frameworks, to ensure that the OSC's decisions are consistent and appropriate.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: If victims write in to the OSC regarding their experience of a specified online harm that is not covered in the first phase, officers will, nevertheless, guide the victims on the appropriate process.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This could be making a report to the platforms, filing a Police report or reaching out to community partners for support.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Ms Cassandra Lee asked about measures to safeguard victims' confidentiality during the reporting process.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I assure Members that all victims' reports will be stored securely, and the agency will adopt practices to ensure victims and all other parties involved are treated with sensitivity and care.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We have also built-in legislative safeguards on preservation of secrecy.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Any information published for public education and awareness will be in an anonymised form.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Members, including Dr Choo Pei Ling and Mr Alex Yeo, sought clarifications on who can or cannot file reports to OSC.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Dr Wan Rizal asked about the process for unions and professional bodies to file a report on behalf of their members.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Where the victim is under 18, their parent or guardian can file a report on their behalf.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Andre Low and Mr Pritam Singh asked for clarity regarding those with a prescribed connection to Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I mentioned in my opening speech that we intend to prescribe foreigners who stay in Singapore for the long term.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For a start, this would include foreign spouses who are in Singapore on a Long-Term Visit Pass.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We are still studying the full scope and will share more details in due course.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Ng Shi Xuan and Mr Alex Yeo had suggested for OSC to take differentiated approaches between groups of victims.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For a start, the response time will likely be shorter for more severe harms.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling and Ms Yeo Wan Ling asked about the measures to prevent devious characters from submitting vexatious reports or weaponising the OSC reporting mechanism.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Dr Choo Pei Ling also asked how OSC can minimise mischief reports.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Those submitting a report will have to explain how the content or conduct is a specified online harmful activity and be required to declare that the information that they have provided is true.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Submitting false information to the OSC will be an offence.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: If these complainants persistently make such reports, the OSC will also not consider any further reports from them.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This would allow the OSC to focus its time and resources to the real victims who need redress.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: On the OSC's assessment of reports, Mr Sharael Taha asked how the threshold for online harassment will be determined; Mr Andre Low asked whether victims who publish identity information of their harasser would be caught under doxxing; Mr Low and Ms Eileen Chong also asked about consistency in the OSC' decisions; and Mr Pritam Singh sought clarifications on the information that OSC will share at the reconsideration stage.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As drafted in the OSRA Bill, OSC will take an objective approach when assessing reports, and the thresholds for online harms are based on objective standards.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: While each case will be fact-specific, the "reasonable person" test is a well-established legal standard, including in tort and criminal law.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The question will not be whether someone personally feels offended, but whether OSC has reason to suspect that online harmful activity was conducted, before issuing a direction.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Members discussed the thresholds of "reasonable grounds to believe" versus "reason to suspect".

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: First, that "reason to suspect" is an established legal threshold that applies in other legislation, such as the Online Criminal Harms Act.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Second, we have assessed this threshold to be appropriate to meet the intent of ensuring that online harms can be stopped in a timely manner.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As mentioned in my opening speech, the OSC will also publish guidelines that will inform its decisions to ensure consistency and objectivity.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: These guidelines will inform the public on the factors that the Commissioner will take into account for present and future cases.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Victims and recipients of OSC's directions will be able to seek OSC's reconsideration if they disagree with it, and appeal to an independent Appeal Committee thereafter.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Ms Cassandra Lee asked about the requirement for victims to file reports to the platforms first before the OSC.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We believe the platforms should be the first port of call or, as Dr Wan Rizal put it, "first responders".

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: They have a duty to protect their users, and the statutory torts will make this clear, especially when notified by the users of harms on their service.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The OSC will continue to work closely with the platforms to ensure that they comply with directions in a timely manner.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr David Hoe, Ms Yeo Wan Ling, Ms Lee Hui Ying and Ms Mariam Jaafar raised broader points on platforms' design and accountability to prevent online harms, beyond OSRA and the OSC.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In this regard, we will also continue working with the major platforms to ensure that they strengthen their online safety measures.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: That said, we recognise that some harms are simply so serious or urgent that they warrant immediate intervention.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Ms Valerie Lee asked for clarification on the categories of online harm that will be prioritised for urgent attention.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For a start, victims can file a report directly to the OSC for the following harms: image-based child abuse, intimate image abuse and doxxing.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In such cases, speed is of the essence to minimise the harm that may be caused to the victims.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Several Members of Parliament, like Mr Ng Shi Xuan, Dr Wan Rizal, Mr Sharael Taha, Mr Cai Yinzhou and Ms Yeo Wan Ling, have asked or spoken about the OSC's service benchmarks to respond to and resolve cases.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr David Hoe also suggested laying out the operational process clearly, so victims are aware of the actions to be taken.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We want to ensure that victims get the help they need, as soon as possible.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Practically, some cases may be more easily resolved than others; for example, it may be easier to make out if the harm of intimate image abuse is present, as compared to a report on online harassment.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For the latter, the OSC officer will have to go through the details more carefully, to understand the nature and the severity of the case.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Ms Valerie Lee asked whether the Commissioner will be required to conduct a preliminary assessment before issuing directions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: OSC will assess if it has reason to suspect that online harmful activity was conducted before issuing a direction.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: To recap, the Commissioner will be empowered to issue directions to stop online harms from continuing to occur or to prevent further online harms from affecting the victim, where there is reason to suspect that the online harm was conducted in respect of the victim or the victim group.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Andre Low raised a few clarifications on specific directions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Low had asked about the scenarios where Engagement Reduction Directions should be considered.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The intent for such a direction would be to stem the virality of online harms, which can spread quickly through similar posts.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Second, Mr Low also asked about potential overreach when the OSC issues a Stop Communication (Class of Material) Direction.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This direction protects victims from floods of harmful content, sharing common identifiers, such as a coordinated harassment campaign.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Rather than requiring the Commissioner to identify each harmful post individually, the direction covers all such content in proportion to the scale of the harm occurring.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Ng Shi Xuan raised the need to keep the playing field level for smaller platforms.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We recognise that we must take a pragmatic approach when engaging the platforms on compliance with directions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This is why we intend to engage online platforms with significant reach or impact first, noting that the harms on such platforms have the potential to travel further and faster.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Such platforms would also have the technical capabilities to implement more complex directions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Sharael Taha asked what qualifies as an online service provider and whether the term extends to closed or encrypted platforms, such as WhatsApp, Telegram and WeChat.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: He and Dr Choo Pei Ling also ask how the Bill would deal with cases arising from private or semi-private chat groups.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: While we have no intentions to proactively intervene in private communications, I believe Members know how quickly something harmful can spread via private messages or in online chat groups.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For all harms except incitement of enmity, if a victim files a report to OSC and brings its attention to the specified online harms made via private communications, the OSC can then assess the case.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I refer Members to the example case given for intimate image abuse in Handout 4.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Here, B posts an intimate image of A in an online chat group, without A’s consent.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In such a case, the OSC can issue a Stop Communication Direction to the administrator of the group to remove B’s post.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: If this online chat group continues to circulate A’s intimate image on subsequent occasions, or intimate images of other persons, if made aware, the OSC could also consider an Access Disabling Direction to the platform whose service the chat group is maintained on.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This will disable access to the chat group for Singapore users.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Next, Members sought clarifications on the OSC's reconsideration and appeal processes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Zhulkarnain urged caution against allowing extensive appellate processes that risk re-traumatising victims.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We are still working through the implementation of the Appeal Committee, including its powers to affirm, revoke, vary or substitute a reconsidered decision by the OSC.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: But I want to assure the public that each case will be given the necessary time and due consideration.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Ms Elysa Chen would also be assured to know that it is possible for persons who are still dissatisfied with the decision of the Appeal Committee to seek to challenge it in the Courts by way of judicial review.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We will provide more details on the appeal process at the later stage.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Ms Elysa Chen and Mr Foo Cexiang asked how the OSC will take enforcement action against bad actors who are overseas, noting the added complexity that technology like VPNs brings.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Ms Lee Hui Ying and Mr Henry Kwek also asked how we would ensure that transnational or cross-border online platforms comply with OSRA directions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This applies as long as the harmful content is communicated in Singapore or accessible by users in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The issuance of these escalatory measures will be carefully considered and used judiciously.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Lastly, the use of VPNs to circumvent restrictions and detection affects all Internet laws and regulations, including the OSRA Bill.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We will have to take a practical approach and do our best to deal with those within the bounds of our law.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Foo Cexiang asked whether the penalties prescribed under OSRA are adequate.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Dr Choo Pei Ling also suggested increasing the maximum penalties.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The Bill sets out maximum penalties for non-compliance with OSC's directions and orders.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: These were determined with reference to similar offences already on the books, such as the Online Criminal Harms Act, the Foreign Interference (Countermeasures) Act, the Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Act and the Broadcasting Act, because these are statutes that have directions similar to the OSC's directions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: You will see that while there are similarities, the penalties are not exactly the same because we have calibrated it against the different purposes of these laws, and the gravity of the situations that would usually give rise to non-compliance.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Foo also asked if guidance could be given on how the Courts should sentence.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Sentencing is a multifactorial exercise and highly context-specific.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It is a matter for the Courts to decide in applying general sentencing principles, with the benefit of submissions by the prosecution and the defence.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The Court would generally treat the maximum penalty in legislation as representing the appropriate sentence for the most serious form of the offence and calibrate accordingly for the case before it.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This can be adjusted in view of aggravating factors, such as defiant conduct, and mitigating factors, like being a first-time offender.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Ms Mariam Jaafar suggested incorporating digital literacy or restorative programmes, especially for younger offenders.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Ms He Ting Ru also asked whether perpetrators could be issues counselling orders to stop them from reoffending.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We agree with the Members that, in some cases, rehabilitation may be the more appropriate action than prosecution.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This may be taken into account when deciding whether to prosecute a person for non-compliance with the OSC's directions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Sharael Taha, Mr Cai Yinzhou and Mr Henry Kwek suggested ways that the OSC can work with partners in the public and people sector to strengthen victim care and support.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Dr Wan Rizal asked whether practical guidelines will be issued to schools, hospitals and care agencies on how to activate the OSC’s remedies.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Better support for victims of online harms is at the heart of what this Bill serves to do.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Should they require further support as they cope with an incident, OSC will refer cases to its appropriate partners.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: One such partner is SHE, who partners with the Singapore Council of Women's Organisations (SCWO) to run SHECARES@SCWO.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The centre is supported by full time counsellors and volunteers, and offers pro bono legal clinics with the support of Pro Bono SG.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Gabriel Lam, Ms Valerie Lee, Ms Tin Pei Ling and Ms Eileen Chong have highlighted the importance of public education in the promotion of responsible online behaviour.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Pritam Singh also asked about outreach and preventive education programmes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As Ms Tin Pei Ling said, social norms and education matter.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In collaboration with community, industry and corporate partners, more ground-up initiatives, such as workshops and webinars, will be organised to foster healthy digital habits and raise awareness of key online safety and digital well-being issues.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: These efforts will equip Singaporeans with practical skills and knowledge to navigate the online space safely and responsibly, and empower them to support others in their communities.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It complements our existing measures to address various harmful online content.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Second, the OSC will provide timely redress for victims of online harms.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This will be done in calibrated manner, starting with most severe and prevalent harms.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Third, the OSRA Bill will strike a balance between protecting victims from online harms, while preserving space for healthy discourse.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The road ahead will bring its share of challenges, but also opportunities to make a real difference.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I seek Members' support for the office of the Commissioner of Online Safety, and your understanding as we refine the details of OSC’s implementation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We are committed to doing right by victims of online harms and to do so in good time, with care.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I urge all Members to support this Bill.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Together, we can foster positive norms of online behaviour, such that Singaporeans can go online safely and confidently.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I also thank all Members who have spoken in support of the Bill and for their thoughtful contributions to this very important debate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I am very heartened to see that actually we are on very common ground, not just in our thoughts and in the way in which we want to advance the Bill and the work of the OSC, but also in our views and in our values on what this means to society.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I think, ultimately, after almost eight hours, I think we are not really disagreeing on much.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I found speeches on both sides of the House thoughtful, with good suggestions, and even if we are not able to take them onboard today, I think, they will be relevant for future iterations of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Members have raised a number of questions, in fact, many questions, and I thought I will take them thematically, as Minister of State Rahayu Mahzam has done.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But I beg your indulgence, that I am not going to be able to respond to every Member’s specific questions, nor I suspect would you want me to.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But let me quickly recap the fundamentals of what this Bill seeks to achieve to set it in perspective.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The law on torts itself is not new.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is established and the jurisprudence is well-established, but to allow victims, individuals, to avail themselves of that framework is something that is new and novel.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In many ways, this has democratised relief for victims.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And as I respond to questions, I would like to say that I hope we can keep it that way because it is a key design feature, as I said at the outset, for this Bill to be speedy, to be efficacious and to allow there to be a low barrier to getting the relief obtained.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I think we would like to keep it that way as far as possible.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I like the way in which Mr Sharael Taha and Mr Xie Yao Quan put it – give it space to grow up, build up and let it take off.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I think that is exactly what we would like to see it do.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Many Members' spoke about the Statutory Torts Framework, and I will respond to this as much as I can.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Courts have contended with issues of establishing liability, quantifying damages and enforcing judgments for as long as the law of torts has existed, and it is not going to be a novel area in which they look at the way you assess breach of duty, the way in which you assess proof of damages and also whether the damage is foreseeable or too remote.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But I think the speeches have put the different issues that are at tension with one another into perspective.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On one hand, Ms Elysa Chen made a very thoughtful speech and cautioned against over-censorship – that administrators and platforms might then remove content too readily.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On the other hand, Mr Henry Kwek said, we should be careful not to allow this to be weaponised.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ms He Ting Ru also said that over-censorship is already happening today.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: People today are already, in some cases, withdrawing from social media entirely.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, you can see the tension, pulling in different directions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: What this Bill tries to do is to set up a framework that allows individual relief but also one which allows you to go to a third party, in this case, the OSC, for quick relief by a regulator.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On top of that, I want to also emphasise that this Bill is, however, not intended to remove discourse.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: You take, for example, the Explanatory Statement on Incitement of Enmity.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: You will see in there that we have specifically provided in the Explanatory Statement that when you have statements that express an opinion, you are free to do so, even if they may be an opinion on the law or on Government policy.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That alone, an opinion, is not something that would fall foul of the provisions of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Neither is expressing a person's belief or the practices of a group of persons inconsistent with another set of beliefs, something, that will fall foul of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: You are entitled to your views, expressing your opinion and pursuing discourse as much as you can, as long as you keep to ensuring that you do not fall into one of the buckets of online harms.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To do this, we have carefully calibrated the Statutory Torts Framework, and I thought I would just reiterate in my answer to Members' questions on how this framework is designed to work.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, we are dealing with online harms with a clearly defined threshold.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There is a formula that is set out in the Bill and in respect of all online harms, the OSC must make an assessment, and the Statutory Torts Framework must reach that standard.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Those are the duties that are set out in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: You must fall below those duties before it becomes actionable.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, there is a threshold that is fairly clear-cut.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In fact, many of them, you will find that these standards are not inconsistent with what the platforms self-profess to be their standards as well.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is not the design architecture of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: When there is an online harm, OSC determines it.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It then makes one of the directions as may be appropriate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It seeks to compensate a victim, sometimes for loss of earnings, sometimes for distress, but it is compensatory in nature, by and large.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And to Mr Henry Kwek's question, the courts will know when a case is frivolous or taken on trivial or unmeritorious grounds.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There are ways in which we can stop a vexatious litigant.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We designed that framework because we do not expect the platforms to trawl the Internet or trawl social media to look out for these harms.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But once you get a notice, then that duty arises and you then have to act in a manner in which the duty would be commensurate with the remedy.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In that situation, unless you have some other reason why you cannot do that very quickly, then otherwise, we expect the timeframe to be much shorter.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In other situations where you might take a bit more time to comply with the order and some steps might be taken, or you might have to make some enquiries or there are some technological issues or challenges, then the framework that we have for "reasonable" allows the Court to take all that into account.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And so, it is not a single standard.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We are not able to say it must be X number of days in every case, but "reasonable" in the context of the particular circumstances of that case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Fifth, we will prescribe the contents and mode of service of these notices.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I know many Members have talked about whether it is going to be difficult to fill up, or is it going to be something that we will have to go back and forth with the platforms.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The answer is, as far as we can, we will prescribe the contents and the way in which we will do service of these notices so that you have, almost like a fixed framework of information that you will have to provide.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And once the platforms receive it, they will have to respond to this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I know what the hon Member Ms Chen said about how there might be an over-reaction.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Platforms might then be a bit more cautious when dealing with online harms.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That with these frameworks, for the platforms, the administrators, the communicators, there is a pause for thought, to think about whether an item crosses the threshold or not and whether you should be doing it.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think that is the kind of mindset that we hope to build – for everyone to be a little bit more cautious, not self-censor in the way which I have told you.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But to have a care, to think about it one more time whether that is something that passes muster for online harms.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I think if they have to take a second look and thereby improve protections for users and for potential victims, then I think we have achieved something.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr David Hoe, Mr Sharael Taha, Ms Lee Hui Ying and Ms He Ting Ru observed that some claimants might lack the means to pursue a claim.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have introduced this now as an additional avenue for our victims to pursue this claim.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Previously, on whatever resources you might have, it was not possible.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But today, you now have an additional framework.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will always, in the context of how we discuss and enhance access to justice, we will have people who fall at the margins and may not be able to be well-resourced enough to pursue the claim.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In those cases, my Ministry, MinLaw, will continue to work on Access to Justice principles to ensure that those who deserve assistance, whether through Legal Aid with the usual means and merits test, or Pro Bono SG or the Community Law Centres, or various other legal clinics or pro bono schemes around Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will continue to support these schemes and ensure that those who are at the end of the spectrum, who are unable to have resources to pursue their own claim, will not be left by the wayside.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In many ways, that is just as an aside, that is precisely why we have also created the OSC framework – that it is simple, really cost-efficient and fast.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: You do not have to pursue a claim in Court to get the immediate relief of having the takedown or right-of-response or any other of the measures that OSC can prescribe.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I note that Ms He Ting Ru talked about the prospect of engaging in court proceedings will be daunting for victims and asked what simplified processes could be introduced.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But the points are taken, and we will see whether there is a way in which we can introduce a simplified framework and process that will be able to handle these cases, particularly the simpler ones, much quicker and much more cost-efficient.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr David Hoe suggested that it should be easy for victims to send "online harm notices" to them and avoid unnecessary information.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will also be working with the platforms to ensure that the process is straightforward and accessible.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, we will be designing this process with them in mind.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They will tell us what is it that they need to identify the harm appropriately and we will work with them as well to design this into the information that will be needed to trigger the process with the platforms.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr David Hoe and I think Ms Cassandra Lee asked whether non-monetary damages or losses can be considered under the Bill's framework, the Statutory Torts Framework.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Of course, the usual tortious principles, as I outlined earlier, will have to apply: is it foreseeable?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ms Cassandra Lee asked if the identifying information of victims who commence civil proceedings can be automatically redacted.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I would say that, whilst redaction is appropriate in some cases, there will also be many where it would not be.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I think you got to put it in context.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: You are now having to face a civil suit, and you have to understand and know who is bringing the claim.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And so, in most cases, I think that would not be the case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And once an assessment has to be made as to whether it is appropriate, then, an automatic reduction upfront would not be suitable for this scheme.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Ng Shi Xuan and Ms Tin Pei Ling asked for clarification on how the Statutory Torts Framework in OSRA might interact with that in POHA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Victims of harassment, doxxing and stalking should continue to sue the communicator or bring action under POHA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Harassment, doxxing and stalking under POHA all have offline dimensions to it as well, which continue to call for protection and it is, therefore, necessary to preserve this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: OSRA deals with online harms, so, we thought it will be more expedient and better coverage to not subsume that under OSRA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Ng also suggested that guidance be issued to help parties understand the interaction.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I noted what the hon Member said, having a healthy online culture and I think that is what we would like to promote.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The OSC and the Courts provide complementary avenues for victims to obtain protection from online harms.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Some Members asked what happens if there are inconsistencies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In most cases, victims will want to use the OSC's directions at the first instance.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I said, it is quick, fast and swift relief.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, you might need to seek an injunction from the Courts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Like OSC's directions, injunctions are also intended to be quick and can protect the victim.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But for tort claims, the claims in Court, it seeks to impose a civil liability on the other party.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And so, for these reasons, the Courts are better placed to address such cases, which sometimes will need a more complex evaluation of the evidential positions on both sides and also considering the legal position and the arguments of parties.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Henry Kwek asked what happens if the OSC and the Courts take a different view on whether an online harm occurred.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The former is an administrative decision by an agency, and the latter is a matter of law decided by the Judiciary.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But the OSC may take the Court's decision, and after a while, a body of case law and jurisprudence into account.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Nothing to stop the OSC from having regard to the body of jurisprudence over time, developed as a result of this framework.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And the OSC is empowered to also revisit past decisions and to vary or cancel them to the extent relevant or appropriate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Andre Low asked whether the OSC would be bound by Minister's clarifications made in the House today.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ms Valerie Lee asked whether the Right-of-Reply Directions which OSC may issue are intended to complement civil remedies for defamation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The short answer is yes, and it is because they serve different purposes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Currently, a successful claim in defamation provides compensation for reputational loss.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But as I said at the outset, not all victims want that financial compensation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They do not want just to go to court for monetary compensation, and we have learned this from many consultations from the stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But the Court may consider the claimant's duty to mitigate loss and if an avenue is available for you to have a right of reply and you do not trigger that for good reason, then, that might be taken into account as part of the claimant's duty to mitigate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Several Members asked questions about the balance between the desire to ensure accountability of wrongdoers and the need to safeguard personal information.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In my opening speech, I covered the safeguards to ensure that information disclosed is not misused.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The OSC may impose any condition in disclosing the information, including limiting the use of the information to the approved purpose.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Further, any misuse of information may be an actionable wrong in itself.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, for example, if the victim uses the information to dox the perpetrator, that may be an offence under POHA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It may also be an offence under OSRA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These safeguards would protect the information disclosed and prevent misuse.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The foregoing answers the questions of Dr Wan Rizal, Mr Henry Kwek and Ms Mariam Jaafar.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Henry Kuek also asked about the OSC's directions under the End- User Identification measures and how they interact with PDPA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ms Eileen Chong also asked, I think, similar questions on the End-User Identification.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Apart from what I have just said, I would like to refer to clause 53, which allows conditions by the OSC to be set in the course of providing information.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I know the hon Member Ms Chong said that these proposals have, and I quote the Member, "real value", and I thank her for that; but that giving information to the victim is a "one-way door".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But likewise, posting an online harm to the world, is also a "one-way door".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And so, the question for us really is, with most of the issues in this Bill, is to grapple with the right balance to be struck.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On the one hand, you have information or a post to the world that is harmful.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Without the identity, you cannot pursue the action and also ensure that the information is not used in a collateral way.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Henry Kwek noted that some anonymous perpetrators may abandon their account when a platform subsequently, after finding out that there is an online harm, attempts to collect their identity through the Collection Notice.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In such cases, the reality is that their information will then not be collected and both OSC and victims will, then, not be able to identify the perpetrator.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But we did consider what the alternative would be.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The alternative would be to require all platforms to collect all information upfront, regardless of whether or not anyone has conducted online harm.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I said at the outset, the vast majority of users will not fall in that category.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, it will inconvenience and in some cases, perhaps, add an additional hurdle, and there is also a burden on platforms.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We know that, with doing that, there is a real risk, that in some cases they will just abandon.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But at the very least, with the provisions that OSC has under this Bill, OSC will be able to take action to deal with the harm being continued online.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I would just want to address Mr Low's point about clause 4.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think he raised a point about clause 4.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The general position in law is that the Government is not bound by legislation unless it provides expressly for that to be so.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Minister Edwin Tong and Minister of State Rahayu have responded to all of your comments comprehensively.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The first observation is that Members agree no one should be beyond accountability when their actions harm others.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Mariam Jaafar was most emphatic about it.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The stories shared by Members today illustrate the mental toll that victims of online harms experience.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They are visceral and emotional, and it is why it is so important to help victims get closure through restitution.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It goes to the heart of the OSC's mission to provide timely, effective and accessible relief for victims of online harms.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: My second observation, Sir, is that Members recognise the complexity and tensions within the online sphere.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Online interactions and the nuances of harmful activities can shift and evolve rapidly.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: No two cases of online harms will be the same.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Every hour that passes by makes a difference to victims.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is why the OSC's work will be very challenging.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Xie Yao Quan posits that it will also be voluminous.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Government has explained how the OSC's processes strike a balance between speed and due process, efficiency and effectiveness.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As much as possible, we will rely on clear criteria for action.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will also provide avenues for independent review of decisions so that outcomes are consistent and fair.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The OSC will not be undertaking this work alone.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have regularly worked together with our network of partners.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Many have been on this journey with us since the beginning.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Bill, itself, has been years in the making.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: At every stage, local community organisations and advocates provided valuable insights that shaped our approach.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Feedback from industry stakeholders further refined our framework.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I am heartened they see Singapore as a determined, yet pragmatic regulator.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I also hope they will continue to actively contribute to improving online safety.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The OSC will draw upon the extensive experience and expertise of our partners.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is essential to how we navigate the evolving digital landscape.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It will also help us improve our practices and stay responsive to victims' needs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: My third observation is that Members agree the OSC must earn the trust of Singaporeans that it is effective and impartial.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There are different thresholds for acting on online harmful activities that may occur.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Commissioner and the OSC have the delicate job of assessing reports and issuing directions on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We need to consider, for example, that what causes distress to a child may not be distressing to an adult.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Sharael Taha, Ms Eileen Chong, Ms Elysa Chen and Mr Alex Yeo have rightly pointed these out.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We may adopt a victim-led approach to filing reports, but OSC will need clear guidelines, adequate oversight and accountability mechanisms.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is so that all parties, whether victims, alleged perpetrators, platforms and administrators know that the OSC makes its assessment based on objective criteria.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The OSC's directions should only go so far to protect any immediate or further harm to victims.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It should not be seen to be taking the side of one party over another.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is important, whether or not political personalities are involved.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Trust in the OSC's objectivity and fairness will be critical to its success.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Clear definitions of each harm have been provided in the Bill, supported by explanatory notes and illustrations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Alex Yeo and Mr Foo Cexiang acknowledged and agree with this approach.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The transparency also ensures that the OSC's decisions can be held to clear standards.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is a necessary safeguard for fairness and consistency.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I hope these assurances address Ms Chong's concerns on the independence of the Commissioner.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To Mr Pritam Singh's question on the use of Ministerial Directions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: An example of a type of direction that may be provided for is on resource prioritisation for the Office of the Commissioner of Online Safety.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: At this juncture, let me also thank Ms He Ting Ru for her proposed amendments to the Bill.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Over the years, many Members of Parliament have given suggestions on strengthening online safety for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I spoke about this when I opened the debate.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As with all well-intentioned suggestions, the Government's approach is to review them carefully and rationally.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Minister of State Rahayu and Minister Edwin have comprehensively addressed why the amendments filed by Ms He are either already provided for in the Bill or could inadvertently limit the work of the OSC in providing relief for the victims.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For instance, we agree that public interest is an important factor.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Under the pretext of public interest, these bad actors can continue to undermine victims' recourse.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To be clear, the Government has no disagreement with the intent behind Ms He's amendments.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will also operationalise the law in the same spirit.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But as with any law, we must strike a careful balance between being specific to make the law clear and operable, and being too specific as to inadvertently make the law less effective.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: MDDI and MinLaw have tried to get this balance right.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We welcome the Workers' Party's (WP's) shared interest in ensuring that OSC is well-positioned to achieve its objectives.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We all want better support for victims of online harms.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I hope Members will agree that our priority is to allow OSC to focus on building its capabilities, clarifying its policies and cultivating its partnerships.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It will take time and things may not work perfectly at first but, step by step, we will get it right.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: We disagree that these changes will cause the protection regime to be problematic or toothless.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Nevertheless, I am grateful that we have had the chance to have a debate on these important issues and to the officeholders who have provided substantial clarifications.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I think we all agree that the legislation covering online harms is very much something that will need continued review, refinement and development as the scale and nature of online harm shifts alongside changes in technology in our society.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: As I stated earlier, both these categories were also rated by respondents as the most egregious of harms and, thus, we believe that they should be explicitly covered.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Regardless, IMDA should work with the new agency under the Bill and study the types of reports received, emerging trends and effectiveness of the Broadcasting Act.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: We believe that victims should more appropriately lodge a report to OSC, not IMDA, to seek redress, and for OSC to issue directions and orders fast.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Additionally, the Broadcasting Act is more of a governance for entities which does not provide recourse for victims.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Also, I believe that the new agency's powers are wider and contain more remedies that will be available to victims.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Thus, will the Minister of State clarify how our concerns outlined above will be addressed?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As I have explained in my opening speech as well as my response, the nature of this particular Bill is really victim-led and in the manner in which there are certain specified online harms that are created as a result of that interaction online.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In the case of sexual grooming, for example, as explained, if the victim realises that he or she is affected and there are actions that are causing harassment, alarm, distress or humiliation and there is content for OSC to act upon, we can act upon it.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, it is the nature in which you are describing that action, because sexual grooming in itself is a whole transaction and it is a crime that can be dealt with better under the Penal Code.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: With regard to the materials that are online, again, if the materials are something that is causing harassment, distress, alarm and humiliation to the victim, that person can file to OSC and we will address it.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, it is really a function of whether the victim sees a particular content that is triggering certain characteristics pursuant to this Bill, they can pursue it through OSC.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, in the event some of these issues are raised to OSC, OSC will assess it and make appropriate references to make sure that the appropriate help is given to the victims.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre
text: Speaker, my clarification is directed to Minister of State Rahayu.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre
text: I just have a quick clarification to make.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre
text: In addressing a point made by hon Member Ms Elysa Chen, I believe Minister of State stated that, "Ms Chen would also be assured to know that it is still possible for persons who are still dissatisfied with the decisions of the Appeal Committee to seek to challenge it in the Courts by way of judicial review.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I am assuming this will be to Minister Tong.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: On one of the clarifications that I had sought – I thank the Minister for addressing a number of those that I had put out.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The point about the Online Criminal Harms Act, a sister legislation; and the implementation direction that the Government had issued to Facebook on their measures against scams, I think they had a timeline: first, end of September; then, end of October.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I asked that question, actually, not specific to that, but just to have a better understanding of how the platforms will respond to the Bill the Government seeks to pass today.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: As an example, Handout 2 states the platform – a victim will essentially go to the platform at first instance, except in a few different circumstances, and these pertain to intimate image abuse, doxxing, image-based child abuse – that one you go straight to OSC.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think this aspect of it is really the substance of that particular clarification, where I sought to understand how promptly and the extent to which the social media platforms would be able to comply.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I understand where the Leader of the Opposition is coming from.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I will not provide information on the first question because that is not the subject of OSRA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But I think on your more general point, the question really is this – two points.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, as I mentioned, we did have extensive consultations, including with the platforms.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The idea here is obviously we do not want to devise a framework in a scheme that will be unworkable and inoperable, practically speaking, so we have been consulting with them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I mean, if truth be told, you start from a blank canvas and you ask the platforms, would they want to see a Bill like this?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The answer probably is, no, if they had a choice.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But we were quite determined to ensure that there would be a Bill of this nature, and a Bill of this nature would not have the teeth if it did not involve the platforms and have powers over the platforms, and I think they quickly understood that.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There will be differences of views on what can be done, what cannot be done, but we have navigated the path forward and we will continue to do so.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To the Member's point about how quickly it can be done in this case, I would like to say that all of the provisions they work with one another.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And, thereafter, their conduct as to what is reasonable will be measured by how easy it is to disable in the case, if it is very easy, then it should be very quick, as I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Or if there is some reason why they cannot do so expeditiously, all that will be taken into account.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But the conduct, they cannot sit on it.
